Teacher-led Geography for ESL learners

Select a lesson. These are the same explanations and checks available on each slide in the classroom player.

The route is planned for 40 minutes. Students listen from their seats and respond briefly when invited. The teacher demonstrates examples and can invite an occasional volunteer to the board.

Timings are planning estimates. Classroom teaching duration has not been measured; the guide contains substantive explanations rather than instructions to prolong a short activity.

Landscape detectives

7A · Week 2 · sections 1.1

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 1.1

On screen: What is here? Where is it? / Classify a feature and explain an interaction

Today's key idea: Geography asks about places. Physical geography studies natural features and processes. Human geography studies people, settlements and activities. Environmental questions connect people and nature: a dam is built by people but changes a river. Categories can overlap. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Which question asks about location?
Listen for: “Where is it?” asks about location.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Geography asks about places

On screen: What is here? Where is it? / Why is it here? How does it affect people?

Geography helps us understand places and the connections between them. Start with our classroom. The building has a location, people use it, and its surroundings influence how we reach it. Now move out to the school, the town and the world. These are different scales of study. A question about one street needs local detail; a question about countries needs a wider view. Geography joins information about nature and people rather than treating a place as a list of names.

Brief check: Which question asks about location?
Listen for: “Where is it?” asks about location.

Physical and human features

On screen: Physical: river, hill, soil. / Human: road, bridge, building.

Physical geography studies natural features and processes. Human geography studies people and their activities. Point to the river and describe its water and banks. Then point to the bridge and describe what people built. A feature can involve both. A farm uses soil, plants and rainfall, but people choose crops and manage the land. Do not tell pupils that every feature must fit only one box. The categories help us explain a place; they do not remove the connections between its parts.

Brief check: Why can a farm involve both categories?
Listen for: Natural soil and rainfall support human farming activities.

People and nature affect each other

On screen: Rain can affect a road. / A road can affect rainwater flow.

An interaction is a connection in which things affect each other. Heavy rain can make a road difficult to use. Building a road can also change the ground: a paved surface may allow less water into soil, so more water may move over the surface. Trace each direction with an arrow. The first starts with a natural process and ends with a human activity. The second starts with construction and ends with water movement. We need evidence to find the size of an effect in a real place.

Brief check: Can the connection work in both directions?
Listen for: Yes. Nature affects people, and people change their environment.

What does “make a link” mean?

On screen: A link explains how two things affect each other. / The bridge crosses the river, so people can reach the other bank.

Compare two sentences. “River, bridge, school” lists three features. “The bridge crosses the river, so pupils can reach the school from the other bank” explains a connection. Point to each feature while saying its part of the sentence. The word so joins an action to an effect. Because introduces a reason. A useful geographical explanation tells us how the connection works. “The bridge is good” gives a judgement without explaining it. Ask the class which words show what the bridge actually does.

Brief check: What is missing from a list of features?
Listen for: The action or process connecting them.

Build it together · Classify a feature and explain an interaction

On screen: Classify a feature and explain an interaction / A reservoir contains water, but a dam built by people changes its storage.

A reservoir contains water, but a dam built by people changes its storage. Name the natural feature, the human action and the effect; do not force every example into one box.

Vegetation is natural material; planting and shelter are human action and purpose.

Teaching question: A farmer plants trees to shelter crops. Which explanation connects people and nature? Correct reasoning: People change vegetation to reduce wind exposure. Contrast this with: Trees cannot be geography because people planted them. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: A farmer plants trees to shelter crops. Which explanation connects people and nature?
Listen for: People change vegetation to reduce wind exposure. Vegetation is natural material; planting and shelter are human action and purpose.

MODEL EXPLANATION River and slope: physical; houses and bridge: human; clearing woodland changes habitat and runoff, an interaction.

METHOD A reservoir contains water, but a dam built by people changes its storage. Name the natural feature, the human action and the effect; do not force every example into one box.

25–31 min · Demonstrate on the board

Class board challenge · Classify a feature and explain an interaction

On screen: Watch your teacher demonstrate one move. / One volunteer can come to the board; everyone else watches.

Introduce the rule before making a move. A reservoir contains water, but a dam built by people changes its storage. Name the natural feature, the human action and the effect; do not force every example into one box. Explain why one choice fits and why the other does not. Vegetation is natural material; planting and shelter are human action and purpose. Then invite a volunteer for one turn if useful. Take one brief response from the class and finish by restating the geographical idea. This is the one core board activity for this topic; the teacher may operate it throughout.

Watch a second example · 1.1

On screen: Explain one possible connection between them.

Fictional field sketch: a wooded slope beside a footpath. Proposed change: trees are removed beside the path. No before-and-after measurements have been made.

Explain one possible connection between them. trees are removed beside the path may lead to less shade and exposed soil. This is a prediction, not a measured result.

Related steps in this same case: Name one natural feature and one human feature. wooded slope: natural; footpath: human. A place contains both.

Explain one possible connection between them. trees are removed beside the path may lead to less shade and exposed soil. This is a prediction, not a measured result.

A pupil says “human and physical geography never overlap”. Repair that claim. The footpath can affect the wooded slope; environmental questions study that connection.

Work through the explanation aloud. Before showing the answer, ask for a short response or a hand signal. Accept an ESL answer with the correct idea even if its grammar is incomplete; restate it accurately.

31–36 min · Explain a changed example

Teacher demonstration · Landscape detectives

On screen: Classify a feature and explain an interaction / Follow your teacher’s explanation of the places, facts and steps.

Our model valley contains a river, wooded slope, houses, bridge and cleared land.

Demonstrate this process on the board: Make three columns: physical, human, interaction. Place five features and explain one overlap.

Explain the result: River and slope: physical; houses and bridge: human; clearing woodland changes habitat and runoff, an interaction.

Use short sentences while tracing or recording each step. Ask one pupil to supply a missing label or operation if appropriate. The teacher completes and explains the whole example; pupils are not assigned independent or partner work.

Now change one condition · 1.1

On screen: What could we observe to test the prediction?

Fictional field sketch: a wooded slope beside a footpath. Proposed change: trees are removed beside the path. No before-and-after measurements have been made.

What could we observe to test the prediction? Compare the affected area with a similar unchanged area; measure the predicted effect at comparable times.

Related steps in this same case: What could we observe to test the prediction? Compare the affected area with a similar unchanged area; measure the predicted effect at comparable times.

A photograph shows the change. Does it prove the effect? It records visible features, but measurements or repeated observations are needed to establish the effect.

Make a two-arrow explanation for the board. trees are removed beside the path → a possible change in the natural feature → an effect on people or wildlife. Accept a specific, qualified link.

Work through the explanation aloud. Before showing the answer, ask for a short response or a hand signal. Accept an ESL answer with the correct idea even if its grammar is incomplete; restate it accurately.

Connection builders

On screen: Watch: hill + road → explain how the hill affects the route. / Watch: river + farm → explain how water can support crops.

Compare two sentences. “River, bridge, school” lists three features. “The bridge crosses the river, so pupils can reach the school from the other bank” explains a connection. Point to each feature while saying its part of the sentence. The word so joins an action to an effect. Because introduces a reason. A useful geographical explanation tells us how the connection works. “The bridge is good” gives a judgement without explaining it. Ask the class which words show what the bridge actually does.

36–39 min · Brief class responses

Explain the important distinction · 1.1

On screen: A farmer plants trees to shelter crops. Which explanation connects people and nature? / Give one short answer when invited.

The key question is: A farmer plants trees to shelter crops. Which explanation connects people and nature? The correct idea is: People change vegetation to reduce wind exposure. Vegetation is natural material; planting and shelter are human action and purpose. Hear one or two brief answers, correct the specific misconception, and close with the accurate geographical explanation.

Your view · 1.1

On screen: Which interaction between people and nature would you investigate around our school? Why? / Say: “I would choose … because …”

Context for this discussion: Our model valley contains a river, wooded slope, houses, bridge and cleared land.

Relevant explanation: River and slope: physical; houses and bridge: human; clearing woodland changes habitat and runoff, an interaction.

Invite one or two brief views, then compare the priorities they name. A preference may vary, while the geographical facts and numerical constraints remain fixed. If an answer contradicts a fact, clarify the fact before accepting the preference. End by connecting the views to the topic rather than turning this into an extended debate.

This is an opinion about priorities. Preferences may differ; geographical facts and stated constraints remain fixed.

39–40 min · Finish and dismiss

As you leave · 1.1

On screen: A farmer plants trees to shelter crops. Which explanation connects people and nature? / Give one spoken sentence as you leave.

Listen for the core meaning rather than perfect English grammar. People change vegetation to reduce wind exposure. Vegetation is natural material; planting and shelter are human action and purpose.

Explain a connection

On screen: Name the feature and the change. / Use “because” or “so”.

Compare two sentences. “River, bridge, school” lists three features. “The bridge crosses the river, so pupils can reach the school from the other bank” explains a connection. Point to each feature while saying its part of the sentence. The word so joins an action to an effect. Because introduces a reason. Build it together · Turn an observation into an investigable exhibit label

On screen: Turn an observation into an investigable exhibit label / An exhibit label needs more than a name.

An exhibit label needs more than a name. “Shaded bench: built seat beneath a tree; is it cooler here at noon?” identifies a feature, a connection and a question that measurements could answer.

The first names comparable surfaces and an observable outcome; the second supplies an unsupported judgement.

Teaching question: Which label could guide a real school investigation? Correct reasoning: Paved path: does rainwater remain longer here than on soil? Contrast this with: Our path: the best path in the world. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: Which label could guide a real school investigation?
Listen for: Paved path: does rainwater remain longer here than on soil? The first names comparable surfaces and an observable outcome; the second supplies an unsupported judgement.

Read the new case together · Build a school geography exhibit

On screen: Listen as your teacher explains the source. / We will use these facts in the demonstration.

CASE SOURCE Choose three places you can actually recall at school: a planted area, a path, a building or another visible feature.

MODEL EXPLANATION A planted area can combine soil and plants with human planting and watering. Ask how shade differs between planted and paved areas.

METHOD An exhibit label needs more than a name. “Shaded bench: built seat beneath a tree; is it cooler here at noon?” identifies a feature, a connection and a question that measurements could answer.

Read the source in small sections. Link each named place, measurement or process to the diagram. Keep the source visible when referring to a number. Demonstrate the relevant operation or connection aloud before inviting an answer. The case is a teaching example; no pupil needs to produce a written response.

Match a tool to a question

On screen: Location: map or atlas. / Direction: north arrow or compass.

Begin with the question before choosing a tool. An atlas contains maps and an index that helps us find places. A compass helps identify direction. A ruler measures a line, but does not tell us which country we are looking at. Show how the same place can be investigated in several ways. To locate it, use a map; to describe its appearance, use a photograph; to estimate a mapped distance, use a ruler and the map scale. No single tool answers every geographical question.

Brief check: Can a ruler tell us which way is north?
Listen for: No. A ruler measures length; direction needs another reference.

Read a map carefully

On screen: Find the title, key and north arrow. / Check the scale before measuring.

A map is a selective drawing of a place. Its title tells us the area or topic. The key explains symbols and colours. The north arrow gives direction, and the scale connects the drawing to real distances. Demonstrate this order before identifying individual features. A blue line might represent a river, but we should confirm it using the key. A large symbol may be easy to see without showing the feature’s exact size. Reading the supporting information prevents us from guessing from appearance alone.

Brief check: Why should we read the key?
Listen for: It tells us what this map’s symbols mean.

Measure and convert

On screen: Start at the ruler’s zero mark. / Map length × scale = ground distance.

Place the zero mark at the start of the line, not the edge of the ruler. State the map measurement in centimetres. If the scale says one centimetre represents forty metres, each centimetre is one equal forty-metre section. A three-centimetre path represents three times forty, or one hundred and twenty metres. The units change because we move from the drawing to the ground. Adding three and forty would mix different quantities. Show the three equal sections before writing the multiplication.

Brief check: Why do we multiply rather than add?
Listen for: Each map centimetre represents another equal section of ground distance.

Record a result others can check

On screen: Name the feature, result and unit. / Say which tool or source you used.

“It is four” is not a complete geographical record. We do not know what was measured or what four means. “Path B measures four centimetres on this map” identifies the object, number and unit. Add the scale when calculating the ground distance. A photograph also needs a place and date if it is used to show change. Clear records let another person check the method instead of trusting an unexplained answer. Model a weak record and improve it aloud, keeping the original visible for comparison.

Brief check: What information is missing from “It is four”?
Listen for: The feature, unit and method are missing.

Build it together · Choose tools by the information they provide

On screen: Choose tools by the information they provide / A photograph can show a path but its perspective distorts length.

A photograph can show a path but its perspective distorts length. For distance, use a measured map line and a scale; for direction, use a north arrow or compass. State what each tool can and cannot tell you.

The index locates the country; a ruler measures length but does not identify countries.

Teaching question: You need to locate Peru within a continent. Which resource helps directly? Correct reasoning: An atlas index and map. Contrast this with: A ruler alone. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: You need to locate Peru within a continent. Which resource helps directly?
Listen for: An atlas index and map. The index locates the country; a ruler measures length but does not identify countries.

Read the new case together · Pack the right kit

On screen: Listen as your teacher explains the source. / We will use these facts in the demonstration.

CASE SOURCE Four jobs: locate a country, find north, measure a map path, record a changing building.

MODEL EXPLANATION Atlas; compass; ruler plus scale; dated photographs. A photo alone does not give exact distance or the reason for change.

METHOD A photograph can show a path but its perspective distorts length. For distance, use a measured map line and a scale; for direction, use a north arrow or compass. State what each tool can and cannot tell you.

Read the source in small sections. Link each named place, measurement or process to the diagram. Keep the source visible when referring to a number. Watch a second example · 1.2

On screen: Calculate the represented distance together.

Equipment bench: a map line measures 4 cm; its scale is 1 cm = 30 m. A broken ruler still has marks 3 cm and 7 cm. North is at the top of the map.

Calculate the represented distance together. 4 × 30 = 120 m. Invite one pupil to choose the operation and another to check the units.

Related steps in this same case: Which two facts are needed to find real distance? Map length (4 cm) and scale (30 m per cm). A ruler alone gives only map length.

Calculate the represented distance together. 4 × 30 = 120 m. Invite one pupil to choose the operation and another to check the units.

A pupil reads only the ruler’s end number. Correct the measurement. 7 − 3 = 4 cm. Subtract the start reading when the line does not begin at zero.

Work through the explanation aloud. Before showing the answer, ask for a short response or a hand signal. Accept an ESL answer with the correct idea even if its grammar is incomplete; restate it accurately.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 1.2

On screen: Location: map or atlas. / Repair an incorrect measurement method

Today's key idea: Match a tool to a question. An atlas locates places; a compass gives direction; a ruler measures map length; a photograph records visible features. 3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Match a tool to a question

On screen: Location: map or atlas. / Direction: north arrow or compass.

Begin with the question before choosing a tool. An atlas contains maps and an index that helps us find places. A compass helps identify direction. A ruler measures a line, but does not tell us which country we are looking at. Show how the same place can be investigated in several ways. To locate it, use a map; to describe its appearance, use a photograph; to estimate a mapped distance, use a ruler and the map scale. No single tool answers every geographical question.

Brief check: Can a ruler tell us which way is north?
Listen for: No. A ruler measures length; direction needs another reference.

Read a map carefully

On screen: Find the title, key and north arrow. / Check the scale before measuring.

A map is a selective drawing of a place. Its title tells us the area or topic. The key explains symbols and colours. The north arrow gives direction, and the scale connects the drawing to real distances. Demonstrate this order before identifying individual features. A blue line might represent a river, but we should confirm it using the key. A large symbol may be easy to see without showing the feature’s exact size. Reading the supporting information prevents us from guessing from appearance alone.

Brief check: Why should we read the key?
Listen for: It tells us what this map’s symbols mean.

Measure and convert

On screen: Start at the ruler’s zero mark. / Map length × scale = ground distance.

Place the zero mark at the start of the line, not the edge of the ruler. State the map measurement in centimetres. If the scale says one centimetre represents forty metres, each centimetre is one equal forty-metre section. A three-centimetre path represents three times forty, or one hundred and twenty metres. The units change because we move from the drawing to the ground. Adding three and forty would mix different quantities. Show the three equal sections before writing the multiplication.

Brief check: Why do we multiply rather than add?
Listen for: Each map centimetre represents another equal section of ground distance.

Record a result others can check

On screen: Name the feature, result and unit. / Say which tool or source you used.

“It is four” is not a complete geographical record. We do not know what was measured or what four means. “Path B measures four centimetres on this map” identifies the object, number and unit. Add the scale when calculating the ground distance. A photograph also needs a place and date if it is used to show change. Clear records let another person check the method instead of trusting an unexplained answer. Model a weak record and improve it aloud, keeping the original visible for comparison.

Brief check: What information is missing from “It is four”?
Listen for: The feature, unit and method are missing.

7A · Week 5 · sections 1.3, 1.3

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 1.3

On screen: Observation: what we can see or measure. / Separate an observation from a possible cause

Today's key idea: Observation and inference. A geographical enquiry moves from a focused question to observations, a pattern and a cautious explanation. Keep time, location and counting rules consistent. A pattern does not by itself establish a cause. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Does a long queue prove a shop is popular?
Listen for: No. Popularity is one possible explanation; other reasons could produce a queue.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Observation and inference

On screen: Observation: what we can see or measure. / Inference: a possible explanation.

An observation comes from a source or measurement. If a photograph shows a queue, we can describe the people visible. Saying that everyone likes the shop is an inference: it suggests a reason that the photograph does not establish. Other reasons are possible, such as slow service or a special event. Use a familiar classroom example before returning to the geographical image. Keep observations and proposed explanations in different columns. This allows pupils to offer ideas while still understanding which claims have actually been checked.

Brief check: Does a long queue prove a shop is popular?
Listen for: No. Popularity is one possible explanation; other reasons could produce a queue.

Make a question measurable

On screen: Choose one place or feature. / Decide what you will count or measure.

“Is our school good?” is too broad for a simple geographical enquiry. “How many people use each gate in five minutes?” tells us what to observe, where and for how long. Explain how a count differs from an opinion. We can count people crossing a line, but happiness requires a different kind of evidence. A good question helps us choose an appropriate method. Before starting, agree exactly what counts as an entry so two observers would make comparable records.

Brief check: Which is easier to investigate: “good school” or “people using each gate”?
Listen for: The gate question gives a clear, countable outcome.

Make comparisons fair

On screen: Use the same counting time. / Use the same rule at each place.

Suppose we count one gate for five minutes and another for ten. The second may have a larger count because we watched longer, not because it is busier. Hold the counting time constant. We also need the same rule for entering and leaving, and comparable observation times. A bag on the boundary between two survey areas should be counted according to one agreed rule. Fairness here means controlling the method so the difference we report is meaningful. It is not about making all results equal.

Brief check: Why could different counting times mislead us?
Listen for: The longer observation has more opportunity to record people.

Repeat before making a broad claim

On screen: A count describes one time. / Repeated counts can reveal variation.

One count is a snapshot. A gate that is busy on Monday may be quieter on Tuesday. Show two days with different results and calculate the combined counts. Discuss why weather, events or lesson times might affect movement, without claiming we know the cause. Repeating a measurement makes us less dependent on one unusual moment. Even repeated counts at two gates do not automatically describe every entrance or every season. A conclusion should name the places and times studied and explain what remains unknown.

Brief check: Does one busy morning prove a gate is always busiest?
Listen for: No. We need comparable repeated observations.

A snapshot describes a moment; repeated timing would be needed to compare service.

Explain the important distinction · 1.3

On screen: A queue is longer at Gate X. What can a single count establish? / Give one short answer when invited.

Explain the important distinction · 1.3

On screen: Which change improves a fair comparison? / Give one short answer when invited.

Your view · 1.3

On screen: Which part of our observation method is most important to make fair? Explain your choice. / Say: “I would choose … because …”

Context for this discussion: At 12:00, Door A has 8 waiting pupils and Door B has 2. No one has asked the pupils why.

Relevant explanation: A has six more waiting pupils. A may serve more rooms or open later; neither is established. Repeat at equal times on several days.

7A · Week 7 · sections 1.1, 1.2, 1.3

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 1.1

On screen: What is here? Where is it? / Turn an observation into an investigable exhibit label

Today's key idea: Geography asks about places. Physical geography studies natural features and processes. Human geography studies people, settlements and activities. Environmental questions connect people and nature: a dam is built by people but changes a river. Categories can overlap. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Which question asks about location?
Listen for: “Where is it?” asks about location.

Today we will understand · 1.2

On screen: Location: map or atlas. / Record a result another investigator can check

Today's key idea: Match a tool to a question. An atlas locates places; a compass gives direction; a ruler measures map length; a photograph records visible features. Choose the tool, take a reading and record the unit. A ruler reading becomes real distance only after applying the map scale. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Can a ruler tell us which way is north?
Listen for: No. A ruler measures length; direction needs another reference.

Today we will understand · 1.3

On screen: Observation: what we can see or measure. / Separate an observation from a possible cause

Today's key idea: Observation and inference. A geographical enquiry moves from a focused question to observations, a pattern and a cautious explanation. Keep time, location and counting rules consistent. A pattern does not by itself establish a cause. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Does a long queue prove a shop is popular?
Listen for: No. Popularity is one possible explanation; other reasons could produce a queue.

3–25 min · Explain and reconnect

Geography asks about places

On screen: What is here? Where is it? / Why is it here? How does it affect people?

Geography helps us understand places and the connections between them. Start with our classroom. The building has a location, people use it, and its surroundings influence how we reach it. Now move out to the school, the town and the world. These are different scales of study. A question about one street needs local detail; a question about countries needs a wider view. Geography joins information about nature and people rather than treating a place as a list of names.

Brief check: Which question asks about location?
Listen for: “Where is it?” asks about location.

Explain a connection

On screen: Name the feature and the change. / Use “because” or “so”.

Compare two sentences. “River, bridge, school” lists three features. “The bridge crosses the river, so pupils can reach the school from the other bank” explains a connection. Point to each feature while saying its part of the sentence. The word so joins an action to an effect. Because introduces a reason. A useful geographical explanation tells us how the connection works. “The bridge is good” gives a judgement without explaining it. Ask the class which words show what the bridge actually does.

Brief check: What is missing from a list of features?
Listen for: The action or process connecting them.

See the method · Turn an observation into an investigable exhibit label

On screen: Turn an observation into an investigable exhibit label / An exhibit label needs more than a name.

An exhibit label needs more than a name. “Shaded bench: built seat beneath a tree; is it cooler here at noon?” identifies a feature, a connection and a question that measurements could answer.

The first names comparable surfaces and an observable outcome; the second supplies an unsupported judgement.

Teaching question: Which label could guide a real school investigation? Correct reasoning: Paved path: does rainwater remain longer here than on soil? Contrast this with: Our path: the best path in the world. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: Which label could guide a real school investigation?
Listen for: Paved path: does rainwater remain longer here than on soil? The first names comparable surfaces and an observable outcome; the second supplies an unsupported judgement.

Match a tool to a question

On screen: Location: map or atlas. / Direction: north arrow or compass.

Begin with the question before choosing a tool. An atlas contains maps and an index that helps us find places. A compass helps identify direction. A ruler measures a line, but does not tell us which country we are looking at. Show how the same place can be investigated in several ways. To locate it, use a map; to describe its appearance, use a photograph; to estimate a mapped distance, use a ruler and the map scale. No single tool answers every geographical question.

Brief check: Can a ruler tell us which way is north?
Listen for: No. A ruler measures length; direction needs another reference.

Record a result others can check

On screen: Name the feature, result and unit. / Say which tool or source you used.

“It is four” is not a complete geographical record. We do not know what was measured or what four means. “Path B measures four centimetres on this map” identifies the object, number and unit. Add the scale when calculating the ground distance. A photograph also needs a place and date if it is used to show change. Clear records let another person check the method instead of trusting an unexplained answer. Model a weak record and improve it aloud, keeping the original visible for comparison.

Brief check: What information is missing from “It is four”?
Listen for: The feature, unit and method are missing.

Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Observation and inference

On screen: Observation: what we can see or measure. / Inference: a possible explanation.

An observation comes from a source or measurement. If a photograph shows a queue, we can describe the people visible. Saying that everyone likes the shop is an inference: it suggests a reason that the photograph does not establish. Other reasons are possible, such as slow service or a special event. Use a familiar classroom example before returning to the geographical image. Keep observations and proposed explanations in different columns. This allows pupils to offer ideas while still understanding which claims have actually been checked.

Brief check: Does a long queue prove a shop is popular?
Listen for: No. Popularity is one possible explanation; other reasons could produce a queue.

Repeat before making a broad claim

On screen: A count describes one time. / Repeated counts can reveal variation.

One count is a snapshot. A gate that is busy on Monday may be quieter on Tuesday. Show two days with different results and calculate the combined counts. Discuss why weather, events or lesson times might affect movement, without claiming we know the cause. Repeating a measurement makes us less dependent on one unusual moment. Even repeated counts at two gates do not automatically describe every entrance or every season. A conclusion should name the places and times studied and explain what remains unknown.

Brief check: Does one busy morning prove a gate is always busiest?
Listen for: No. We need comparable repeated observations.

See the method · Separate an observation from a possible cause

On screen: Separate an observation from a possible cause / If one gate has 9 people and another has 3, the difference is 6.

If one gate has 9 people and another has 3, the difference is 6. This establishes a count, not why people chose the gate. Turn a suggested reason into a question you could investigate.

A snapshot describes a moment; repeated timing would be needed to compare service.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Observation and inference

On screen: Observation: what we can see or measure. / Inference: a possible explanation.

An observation comes from a source or measurement. If a photograph shows a queue, we can describe the people visible. Saying that everyone likes the shop is an inference: it suggests a reason that the photograph does not establish. Other reasons are possible, such as slow service or a special event. Use a familiar classroom example before returning to the geographical image. Keep observations and proposed explanations in different columns. This allows pupils to offer ideas while still understanding which claims have actually been checked.

Brief check: Does a long queue prove a shop is popular?
Listen for: No. Popularity is one possible explanation; other reasons could produce a queue.

Make a question measurable

On screen: Choose one place or feature. / Decide what you will count or measure.

“Is our school good?” is too broad for a simple geographical enquiry. “How many people use each gate in five minutes?” tells us what to observe, where and for how long. Explain how a count differs from an opinion. We can count people crossing a line, but happiness requires a different kind of evidence. A good question helps us choose an appropriate method. Before starting, agree exactly what counts as an entry so two observers would make comparable records.

Brief check: Which is easier to investigate: “good school” or “people using each gate”?
Listen for: The gate question gives a clear, countable outcome.

Make comparisons fair

On screen: Use the same counting time. / Use the same rule at each place.

Suppose we count one gate for five minutes and another for ten. The second may have a larger count because we watched longer, not because it is busier. Hold the counting time constant. We also need the same rule for entering and leaving, and comparable observation times. A bag on the boundary between two survey areas should be counted according to one agreed rule. Fairness here means controlling the method so the difference we report is meaningful. It is not about making all results equal.

Brief check: Why could different counting times mislead us?
Listen for: The longer observation has more opportunity to record people.

Repeat before making a broad claim

On screen: A count describes one time. / Repeated counts can reveal variation.

One count is a snapshot. A gate that is busy on Monday may be quieter on Tuesday. Show two days with different results and calculate the combined counts. Discuss why weather, events or lesson times might affect movement, without claiming we know the cause. Repeating a measurement makes us less dependent on one unusual moment. Even repeated counts at two gates do not automatically describe every entrance or every season. A conclusion should name the places and times studied and explain what remains unknown.

Brief check: Does one busy morning prove a gate is always busiest?
Listen for: No. We need comparable repeated observations.

Build it together · Design a small enquiry with honest limits

On screen: Design a small enquiry with honest limits / Choose two zones, define what counts, record the same length of time and repeat.

Choose two zones, define what counts, record the same length of time and repeat. A bag touching a boundary needs a rule agreed before counting. Report “our two zones”, not “the whole school”.

A shared rule prevents double counting and inconsistent results.

Teaching question: A bag lies on a zone boundary. What should the team do? Correct reasoning: Apply the agreed boundary rule once. Contrast this with: Count it in both zones to be safe. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: A bag lies on a zone boundary. What should the team do?
Listen for: Apply the agreed boundary rule once. A shared rule prevents double counting and inconsistent results.

Read the new case together · Evidence before explanation

On screen: Listen as your teacher explains the source. / We will use these facts in the demonstration.

CASE SOURCE Observe two classroom zones for 30 seconds without moving: count visible bags using the same rule in each zone.

MODEL EXPLANATION A valid record states the zones, time and rule. Counts describe this observation only; placement and class routines are possible explanations to test.

METHOD Choose two zones, define what counts, record the same length of time and repeat. A bag touching a boundary needs a rule agreed before counting. Report “our two zones”, not “the whole school”.

Read the source in small sections. Link each named place, measurement or process to the diagram. Keep the source visible when referring to a number. Demonstrate the relevant operation or connection aloud before inviting an answer. The case is a teaching example; no pupil needs to produce a written response.

Ironbridge Gorge: a changing industrial landscape

On screen: Ironbridge Gorge is in Shropshire, beside the River Severn. / Industry, transport and settlement changed the landscape.

Ironbridge Gorge is a real place in Shropshire associated with the Industrial Revolution. The River Severn runs through the gorge. Its historic industrial landscape includes evidence of manufacturing, transport and homes, while the iron bridge is an important example of early large-scale structural use of cast iron. Explain why this is more than a story about one bridge: industry changes land use, creates connections between workplaces and housing, and leaves material traces. Today, historical remains can also serve heritage and visitor purposes. Use this factual background to introduce change, while keeping our imagined before-and-after drawings separate from verified historical records. We can practise comparison with a schematic, but cannot use invented building counts to describe the actual gorge’s history.

Brief check: Why should the fictional drawing’s counts not become historical Ironbridge facts?
Listen for: They are classroom data rather than historical records.

Places change over time

On screen: Look at the same place on two dates. / Separate what stayed from what changed.

A place can change in its buildings, transport, land use and environment. Put two views of the same place side by side. Start with a feature that appears in both so pupils know they are comparing the same area. Then identify a feature added, removed or altered. A stayed-and-changed table prevents us from treating the whole place as new. Dates matter: an undated photograph can show appearance, but cannot reliably establish which view came first. Keep imagined classroom scenes separate from verified historical photographs.

Brief check: Why do the dates matter?
Listen for: They establish the order of the changes.

A crossing changes access

On screen: A ferry crosses water in separate trips. / A bridge provides a fixed crossing when open.

A river can connect places by water while also making travel between its banks difficult. A ferry carries people or goods in trips. A bridge creates a fixed crossing, but it still needs suitable access and can close. Trace a journey before and after a crossing is added. Explain the mechanism: a shorter or more reliable route may make a destination easier to reach. We should not leap from a bridge symbol to a precise claim about jobs or income; those require separate records.

Brief check: What can a new crossing change directly?
Listen for: The routes people can use to move between the banks.

Describe first, explain second

On screen: “A workshop appeared” describes change. / “Access may have helped” suggests a cause.

Descriptions tell us what differs between the sources. Explanations suggest why that difference occurred. A new workshop beside a bridge may lead us to ask whether improved access helped the business. Its location alone does not prove that cause. The workshop might have opened for another reason or before the bridge. Demonstrate both sentence types using the same image. Accurate description is the starting point; a causal explanation needs evidence linking the change in transport to the change in activity.

Brief check: Does being close to a bridge prove a business opened because of it?
Listen for: No. Location alone does not establish cause.

Test the proposed cause

On screen: A cause must come before its effect. / Use dates, records and comparisons.

If a shop opened in 2015 and the bridge opened in 2020, the bridge cannot explain the shop’s original opening. It could still affect later customer numbers. Split those two claims rather than accepting or rejecting everything at once. To investigate later effects, compare suitable records before and after the crossing, and consider other changes. This is how historical geography joins the story of a place to evidence. A convincing explanation identifies a possible mechanism and checks whether the timing and records support it.

Brief check: What does an earlier shop opening rule out?
Listen for: The later bridge cannot have caused that original opening.

Build it together · Explain a transport change without inventing history

On screen: Explain a transport change without inventing history / A ferry carries people across in batches; a bridge provides a fixed connection when open.

A ferry carries people across in batches; a bridge provides a fixed connection when open. This suggests an access mechanism, but does not prove how many jobs were created. Label historical facts separately from predictions in a model.

A precise economic change requires records; it cannot be read from the crossing symbol.

Teaching question: An imagined bridge opens. Which claim needs additional evidence? Correct reasoning: Local trade increased by 50%. Contrast this with: The model now shows a fixed crossing. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: An imagined bridge opens. Which claim needs additional evidence?
Listen for: Local trade increased by 50%. A precise economic change requires records; it cannot be read from the crossing symbol.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Identify means name

On screen: Give the requested feature. / Use the correct geographical term.

Command words tell us what kind of answer is needed. Identify means name or recognise. If the question asks us to identify the crossing, “footbridge” may be sufficient. A long story about why people need transport answers a different question. Point to the feature before naming it so pupils link the term to the visual. If several crossings are shown, add enough location information to distinguish the requested one. Accuracy comes before length: a short relevant answer can be better than a long unrelated one.

Brief check: Does “people travel faster” identify a crossing?
Listen for: No. It explains a possible effect rather than naming the feature.

Describe means say what it is like

On screen: Use position, shape and number. / Describe the visible pattern.

To describe a settlement, say where its buildings lie and how they are arranged. “Six homes are beside the bridge and two are farther away” gives a count and location. “People want jobs” is a possible explanation, not a description of the visible pattern. Move a finger across the image as you describe it so pupils can match each phrase to evidence. Useful description words include near, beside, north of, scattered and clustered. The relevant words depend on the feature being studied.

Brief check: Which adds detail: “some homes” or “six homes beside the bridge”?
Listen for: The second gives both number and location.

Explain means give the connection

On screen: Give a reason or process. / Show how it leads to the result.

An explanation needs more than the word because. “The homes are here because they are here” adds no cause. “A crossing may improve access, so people may choose nearby homes” supplies a mechanism. When the source shows only a pattern, use cautious language rather than pretending the cause was measured. Explain by tracing the sequence: crossing, easier access, possible location choice. The explanation should remain connected to the actual place or source in the question rather than becoming a memorised sentence about any settlement.

Brief check: What makes an explanation useful?
Listen for: It connects a reason or process to the result.

Answer the question asked

On screen: Find the command word. / Then find the place and evidence required.

Read a question in three parts: what to do, which feature or place, and which source to use. A pupil may know a correct fact but still fail to answer the question. Show a deliberate mismatch, such as a cause given when the question asks for a pattern. Repair the response by keeping any useful detail and replacing the irrelevant part. This is a method pupils can apply across Geography. A good answer is relevant, accurate and supported; its length depends on the task rather than on filling space.

On screen: Listen as your teacher explains the source. / We will use these facts in the demonstration.

MODEL EXPLANATION The answer supplies reasons, not the visible distribution. A good description states the cluster and contrasting locations.

A claim needs support

On screen: Claim: what you say is true. / Evidence: the detail that supports it.

A claim states an idea about a place. Evidence is the observation, count or source detail we use to support that idea. “Shops cluster near the stop” is a claim. “Twelve of sixteen shops are within two hundred metres” makes the pattern more precise. Explain that evidence must be relevant: the colour of a shop sign does not test a claim about customer transport. We should be able to point to the supporting information and explain why it bears on the claim.

Brief check: Which supports clustering: a shop colour or a count with distance?
Listen for: The count and distance are relevant to the pattern.

Join evidence to the explanation

On screen: Say what the detail shows. / Explain why it matters.

A number does not explain itself. After giving a count, say what it tells us about the distribution. Then separate that pattern from a proposed cause. Many shops near a bus stop may be consistent with customers valuing access, but the count alone does not show why each business opened. Use two arrows: count to pattern, then possible access mechanism to explanation. The first can be directly supported by the count; the second needs more information about customers or business decisions.

Brief check: Can a location count tell us every business owner’s reason?
Listen for: No. It establishes the pattern, not every cause.

Ask for relevant new evidence

On screen: Customer survey: how did you travel? / Business records: when did the shop open?

The best next source depends on the claim being tested. If we want to know whether a bus stop brings customers, ask customers about travel and reasons for visiting. If we want to know whether the stop caused shops to open, compare opening dates and the stop’s history. Different questions need different evidence. More information is useful only if it addresses the uncertainty. Demonstrate a relevant and an irrelevant question, then explain why the relevant one could change our confidence in the proposed connection.

Brief check: Which evidence tests original opening: paint colour or dates?
Listen for: Dates can test whether the proposed cause came first.

State a useful limit

On screen: Say what is supported. / Say what still needs checking.

A limitation is a boundary on what we can conclude. It does not mean the investigation was worthless. We may accurately report that shops cluster in our mapped area while admitting that we did not measure the reasons for their location. Avoid extremes such as “we know everything” or “we know nothing”. Model a balanced conclusion: the source supports this pattern, a mechanism may explain it, and this further evidence would test that mechanism. Changing a claim when new evidence appears is part of good geographical reasoning.

Brief check: Does recognising a limit make all the evidence useless?
Listen for: No. Keep the supported finding and qualify the uncertain part.

3–25 min · Explain and reconnect

Ironbridge Gorge: a changing industrial landscape

On screen: Ironbridge Gorge is in Shropshire, beside the River Severn. / Industry, transport and settlement changed the landscape.

Ironbridge Gorge is a real place in Shropshire associated with the Industrial Revolution. The River Severn runs through the gorge. Its historic industrial landscape includes evidence of manufacturing, transport and homes, while the iron bridge is an important example of early large-scale structural use of cast iron. Explain why this is more than a story about one bridge: industry changes land use, creates connections between workplaces and housing, and leaves material traces. Today, historical remains can also serve heritage and visitor purposes. Use this factual background to introduce change, while keeping our imagined before-and-after drawings separate from verified historical records. We can practise comparison with a schematic, but cannot use invented building counts to describe the actual gorge’s history.

Brief check: Why should the fictional drawing’s counts not become historical Ironbridge facts?
Listen for: They are classroom data rather than historical records.

Test the proposed cause

On screen: A cause must come before its effect. / Use dates, records and comparisons.

If a shop opened in 2015 and the bridge opened in 2020, the bridge cannot explain the shop’s original opening. It could still affect later customer numbers. Split those two claims rather than accepting or rejecting everything at once. To investigate later effects, compare suitable records before and after the crossing, and consider other changes. This is how historical geography joins the story of a place to evidence. A convincing explanation identifies a possible mechanism and checks whether the timing and records support it.

Brief check: What does an earlier shop opening rule out?
Listen for: The later bridge cannot have caused that original opening.

Match the same feature across the two sources before describing change.

Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Identify means name

On screen: Give the requested feature. / Use the correct geographical term.

Command words tell us what kind of answer is needed. Identify means name or recognise. If the question asks us to identify the crossing, “footbridge” may be sufficient. A long story about why people need transport answers a different question. Point to the feature before naming it so pupils link the term to the visual. If several crossings are shown, add enough location information to distinguish the requested one. Accuracy comes before length: a short relevant answer can be better than a long unrelated one.

Brief check: Does “people travel faster” identify a crossing?
Listen for: No. It explains a possible effect rather than naming the feature.

Answer the question asked

On screen: Find the command word. / Then find the place and evidence required.

Read a question in three parts: what to do, which feature or place, and which source to use. A pupil may know a correct fact but still fail to answer the question. Show a deliberate mismatch, such as a cause given when the question asks for a pattern. Repair the response by keeping any useful detail and replacing the irrelevant part. This is a method pupils can apply across Geography. A good answer is relevant, accurate and supported; its length depends on the task rather than on filling space.

Brief check: What should we check before adding more sentences?

A claim needs support

On screen: Claim: what you say is true. / Evidence: the detail that supports it.

A claim states an idea about a place. Evidence is the observation, count or source detail we use to support that idea. “Shops cluster near the stop” is a claim. “Twelve of sixteen shops are within two hundred metres” makes the pattern more precise. Explain that evidence must be relevant: the colour of a shop sign does not test a claim about customer transport. We should be able to point to the supporting information and explain why it bears on the claim.

Brief check: Which supports clustering: a shop colour or a count with distance?
Listen for: The count and distance are relevant to the pattern.

State a useful limit

On screen: Say what is supported. / Say what still needs checking.

A limitation is a boundary on what we can conclude. It does not mean the investigation was worthless. We may accurately report that shops cluster in our mapped area while admitting that we did not measure the reasons for their location. Avoid extremes such as “we know everything” or “we know nothing”. Model a balanced conclusion: the source supports this pattern, a mechanism may explain it, and this further evidence would test that mechanism. Changing a claim when new evidence appears is part of good geographical reasoning.

Brief check: Does recognising a limit make all the evidence useless?
Listen for: No. Keep the supported finding and qualify the uncertain part.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 1.6

On screen: Claim: what you say is true. / Replace certainty with a testable explanation

Today's key idea: A claim needs support. Build an explanation with a claim, specific evidence and a link showing why the evidence matters. Evidence can support a pattern without proving its cause. A limitation identifies what information is missing. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

A claim needs support

On screen: Claim: what you say is true. / Evidence: the detail that supports it.

A claim states an idea about a place. Evidence is the observation, count or source detail we use to support that idea. “Shops cluster near the stop” is a claim. “Twelve of sixteen shops are within two hundred metres” makes the pattern more precise. Explain that evidence must be relevant: the colour of a shop sign does not test a claim about customer transport. We should be able to point to the supporting information and explain why it bears on the claim.

Brief check: Which supports clustering: a shop colour or a count with distance?
Listen for: The count and distance are relevant to the pattern.

Join evidence to the explanation

On screen: Say what the detail shows. / Explain why it matters.

A number does not explain itself. After giving a count, say what it tells us about the distribution. Then separate that pattern from a proposed cause. Many shops near a bus stop may be consistent with customers valuing access, but the count alone does not show why each business opened. Use two arrows: count to pattern, then possible access mechanism to explanation. The first can be directly supported by the count; the second needs more information about customers or business decisions.

Brief check: Can a location count tell us every business owner’s reason?
Listen for: No. It establishes the pattern, not every cause.

Ask for relevant new evidence

On screen: Customer survey: how did you travel? / Business records: when did the shop open?

The best next source depends on the claim being tested. If we want to know whether a bus stop brings customers, ask customers about travel and reasons for visiting. If we want to know whether the stop caused shops to open, compare opening dates and the stop’s history. Different questions need different evidence. More information is useful only if it addresses the uncertainty. Demonstrate a relevant and an irrelevant question, then explain why the relevant one could change our confidence in the proposed connection.

Brief check: Which evidence tests original opening: paint colour or dates?
Listen for: Dates can test whether the proposed cause came first.

State a useful limit

On screen: Say what is supported. / Say what still needs checking.

A limitation is a boundary on what we can conclude. It does not mean the investigation was worthless. We may accurately report that shops cluster in our mapped area while admitting that we did not measure the reasons for their location. Avoid extremes such as “we know everything” or “we know nothing”. Model a balanced conclusion: the source supports this pattern, a mechanism may explain it, and this further evidence would test that mechanism. Changing a claim when new evidence appears is part of good geographical reasoning.

Brief check: Does recognising a limit make all the evidence useless?
Listen for: No. Keep the supported finding and qualify the uncertain part.

7A · Week 19 · sections 1.7, 1.7

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 1.7

On screen: Trace every section in order. / Evaluate a route for a named traveller

Today's key idea: Routes connect a start and destination. Compare options using the same criteria. An evaluation weighs advantages and disadvantages for a named user. Shortest is not always most suitable: access, safety and time can matter as well as distance. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Why might the straight line fail?
Listen for: It may cross a barrier or an inaccessible area.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Routes connect a start and destination

On screen: Trace every section in order. / A straight line may not be a usable route.

A route is a sequence of connected sections between places. Trace the start, crossings, turns and destination. A straight line may be shorter on a map but could cross a fence, river or private land. The route must be usable by the traveller. Explain why geography considers the arrangement of places and the connections between them. Looking at distance alone ignores how the journey actually works. Before comparing routes, make sure each one begins and ends at the required locations and has no missing connection.

Brief check: Why might the straight line fail?
Listen for: It may cross a barrier or an inaccessible area.

Different travellers have different needs

On screen: Stairs can be a barrier. / Surface and slope affect access.

Imagine a traveller using a wheelchair and another walking without luggage. A staircase shortcut may work for one and prevent the other from travelling. A ramp label helps, but its gradient, width and surface condition still matter. Accessibility is a practical question about whether this person can use this route. It is not a judgement that one traveller is better than another. Point to the obstacle and explain its effect before comparing convenience. The shortest route may fail a necessary access condition.

Brief check: Should we choose stairs for every traveller because they are shorter?
Listen for: No. Check whether the traveller can use them.

Constraints and preferences

On screen: Constraint: a condition that must be met. / Preference: something we would like.

A constraint rules out a route when a required condition fails. A closed gate or unusable staircase can stop a journey. A preference helps choose between routes that work, such as a shorter distance or quieter surroundings. Establish feasibility before choosing favourites. Show a short closed route and a longer open route. The closed one cannot become feasible simply because we prefer it. This order makes a recommendation clear: first explain why the route can be used, then explain why it is the preferred usable option.

Brief check: Is an open route a preference or a necessary condition?
Listen for: Availability is a necessary condition.

Revise when conditions change

On screen: A closure can change the best route. / Check current conditions before travelling.

Maps describe locations and selected features, but they may not include a closure that happened this morning. A route that was suitable yesterday may be unavailable today. Show the old recommendation, add one changed condition and reconsider it aloud. Keep unchanged facts, such as the destination, while revising the affected route. Ask what information is needed before using an alternative: surface, crossing, opening hours or other relevant conditions. A good decision responds to evidence rather than defending an answer after its conditions have failed.

Brief check: What should happen to a recommendation after a route closes?
Listen for: Check alternatives and revise the route.

Access labels alone do not establish practical usability.

Teaching question: Which missing detail matters most to whether a ramp can be used? Correct reasoning: Its gradient and surface condition. Contrast this with: The colour of nearby houses. Explain the important distinction · 1.7

On screen: Two users choose different routes. What is the strongest comparison? / Give one short answer when invited.

The key question is: Two users choose different routes. What is the strongest comparison? The correct idea is: Check each user's needs against the same route evidence. Different priorities can justify different choices from the same evidence. Hear one or two brief answers, correct the specific misconception, and close with the accurate geographical explanation.

On screen: For the traveller in this source, which route condition would you check first? Why? / Say: “I would choose … because …”

Relevant explanation: B offers a ramp despite being 200 m longer. Check ramp gradient, condition and access; a ramp label does not guarantee suitability.

If an answer contradicts a fact, clarify the fact before accepting the preference. End by connecting the views to the topic rather than turning this into an extended debate.

Shortest is not always most suitable: access, safety and time can matter as well as distance. Start by pointing to the named features. 3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Routes connect a start and destination

On screen: Trace every section in order. / A straight line may not be a usable route.

A route is a sequence of connected sections between places. Trace the start, crossings, turns and destination. A straight line may be shorter on a map but could cross a fence, river or private land. The route must be usable by the traveller. Explain why geography considers the arrangement of places and the connections between them. Looking at distance alone ignores how the journey actually works. Before comparing routes, make sure each one begins and ends at the required locations and has no missing connection.

Brief check: Why might the straight line fail?
Listen for: It may cross a barrier or an inaccessible area.

Different travellers have different needs

On screen: Stairs can be a barrier. / Surface and slope affect access.

Imagine a traveller using a wheelchair and another walking without luggage. A staircase shortcut may work for one and prevent the other from travelling. A ramp label helps, but its gradient, width and surface condition still matter. Accessibility is a practical question about whether this person can use this route. It is not a judgement that one traveller is better than another. Point to the obstacle and explain its effect before comparing convenience. The shortest route may fail a necessary access condition.

Brief check: Should we choose stairs for every traveller because they are shorter?
Listen for: No. Check whether the traveller can use them.

Constraints and preferences

On screen: Constraint: a condition that must be met. / Preference: something we would like.

A constraint rules out a route when a required condition fails. A closed gate or unusable staircase can stop a journey. A preference helps choose between routes that work, such as a shorter distance or quieter surroundings. Establish feasibility before choosing favourites. Show a short closed route and a longer open route. The closed one cannot become feasible simply because we prefer it. This order makes a recommendation clear: first explain why the route can be used, then explain why it is the preferred usable option.

Brief check: Is an open route a preference or a necessary condition?
Listen for: Availability is a necessary condition.

Revise when conditions change

On screen: A closure can change the best route. / Check current conditions before travelling.

Maps describe locations and selected features, but they may not include a closure that happened this morning. A route that was suitable yesterday may be unavailable today. Show the old recommendation, add one changed condition and reconsider it aloud. Keep unchanged facts, such as the destination, while revising the affected route. Ask what information is needed before using an alternative: surface, crossing, opening hours or other relevant conditions. A good decision responds to evidence rather than defending an answer after its conditions have failed.

Brief check: What should happen to a recommendation after a route closes?
Listen for: Check alternatives and revise the route.

Build it together · Treat availability as a constraint

On screen: Treat availability as a constraint / A closed path is not an option today even if its recorded length is shortest.

A closed path is not an option today even if its recorded length is shortest. Cross unavailable choices out before ranking what remains. A recommendation needs both a route and the conditions under which it works.

A measured advantage cannot override an unavailable connection.

Teaching question: The shorter bridge is closed. Which action comes first? Correct reasoning: Find an open crossing before comparing journey lengths. Contrast this with: Recommend it because it is still shortest. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: The shorter bridge is closed. Which action comes first?
Listen for: Find an open crossing before comparing journey lengths. A measured advantage cannot override an unavailable connection.

Read the new case together · The missing criterion

On screen: Listen as your teacher explains the source. / We will use these facts in the demonstration.

CASE SOURCE A new report says Route A is closed today. Route B remains open; distances are unchanged.

MODEL EXPLANATION Recommend open Route B; availability overrides the shorter measured distance.

METHOD A closed path is not an option today even if its recorded length is shortest. Cross unavailable choices out before ranking what remains. A recommendation needs both a route and the conditions under which it works.

Read the source in small sections. Link each named place, measurement or process to the diagram. Keep the source visible when referring to a number. Demonstrate the relevant operation or connection aloud before inviting an answer. The case is a teaching example; no pupil needs to produce a written response.

Map making has developed

On screen: Surveying improved position and distance information. / Digital maps combine data in changeable layers.

Maps have been made for navigation, ownership, government, exploration and many other purposes. Their development is not simply a move from bad pictures to good ones. Different maps serve different needs. Surveying methods improved the measurement of positions and distances; printing helped reproduce maps; aerial and satellite observations supplied further information. Digital systems can combine layers and update selected data. A satellite image is still not identical to a road map: it records visible information that must be interpreted and combined with other sources. Explain what each development makes possible, then keep the key questions unchanged: who made the map, for what purpose, at what date and scale? Technology can improve the information available without making every map complete or suitable for every journey.

Brief check: Is a satellite image automatically the same as a usable road map?
Listen for: No. A road map selects and explains information for a particular purpose.

A map has a purpose

On screen: Maps select information. / Different users need different detail.

A map represents selected information about a place. A road map helps drivers see routes; a historical map may show former buildings or industries; a weather map presents a different kind of information. No map can display every detail clearly at once. Ask who will use the map and which question it should answer. The omission of a feature may reflect the purpose or scale, rather than proving that the feature does not exist. Start by reading the title instead of treating every map as a complete picture.

Brief check: Does an absent symbol always prove a feature is absent on the ground?
Listen for: No. The map may omit it.

Direction needs a reference

On screen: Use the north arrow. / East and west are opposite directions.

On a north-up map, north is towards the top and east towards the right. However, a rotated map changes screen positions without changing real directions. Point to the north arrow first, then identify east, south and west relative to it. Use a route between two features to demonstrate a directional sentence. Direction describes one place relative to another, so reversing the journey can reverse the description. Do not use left and right as substitutes for compass directions unless the reference is clear.

Brief check: If we rotate a map, does the town move to a new real location?
Listen for: No. The view changes; the location does not.

A key translates symbols

On screen: Symbols simplify features. / The key explains their meanings.

A symbol stands for a feature so the map can be read without drawing every detail. A dot may mark a city, and a line may mark a road or river. Colours and shapes should be interpreted using the supplied key, not by assuming they always mean the same thing. Compare two possible keys for the same drawing. If a circle means a pond in one map and a town in another, the keys prevent confusion. Good map design keeps the meanings consistent within a map.

Brief check: Can we decide a symbol’s meaning from its colour alone?
Listen for: Use the key; colour alone may be ambiguous.

Check the date and scale

On screen: The date affects how current the map is. / The scale affects distance and detail.

A map may be excellent for one question and unsuitable for another. An old map can show past land use but may miss new roads. A small-scale regional map covers a broad area but may omit a local path. A large-scale map usually has more space for local detail. Date and scale therefore affect interpretation, alongside purpose. Demonstrate choosing a map for a local walking route and another for locating a country. The best map is the one whose information matches the geographical question.

Brief check: Which matters when checking a recently built road?
Listen for: The map’s date and whether it shows that level of detail.

Build it together · Select a map by its purpose and date

On screen: Select a map by its purpose and date / A factory map from the past can locate former industry; a current transport map can show bus connections.

A factory map from the past can locate former industry; a current transport map can show bus connections. Detail is selected for a purpose. Older does not automatically mean useless.

Historical land use directly addresses former industry, though its date and coverage still matter.

Teaching question: Which map would best investigate former mills? Correct reasoning: A dated historical land-use map. Contrast this with: Only today's bus timetable. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: Which map would best investigate former mills?
Listen for: A dated historical land-use map. Historical land use directly addresses former industry, though its date and coverage still matter.

Watch a second example · 1.7

Fictional routes: A is 350 m with stairs; B is 550 m with a ramp. Both are open. First traveller: a wheelchair user. Second traveller: a walker carrying a light bag. Ramp condition has not been checked.

Which route would you investigate first for the wheelchair user? B, because it has a ramp. Check gradient, width and surface before calling it accessible.

Could the walker reasonably choose differently? Yes. A may suit someone who can use stairs and values distance; safety and condition still matter.
