Now change one condition · 3.1

On screen: Budget rises to 80 tokens. What is newly possible?

Fictional travel briefing: a group leaves Wales for Northern Ireland. Ferry package: 8 hours, 40 tokens. Air package: 5 hours, 75 tokens. Budget 60 tokens. The map shows the Irish Sea between the islands; it is not a timetable.

Budget rises to 80 tokens. What is newly possible? Both packages would be affordable if available; the cancelled ferry still cannot be used.

Related steps in this same case: Budget rises to 80 tokens. What is newly possible? Both packages would be affordable if available; the cancelled ferry still cannot be used.

What does the map establish, and what does it not establish? It shows locations and the sea crossing. It does not establish current departures, availability or prices.

Suggest two questions before booking a real journey. Check service availability and total price, including connections; access needs and travel conditions may also matter.

As you leave · 3.1

On screen: A new journey costs 42 tokens; the budget is 40. / As you leave, say its pictured total time and whether the budget is enough.

The pictured legs total 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 5 hours. Its cost is 42 tokens, exceeding the 40-token budget by 2. It is not feasible within that budget even if the service runs. Accept that meaning in a short ESL response.

Build two map keys

7B · Week 3 · Lesson 1 · sections 3.2

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 3.2

On screen: Countries and boundaries are political information. / Separate political information from physical relief

Today's key idea: Political maps show territories. Political maps show borders and territories; physical maps show features such as relief and rivers. A boundary and a mountain range are different kinds of information; overlays let us compare them. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Does a green country automatically mean low land?
Listen for: No. Its colour may simply identify the country.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Political maps show territories

On screen: Countries and boundaries are political information. / Read what each colour represents.

A political map shows divisions such as countries and their boundaries. Colours make neighbouring territories easier to distinguish; they do not automatically represent temperature or height. Point to Wales and England and identify the line separating them. A country can contain rivers, cities and mountains, but its outline is not the shape of one landform. Begin with the legend to understand the layer we are reading. Different maps of the same area may use different colours while describing the same political division.

Brief check: Does a green country automatically mean low land?
Listen for: No. Its colour may simply identify the country.

Physical maps show land and water

On screen: Relief describes the shape and height of land. / Rivers and mountains are physical features.

A physical map focuses on natural features such as land height, mountains and rivers. Relief means the shape and height differences of the land. The Scottish Highlands are an upland region in northern Great Britain; they are not another country. Compare the Highlands label with the Scotland boundary so the two kinds of information remain distinct. Rivers can cross territorial boundaries because water follows the landscape rather than stopping at a political line. The key tells us whether shading represents height, land cover or another physical property.

Brief check: Is a mountain region the same thing as a country?
Listen for: No. They describe different kinds of area.

Combine layers for a better question

On screen: Country layer: where is the territory? / Relief layer: what is the land like?

Layers allow us to examine different information about the same place. A country layer locates Wales, while a relief layer helps us examine high and low ground. A river layer adds drainage information. Switch layers without changing the location, then explain what each contributes. A question about a route across high land may need more than a country boundary. However, adding many layers at once can make a map harder to read. Select the layers that help answer the geographical question rather than treating more information as automatically better.

Brief check: Which layer helps identify high ground?
Listen for: An elevation or relief layer.

Boundaries and symbols need interpretation

On screen: A border need not follow a ridge. / A city dot marks location, not exact city size.

Some boundaries follow natural features, while others do not. We must compare their positions instead of assuming every border is a mountain ridge or river. Point symbols also simplify information. A large city dot may be drawn for visibility and does not necessarily show the city’s actual area. Explain the difference between a symbol’s function and its physical appearance. Careful map reading uses the legend, scale and layers together. It avoids converting a convenient drawing convention into an unsupported statement about the ground.

Brief check: Does a large city dot necessarily show the city’s ground area?
Listen for: No. It may be a point symbol chosen for visibility.

Build it together · Separate political information from physical relief

On screen: Separate political information from physical relief / A country boundary marks a territorial division; a ridge describes elevated land.

A country boundary marks a territorial division; a ridge describes elevated land. They may coincide but need not. A map key should use different symbols so a reader does not mistake every border for a mountain.

Physical layers describe landscape features; political layers describe territorial organisation.

Teaching question: Which pair belongs on a physical layer? Correct reasoning: Rivers and uplands. Contrast this with: National borders and capital-city status. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: Which pair belongs on a physical layer?
Listen for: Rivers and uplands. Physical layers describe landscape features; political layers describe territorial organisation.

Watch a second example · 3.2

On screen: Which two features are physical?

Map layers: country boundary for Wales; approximate upland area labelled Scottish Highlands; river line labelled Thames. A city point is also marked. Colours and symbols are explained in the key.

Which two features are physical? Scottish Highlands and Thames: relief and a river, rather than a country boundary.

7B · Week 3 · Lesson 2 · sections 3.2

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 3.2

On screen: Countries and boundaries are political information. / Combine layers to answer a specific question

Today's key idea: Political maps show territories. Political maps show borders and territories; physical maps show features such as relief and rivers. A boundary and a mountain range are different kinds of information; overlays let us compare them. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Does a green country automatically mean low land?
Listen for: No. Its colour may simply identify the country.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Political maps show territories

On screen: Countries and boundaries are political information. / Read what each colour represents.

A political map shows divisions such as countries and their boundaries. Colours make neighbouring territories easier to distinguish; they do not automatically represent temperature or height. Point to Wales and England and identify the line separating them. A country can contain rivers, cities and mountains, but its outline is not the shape of one landform. Begin with the legend to understand the layer we are reading. Different maps of the same area may use different colours while describing the same political division.

Brief check: Does a green country automatically mean low land?
Listen for: No. Its colour may simply identify the country.

Physical maps show land and water

On screen: Relief describes the shape and height of land. / Rivers and mountains are physical features.

A physical map focuses on natural features such as land height, mountains and rivers. Relief means the shape and height differences of the land. The Scottish Highlands are an upland region in northern Great Britain; they are not another country. Compare the Highlands label with the Scotland boundary so the two kinds of information remain distinct. Rivers can cross territorial boundaries because water follows the landscape rather than stopping at a political line. The key tells us whether shading represents height, land cover or another physical property.

Brief check: Is a mountain region the same thing as a country?
Listen for: No. They describe different kinds of area.

Combine layers for a better question

On screen: Country layer: where is the territory? / Relief layer: what is the land like?

Layers allow us to examine different information about the same place. A country layer locates Wales, while a relief layer helps us examine high and low ground. A river layer adds drainage information. Switch layers without changing the location, then explain what each contributes. A question about a route across high land may need more than a country boundary. However, adding many layers at once can make a map harder to read. Select the layers that help answer the geographical question rather than treating more information as automatically better.

Brief check: Which layer helps identify high ground?
Listen for: An elevation or relief layer.

Boundaries and symbols need interpretation

On screen: A border need not follow a ridge. / A city dot marks location, not exact city size.

Some boundaries follow natural features, while others do not. We must compare their positions instead of assuming every border is a mountain ridge or river. Point symbols also simplify information. A large city dot may be drawn for visibility and does not necessarily show the city’s actual area. Explain the difference between a symbol’s function and its physical appearance. Careful map reading uses the legend, scale and layers together. It avoids converting a convenient drawing convention into an unsupported statement about the ground.

Brief check: Does a large city dot necessarily show the city’s ground area?
Listen for: No. It may be a point symbol chosen for visibility.

Build it together · Combine layers to answer a specific question

On screen: Combine layers to answer a specific question / For a proposed route, the political layer identifies which territories it crosses; the relief layer indicates hills and valleys.

For a proposed route, the political layer identifies which territories it crosses; the relief layer indicates hills and valleys. Keep the layers separate until you ask how one route intersects both.

A boundary describes jurisdiction, not a guaranteed change of height.

Teaching question: A route crosses a country boundary. What cannot be concluded from that alone? Correct reasoning: That it climbs a mountain. Contrast this with: That it moves between the mapped territories. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: A route crosses a country boundary. What cannot be concluded from that alone?
Listen for: That it climbs a mountain. A boundary describes jurisdiction, not a guaranteed change of height.

7B · Week 4 · Lesson 1 · sections 3.3

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 3.3

On screen: Weather: conditions at a time and place. / Compare weather measurements without calling them climate

Today's key idea: Weather and climate use different time scales. Weather is short-term atmospheric conditions; climate summarises patterns over many years. Moist air rising over high ground cools; condensation and rainfall can make windward slopes wetter. This is one influence, not a daily guarantee. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Does one cold day prove a cold climate?
Listen for: No. Climate needs long-term observations.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Weather and climate use different time scales

On screen: Weather: conditions at a time and place. / Climate: long-term patterns of weather.

Weather describes conditions such as temperature, rainfall and wind at a particular time and place. Climate describes their long-term patterns and variation. A rainy afternoon is weather; it does not by itself establish a place’s typical rainfall. Show two station readings and state their dates before comparing them. Then explain why many observations across years are needed to investigate climate. Avoid saying that weather is random or that climate never changes. They concern related atmospheric conditions examined over different time scales.

Brief check: Does one cold day prove a cold climate?
Listen for: No. Climate needs long-term observations.

Read the measurements and units

On screen: Temperature is measured in degrees Celsius here. / Rainfall is measured in millimetres here.

A temperature value and a rainfall value measure different things. Degrees Celsius describe temperature; rainfall depth in millimetres describes an amount over the stated period. Read the station, date, unit and observation period before comparing numbers. Ten millimetres recorded in one hour cannot be interpreted in the same way as ten millimetres spread across a month. Compare like measurements over like periods. A weather table can show which station was wetter in the exercise without proving why that difference occurred.

Brief check: What must be checked besides the rainfall number?
Listen for: The unit, location and period over which it was recorded.

Mountains can force moist air to rise

On screen: Air rises on the windward side. / Rising air cools; cloud and rain can form.

Wind brings air towards a mountain. On the side facing the incoming wind, moist air is forced upwards. As the air rises, it expands and cools. Cooling can allow water vapour to condense into cloud droplets, and precipitation may result. Trace the rising arrow, then point to the cloud and rain. The sequence connects the mountain, air movement and rainfall rather than merely saying that mountains are wet. Windward describes the side facing the incoming wind, so that side can change when the wind direction changes.

Brief check: What happens to the air as it rises in this explanation?
Listen for: It cools, helping cloud droplets form.

The leeward side may be drier

On screen: Leeward is away from the incoming wind. / Descending air warms; a rain shadow may form.

After crossing the high ground, air can descend on the leeward side. Descending air warms, which can reduce relative humidity and discourage cloud formation. This helps explain a rain-shadow pattern. It does not mean that the leeward side can never receive rain: other weather systems and conditions also matter. Reverse the wind arrow and reconsider which side is windward. In the UK, western uplands often enhance rainfall from moist westerly air, but a simplified diagram does not predict every day’s weather at every station.

Brief check: If the wind reverses, must the windward side stay the same?
Listen for: No. It is defined by the incoming wind direction.

Build it together · Compare weather measurements without calling them climate

On screen: Compare weather measurements without calling them climate / A station at 11°C and another at 15°C differ by 4°C.

A station at 11°C and another at 15°C differ by 4°C. Rainfall in millimetres is a separate variable. One wet day is weather; climate needs records across many years, not just a larger number from one day.

The subtraction describes this day's difference, not a long-term pattern.

Teaching question: Station A has 16 mm and B 6 mm today. What is supported? Correct reasoning: A received 10 mm more rain today. Contrast this with: A always has the wetter climate. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: Station A has 16 mm and B 6 mm today. What is supported?
Listen for: A received 10 mm more rain today. The subtraction describes this day's difference, not a long-term pattern.

METHOD A station at 11°C and another at 15°C differ by 4°C. Rainfall in millimetres is a separate variable. One wet day is weather; climate needs records across many years, not just a larger number from one day.

The subtraction describes this day's difference, not a long-term pattern. Then invite a volunteer for one turn if useful. 7B · Week 5 · Lesson 1 · sections 3.4

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 3.4

On screen: Population: people living in an area. / Count overlapping groups once

Today's key idea: Population, community and identity. Population descriptions use data about people; averages and samples do not describe every individual. Overlapping categories must not be counted twice when finding a total. Avoid stereotypes about a whole country. Start by pointing to the named features. Listen for: Yes. Communities and identities can overlap.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Population, community and identity

On screen: Population: people living in an area. / People can belong to several communities.

A population is the people living in a defined area. It contains individuals with different ages, experiences, backgrounds and interests. A community can be connected by place or by shared activities, while identity concerns how people understand themselves and their connections. These groups can overlap: someone can belong to a local neighbourhood, a language community and a sports club. The UK is not one uniform group of people who all have the same experiences or preferences. Nor should we assume that every member of a cultural group thinks alike. When we examine population information, ask which aspect was measured. A hobby survey tells us about hobbies in its sample; it does not establish someone’s whole identity or describe all people in the country.

Brief check: Can one person belong to several communities?
Listen for: Yes. Communities and identities can overlap.

Describe diversity without stereotyping

On screen: Culture includes practices, language and traditions. / A group label does not predict every individual.

Culture includes shared practices, languages, traditions and ways of expressing meaning. Cultures change and can interact, while individuals participate in them differently. Use everyday examples such as different celebrations, foods or languages without ranking them or assuming everyone in a country follows one tradition. Population data can describe a distribution when it has a defined source and category, but cannot tell us every individual’s opinions. Distinguish a careful statement about a measured group from a stereotype. If we ask a small group about music or sport, report its actual responses and overlap. Do not turn that exercise into a statement that every person in the UK likes the same things.

Brief check: Does a community label establish each member’s favourite activity?
Listen for: No. Individuals within a community can differ.

People and data are not the same thing

On screen: Population: the group we want to describe. / Sample: the people we actually study.

Population can mean the total people in an area or, in a survey, the whole group we want to learn about. A sample is the smaller group actually studied. If we ask ten residents, we know their answers; we have not automatically heard from every resident. Explain why surveys use samples and why selection matters. Volunteers from one club may share interests that differ from other residents. A larger sample can still be biased if it repeatedly selects the same narrow kind of participant.

Brief check: Does asking more members of one club guarantee a representative sample?
Listen for: No. The selection may still be restricted.

Counts and proportions answer different questions

On screen: Count: how many? / Proportion: how many out of the total?

A count tells us the number in a category. A proportion relates that number to the whole group. Six out of ten is a larger proportion than twelve out of thirty, even though twelve is the larger count. Use groups of drawn people to show the numerator and denominator before calculating percentages. The question determines which comparison is useful. Counts can matter for service demand, while proportions help compare groups of different sizes. Neither should be substituted for the other without explaining the change.

Brief check: Which has the higher proportion: 6 of 10 or 12 of 30?
Listen for: 6 of 10: 60%, compared with 40%.

Overlapping groups need care

On screen: A person can belong to two groups. / Do not count the overlap twice in the total.

Suppose some pupils both walk and cycle on different days. Adding the walking count and cycling count may count those pupils twice. Draw two overlapping circles and put the shared pupils in the middle. To find the number in at least one group, add both counts and subtract the overlap once. Explain that the categories and question must be clear before calculating. A survey about usual travel mode may use different rules from a survey asking every mode used during the week.

Brief check: Why can adding two group counts overestimate the number of people?
Listen for: Some people may belong to both groups.

Write a headline that fits the survey

On screen: Name who was asked. / Do not turn a sample into “everyone”.

A headline should reflect the evidence’s scope. If a survey asks cycling-club volunteers, report their responses rather than claiming all residents have the same views. Explain how a word such as everyone can make a statement much stronger than the data support. Keep useful findings while correcting the population claim. A careful geographical report includes the sample, question and relevant period. It can also say which other groups should be studied before making a wider conclusion about the town.

Brief check: How should a limited survey’s headline be qualified?
Listen for: Name the sampled group rather than claiming it describes everyone.

Of 10 walkers and 7 cyclists, 4 do both. Put 4 in the overlap, then 6 walkers only and 3 cyclists only: total 13. Adding 10 and 7 without subtracting the overlap counts four people twice.

8 + 6 - 3 = 11 distinct people.

Today we will understand · 3.2

On screen: Countries and boundaries are political information. / Combine layers to answer a specific question

Today's key idea: Political maps show territories. Political maps show borders and territories; physical maps show features such as relief and rivers. A boundary and a mountain range are different kinds of information; overlays let us compare them. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Does a green country automatically mean low land?
Listen for: No. Its colour may simply identify the country.

Today we will understand · 3.3

On screen: Weather: conditions at a time and place. / Compare weather measurements without calling them climate

Today's key idea: Weather and climate use different time scales. Weather is short-term atmospheric conditions; climate summarises patterns over many years. Moist air rising over high ground cools; condensation and rainfall can make windward slopes wetter. This is one influence, not a daily guarantee. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Does one cold day prove a cold climate?
Listen for: No. Climate needs long-term observations.

Listen for: Yes. Communities and identities can overlap.

3–25 min · Explain and reconnect

Political maps show territories

On screen: Countries and boundaries are political information. / Read what each colour represents.

A political map shows divisions such as countries and their boundaries. Colours make neighbouring territories easier to distinguish; they do not automatically represent temperature or height. Point to Wales and England and identify the line separating them. A country can contain rivers, cities and mountains, but its outline is not the shape of one landform. Begin with the legend to understand the layer we are reading. Different maps of the same area may use different colours while describing the same political division.

Brief check: Does a green country automatically mean low land?
Listen for: No. Its colour may simply identify the country.

Boundaries and symbols need interpretation

On screen: A border need not follow a ridge. / A city dot marks location, not exact city size.

Some boundaries follow natural features, while others do not. We must compare their positions instead of assuming every border is a mountain ridge or river. Point symbols also simplify information. A large city dot may be drawn for visibility and does not necessarily show the city’s actual area. Explain the difference between a symbol’s function and its physical appearance. Careful map reading uses the legend, scale and layers together. It avoids converting a convenient drawing convention into an unsupported statement about the ground.

Brief check: Does a large city dot necessarily show the city’s ground area?
Listen for: No. It may be a point symbol chosen for visibility.

See the method · Combine layers to answer a specific question

On screen: Combine layers to answer a specific question / For a proposed route, the political layer identifies which territories it crosses; the relief layer indicates hills and valleys.

For a proposed route, the political layer identifies which territories it crosses; the relief layer indicates hills and valleys. Keep the layers separate until you ask how one route intersects both.

A boundary describes jurisdiction, not a guaranteed change of height.

Teaching question: A route crosses a country boundary. What cannot be concluded from that alone? Correct reasoning: That it climbs a mountain. Contrast this with: That it moves between the mapped territories. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: A route crosses a country boundary. What cannot be concluded from that alone?
Listen for: That it climbs a mountain. A boundary describes jurisdiction, not a guaranteed change of height.

Method note: For a proposed route, the political layer identifies which territories it crosses; the relief layer indicates hills and valleys. Keep the layers separate until you ask how one route intersects both.

MODEL EXPLANATION Correction: That it climbs a mountain. A boundary describes jurisdiction, not a guaranteed change of height. A complete response must explain the method, not simply copy the correct choice. For a changed case, accept different answers only when the new condition actually supports them.

METHOD For a proposed route, the political layer identifies which territories it crosses; the relief layer indicates hills and valleys. Keep the layers separate until you ask how one route intersects both.

Read the source in small sections. Link each named place, measurement or process to the diagram. Keep the source visible when referring to a number. Demonstrate the relevant operation or connection aloud before inviting an answer. The case is a teaching example; no pupil needs to produce a written response.

Weather and climate use different time scales

On screen: Weather: conditions at a time and place. / Climate: long-term patterns of weather.

Weather describes conditions such as temperature, rainfall and wind at a particular time and place. Climate describes their long-term patterns and variation. A rainy afternoon is weather; it does not by itself establish a place’s typical rainfall. Show two station readings and state their dates before comparing them. Then explain why many observations across years are needed to investigate climate. Avoid saying that weather is random or that climate never changes. They concern related atmospheric conditions examined over different time scales.

Brief check: Does one cold day prove a cold climate?
Listen for: No. Climate needs long-term observations.

The leeward side may be drier

On screen: Leeward is away from the incoming wind. / Descending air warms; a rain shadow may form.

After crossing the high ground, air can descend on the leeward side. Descending air warms, which can reduce relative humidity and discourage cloud formation. This helps explain a rain-shadow pattern. It does not mean that the leeward side can never receive rain: other weather systems and conditions also matter. Reverse the wind arrow and reconsider which side is windward. In the UK, western uplands often enhance rainfall from moist westerly air, but a simplified diagram does not predict every day’s weather at every station.

Brief check: If the wind reverses, must the windward side stay the same?
Listen for: No. It is defined by the incoming wind direction.

See the method · Compare weather measurements without calling them climate

On screen: Compare weather measurements without calling them climate / A station at 11°C and another at 15°C differ by 4°C.

A station at 11°C and another at 15°C differ by 4°C. Rainfall in millimetres is a separate variable. One wet day is weather; climate needs records across many years, not just a larger number from one day.

The subtraction describes this day's difference, not a long-term pattern.

Teaching question: Station A has 16 mm and B 6 mm today. What is supported? Correct reasoning: A received 10 mm more rain today. Contrast this with: A always has the wetter climate. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: Station A has 16 mm and B 6 mm today. What is supported?
Listen for: A received 10 mm more rain today. The subtraction describes this day's difference, not a long-term pattern.

CASE SOURCE Review case: Station A has 16 mm and B 6 mm today. What is supported? Proposed answer: “A always has the wetter climate.”. Method note: A station at 11°C and another at 15°C differ by 4°C. Rainfall in millimetres is a separate variable. One wet day is weather; climate needs records across many years, not just a larger number from one day.

MODEL EXPLANATION Correction: A received 10 mm more rain today. The subtraction describes this day's difference, not a long-term pattern. Population, community and identity

On screen: Population: people living in an area. / People can belong to several communities.

A population is the people living in a defined area. It contains individuals with different ages, experiences, backgrounds and interests. A community can be connected by place or by shared activities, while identity concerns how people understand themselves and their connections. These groups can overlap: someone can belong to a local neighbourhood, a language community and a sports club. The UK is not one uniform group of people who all have the same experiences or preferences. Nor should we assume that every member of a cultural group thinks alike. Political maps show territories

On screen: Countries and boundaries are political information. / Read what each colour represents.

A political map shows divisions such as countries and their boundaries. Colours make neighbouring territories easier to distinguish; they do not automatically represent temperature or height. Point to Wales and England and identify the line separating them. A country can contain rivers, cities and mountains, but its outline is not the shape of one landform. Begin with the legend to understand the layer we are reading. Different maps of the same area may use different colours while describing the same political division.

Brief check: Does a green country automatically mean low land?
Listen for: No. Its colour may simply identify the country.

Boundaries and symbols need interpretation

On screen: A border need not follow a ridge. / A city dot marks location, not exact city size.

Some boundaries follow natural features, while others do not. We must compare their positions instead of assuming every border is a mountain ridge or river. Point symbols also simplify information. A large city dot may be drawn for visibility and does not necessarily show the city’s actual area. Explain the difference between a symbol’s function and its physical appearance. Careful map reading uses the legend, scale and layers together. It avoids converting a convenient drawing convention into an unsupported statement about the ground.

Brief check: Does a large city dot necessarily show the city’s ground area?
Listen for: No. It may be a point symbol chosen for visibility.

Weather and climate use different time scales

On screen: Weather: conditions at a time and place. / Climate: long-term patterns of weather.

Weather describes conditions such as temperature, rainfall and wind at a particular time and place. Climate describes their long-term patterns and variation. A rainy afternoon is weather; it does not by itself establish a place’s typical rainfall. Show two station readings and state their dates before comparing them. Then explain why many observations across years are needed to investigate climate. Avoid saying that weather is random or that climate never changes. They concern related atmospheric conditions examined over different time scales.

Brief check: Does one cold day prove a cold climate?
Listen for: No. Climate needs long-term observations.

The leeward side may be drier

On screen: Leeward is away from the incoming wind. / Descending air warms; a rain shadow may form.

After crossing the high ground, air can descend on the leeward side. Descending air warms, which can reduce relative humidity and discourage cloud formation. This helps explain a rain-shadow pattern. It does not mean that the leeward side can never receive rain: other weather systems and conditions also matter. Reverse the wind arrow and reconsider which side is windward. In the UK, western uplands often enhance rainfall from moist westerly air, but a simplified diagram does not predict every day’s weather at every station.

Brief check: If the wind reverses, must the windward side stay the same?
Listen for: No. It is defined by the incoming wind direction.

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 3.2

On screen: Countries and boundaries are political information. / Separate political information from physical relief

Today's key idea: Political maps show territories. Political maps show borders and territories; physical maps show features such as relief and rivers. A boundary and a mountain range are different kinds of information; overlays let us compare them. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Does a green country automatically mean low land?
Listen for: No. Its colour may simply identify the country.

Today we will understand · 3.3

On screen: Weather: conditions at a time and place. / Explain relief rainfall as a connected process

Today's key idea: Weather and climate use different time scales. Weather is short-term atmospheric conditions; climate summarises patterns over many years. Moist air rising over high ground cools; condensation and rainfall can make windward slopes wetter. This is one influence, not a daily guarantee. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Does one cold day prove a cold climate?
Listen for: No. Climate needs long-term observations.

Today we will understand · 3.4

On screen: Population: people living in an area. / Count overlapping groups once

Today's key idea: Population, community and identity. Population descriptions use data about people; averages and samples do not describe every individual. Overlapping categories must not be counted twice when finding a total. Avoid stereotypes about a whole country. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Can one person belong to several communities?
Listen for: Yes. Communities and identities can overlap.

3–25 min · Explain and reconnect

Political maps show territories

On screen: Countries and boundaries are political information. / Read what each colour represents.

A political map shows divisions such as countries and their boundaries. Colours make neighbouring territories easier to distinguish; they do not automatically represent temperature or height. Point to Wales and England and identify the line separating them. A country can contain rivers, cities and mountains, but its outline is not the shape of one landform. Begin with the legend to understand the layer we are reading. Different maps of the same area may use different colours while describing the same political division.

Brief check: Does a green country automatically mean low land?
Listen for: No. Its colour may simply identify the country.

Boundaries and symbols need interpretation

On screen: A border need not follow a ridge. / A city dot marks location, not exact city size.

Some boundaries follow natural features, while others do not. We must compare their positions instead of assuming every border is a mountain ridge or river. Point symbols also simplify information. A large city dot may be drawn for visibility and does not necessarily show the city’s actual area. Explain the difference between a symbol’s function and its physical appearance. Careful map reading uses the legend, scale and layers together. It avoids converting a convenient drawing convention into an unsupported statement about the ground.

Brief check: Does a large city dot necessarily show the city’s ground area?
Listen for: No. It may be a point symbol chosen for visibility.

See the method · Separate political information from physical relief

On screen: Separate political information from physical relief / A country boundary marks a territorial division; a ridge describes elevated land.

A country boundary marks a territorial division; a ridge describes elevated land. They may coincide but need not. A map key should use different symbols so a reader does not mistake every border for a mountain.

Physical layers describe landscape features; political layers describe territorial organisation.

Teaching question: Which pair belongs on a physical layer? Correct reasoning: Rivers and uplands. Contrast this with: National borders and capital-city status. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: Which pair belongs on a physical layer?
Listen for: Rivers and uplands. Physical layers describe landscape features; political layers describe territorial organisation.

Weather and climate use different time scales

On screen: Weather: conditions at a time and place. / Climate: long-term patterns of weather.

Weather describes conditions such as temperature, rainfall and wind at a particular time and place. Climate describes their long-term patterns and variation. A rainy afternoon is weather; it does not by itself establish a place’s typical rainfall. Show two station readings and state their dates before comparing them. Then explain why many observations across years are needed to investigate climate. Avoid saying that weather is random or that climate never changes. They concern related atmospheric conditions examined over different time scales.

Brief check: Does one cold day prove a cold climate?
Listen for: No. Climate needs long-term observations.

The leeward side may be drier

On screen: Leeward is away from the incoming wind. / Descending air warms; a rain shadow may form.

After crossing the high ground, air can descend on the leeward side. Descending air warms, which can reduce relative humidity and discourage cloud formation. This helps explain a rain-shadow pattern. It does not mean that the leeward side can never receive rain: other weather systems and conditions also matter. Reverse the wind arrow and reconsider which side is windward. In the UK, western uplands often enhance rainfall from moist westerly air, but a simplified diagram does not predict every day’s weather at every station.

Brief check: If the wind reverses, must the windward side stay the same?
Listen for: No. It is defined by the incoming wind direction.

See the method · Explain relief rainfall as a connected process

On screen: Explain relief rainfall as a connected process / Moist air rises over high ground and cools.

Moist air rises over high ground and cools. Condensation can form cloud and precipitation. Descending air on the other side may be drier; wind and moisture supply matter, so a mountain does not guarantee rain every day.

Cooling changes conditions for condensation; it does not create water.

Teaching question: The incoming air becomes much drier. What prediction follows, other things equal? Correct reasoning: Less moisture is available for precipitation. Contrast this with: The mountain creates the missing water. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: The incoming air becomes much drier. What prediction follows, other things equal?
Listen for: Less moisture is available for precipitation. Cooling changes conditions for condensation; it does not create water.

Population, community and identity

On screen: Population: people living in an area. / People can belong to several communities.

A population is the people living in a defined area. It contains individuals with different ages, experiences, backgrounds and interests. A community can be connected by place or by shared activities, while identity concerns how people understand themselves and their connections. These groups can overlap: someone can belong to a local neighbourhood, a language community and a sports club. The UK is not one uniform group of people who all have the same experiences or preferences. Nor should we assume that every member of a cultural group thinks alike. When we examine population information, ask which aspect was measured. A hobby survey tells us about hobbies in its sample; it does not establish someone’s whole identity or describe all people in the country.

Brief check: Can one person belong to several communities?
Listen for: Yes. Communities and identities can overlap.

Write a headline that fits the survey

On screen: Name who was asked. / Do not turn a sample into “everyone”.

A headline should reflect the evidence’s scope. If a survey asks cycling-club volunteers, report their responses rather than claiming all residents have the same views. Explain how a word such as everyone can make a statement much stronger than the data support. Keep useful findings while correcting the population claim. A careful geographical report includes the sample, question and relevant period. It can also say which other groups should be studied before making a wider conclusion about the town.

Brief check: How should a limited survey’s headline be qualified?
Listen for: Name the sampled group rather than claiming it describes everyone.

See the method · Count overlapping groups once

On screen: Count overlapping groups once / Of 10 walkers and 7 cyclists, 4 do both.

Of 10 walkers and 7 cyclists, 4 do both. Put 4 in the overlap, then 6 walkers only and 3 cyclists only: total 13. Adding 10 and 7 without subtracting the overlap counts four people twice.

8 + 6 - 3 = 11 distinct people.

Teaching question: Eight swim, six run and three do both; everyone does at least one. How many people? Correct reasoning: 11. Contrast this with: 14. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: Eight swim, six run and three do both; everyone does at least one. How many people?
Listen for: 11. 8 + 6 - 3 = 11 distinct people.

Why is adding the two activity totals misleading? The 16 pupils in both groups would be counted twice.

A city is drawn with a large dot. Is the city that size on the ground? Not necessarily. A point symbol locates it; its drawn size may be chosen for visibility.

Teacher demonstration · Design a counterexample · Explain relief rainfall as a connected process

On screen: Explain relief rainfall as a connected process / Follow your teacher’s explanation of the places, facts and steps.

Review case: The incoming air becomes much drier. What prediction follows, other things equal? Proposed answer: “The mountain creates the missing water.”. Method note: Moist air rises over high ground and cools. Condensation can form cloud and precipitation. Descending air on the other side may be drier; wind and moisture supply matter, so a mountain does not guarantee rain every day.

Demonstrate this process on the board: Station 2: Create a changed case in which a tempting answer fails. Show the original reasoning, change one condition and explain what must now be reconsidered.

Explain the result: Correction: Less moisture is available for precipitation. Cooling changes conditions for condensation; it does not create water. A complete response must explain the method, not simply copy the correct choice. For a changed case, accept different answers only when the new condition actually supports them.

On screen: Does this one day establish the climate?

Fictional weather on one day: West station 24°C and 28 mm rain; East station 27°C and 2 mm rain. A mountain stands between them. Incoming air is moist and blows from the west.

Does this one day establish the climate? No. Climate needs long-term patterns, not one day’s weather.

Related steps in this same case: Does this one day establish the climate? No. Climate needs long-term patterns, not one day’s weather.

Keep the mountain but replace moist air with dry air. Predict the effect. Less available moisture limits rainfall. A mountain does not create water from nothing.

What should a fair station comparison keep consistent? Measurement period, instruments and recording method; also examine height and exposure when interpreting differences.

7B · Week 9 · Lesson 1 · sections 3.5

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 3.5

On screen: A settlement can be small or large. / Read settlement pattern before guessing its cause

Today's key idea: Settlements are places where people live. Nucleated settlements cluster; linear settlements follow a line; dispersed settlements are spread out. Describe a pattern before suggesting reasons; roads, relief and services may influence settlement. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Does pattern mean only the number of residents?
Listen for: No. It describes spatial arrangement.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Settlements are places where people live

On screen: A settlement can be small or large. / Its pattern describes the arrangement of buildings.

A settlement is a place where people live. Settlements differ in size, form and functions. A pattern concerns how buildings are arranged, not just how many people live there. Begin with a simple map of buildings and describe positions without guessing causes. Then introduce the pattern terms. A settlement may grow over time and contain several different arrangements. The map’s scale and the area selected influence what pattern is visible, so a small detail should not automatically become a description of the whole town.

Brief check: Does pattern mean only the number of residents?
Listen for: No. It describes spatial arrangement.

Nucleated, linear and dispersed

On screen: Nucleated: buildings clustered together. / Linear: buildings follow a line; dispersed: spread apart.

A nucleated pattern has a cluster of buildings, often around a focal point. A linear pattern follows a line such as a road or valley. A dispersed pattern has buildings separated across an area. Trace each arrangement on the diagram and use spacing and alignment as evidence. These terms describe the visible form; they do not prove why it developed. A single settlement can combine a roadside strip with a separate cluster. Good description names the distinct parts instead of forcing everything into one label.

Brief check: What visible evidence supports “linear”?
Listen for: Buildings follow a line, such as along a road.

Site and situation explain different relationships

On screen: Site: the land where the settlement stands. / Situation: its position relative to other places.

Site refers to the local land occupied by a settlement: slope, water access and ground conditions are examples. Situation concerns its relationships with surrounding places and routes. A settlement may stand on a valley floor and lie near a river crossing used by travellers. Separate these two scales while pointing to the map. Neither guarantees one cause of growth. To investigate why people settled there, examine historical information and relevant conditions instead of assuming that a convenient-looking location explains every decision.

Brief check: Is being near another town a site or situation detail?
Listen for: Situation: it describes the relationship with another place.

Growth can create mixed patterns

On screen: New buildings can change the visible form. / Describe each part before making a general label.

Add a new housing cluster to a previously linear settlement. The original roadside buildings remain, while the new development creates another arrangement. Describe both and compare before and after. A new road, service or development plan may help explain the change, but the map alone does not establish the developer’s reasons. Distinguish observation from explanation. Mixed patterns are not errors in classification; they show that settlements develop through several changes rather than following one simple shape forever.

Brief check: Should a new cluster erase the description of the original roadside strip?
Listen for: No. Describe the linear section and the separate cluster.

A cluster around a junction is nucleated; a row along a road is linear; isolated farms are dispersed. First describe locations. A road may influence development, but the drawing alone cannot prove residents' reasons.

The buildings follow a line rather than being scattered independently.

Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

7B · Week 10 · Lesson 1 · sections 3.6

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 3.6

On screen: Health, safety, housing and access matter. / Evaluate quality of life using more than income

Today's key idea: Quality of life has several dimensions. Quality of life includes access to services, income, environment and other factors. Compare several indicators and whose needs they represent. Averages can hide differences within a place. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Does income alone tell us everything about quality of life?
Listen for: No. Other conditions and access also matter.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Quality of life has several dimensions

On screen: Health, safety, housing and access matter. / Income is one part of the picture.

Quality of life concerns how people live and experience their surroundings. Income matters, but health services, housing, safety, environmental conditions and access to opportunities also matter. A wealthy area may still have a long journey to a clinic or polluted surroundings. Introduce several indicators before judging a place. Explain that indicators measure selected aspects rather than a complete human experience. People can also value the same features differently, so factual measurements and personal priorities should be kept distinguishable.

Brief check: Does income alone tell us everything about quality of life?
Listen for: No. Other conditions and access also matter.

Use indicators to make a comparison

On screen: Compare the same measure and unit. / Read what the measure actually represents.

An indicator is a measurable sign of a condition. Clinic travel time can indicate access to care, while a housing measure may describe living conditions. Compare the same indicator across places using compatible units and periods. A shorter travel time does not prove that the clinic offers every required service. Read the definition before deciding what the measurement tells us. Show a table in which one place has higher income but a longer clinic journey, then explain why the choice depends on more than one column.

Brief check: What does clinic travel time measure directly?
Listen for: The journey time to the clinic, not every aspect of healthcare quality.

Averages can hide uneven experiences

On screen: An average describes a group. / It does not describe every person equally.

An average travel time can improve while some residents experience longer journeys. Use a central district and a remote district to illustrate this. If many people benefit, the overall average may fall even though a smaller group is worse off. A geographical evaluation should therefore examine the distribution of benefits and costs as well as the average. Ask who gains, who loses and where they live. This is especially important when deciding whether a new service location improves access fairly across an area.

Brief check: Can an improved average coexist with worse access for one district?
Listen for: Yes. Group averages can hide different local outcomes.

Explain the trade-off

On screen: A proposal can have benefits and costs. / Use evidence for both sides.

A new service may improve one condition while weakening another. For example, a larger central clinic could offer more facilities but increase travel for remote residents. Explain each effect through its mechanism rather than labelling the proposal simply good or bad. Then identify what evidence could help compare the effects: travel times, service capacity and the needs of different users. An opinion about priorities is legitimate, but it should be distinguished from a measurable claim about what the proposal will do.

Brief check: What should a balanced recommendation include?
Listen for: Supported benefits, supported costs and the needs of affected groups.

Quality of life has several dimensions

A wealthy area may still have a long journey to a clinic or polluted surroundings. Introduce several indicators before judging a place. Explain that indicators measure selected aspects rather than a complete human experience. People can also value the same features differently, so factual measurements and personal priorities should be kept distinguishable.

An opinion about priorities is legitimate, but it should be distinguished from a measurable claim about what the proposal will do.

Brief check: What should a balanced recommendation include?
Listen for: Supported benefits, supported costs and the needs of affected groups.

7B · Week 11 · Lesson 1 · sections 3.7

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 3.7

On screen: London is in south-east England, on the River Thames. / Explain links between city functions

Today's key idea: London is the UK’s capital. Cities have multiple functions: government, culture, work, housing and transport can depend on one another. A connection may benefit some users more than others. London is on the Thames in south-east England. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Does being the capital mean all UK residents live there?
Listen for: No. It describes the city’s national role.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

London is the UK’s capital

On screen: London is in south-east England, on the River Thames. / Its capital role includes national government.

London is the United Kingdom’s capital and lies in south-east England on the River Thames. Locate it within England, then within the UK, before discussing its functions. Parliament meets at Westminster, giving a concrete example of the city’s national government role. London is also a place where people live, work, study and visit. A capital is not defined as a place where everyone in the country lives or as the only city with important activities. Its role connects a particular location to national decision-making. Link the map location to the river and transport connections, while avoiding the assumption that river location alone completely explains the history or importance of the city.

Brief check: Does being the capital mean all UK residents live there?
Listen for: No. It describes the city’s national role.

A city serves residents and visitors

On screen: Government, transport, work, education and culture are functions. / Connections help people reach these activities.

A function is an activity or role served by a place. London’s functions include government, employment, education, culture, commerce and transport. Use Parliament for government, museums for culture and stations for transport as concrete examples. The same visitor may use several functions in one day: arriving by train, visiting a museum and using a shop. Residents have additional everyday needs such as homes and services. Transport can support other functions by connecting users to them, while congestion can make those connections harder. Show the nodes and routes only after identifying the real activities they connect. This keeps a network explanation rooted in London rather than turning the topic into an anonymous set of lines.

Brief check: How can a station support a museum’s function?
Listen for: It can help residents and visitors reach the museum.

Towns have connected functions

On screen: Homes, work, shops and services have different roles. / People and goods move between them.

A town contains activities that serve different needs. Residential areas provide homes; shops supply goods; workplaces provide jobs; services include education and healthcare. Their locations matter because people travel between them. Trace a journey from home to school and another from a delivery depot to shops. These movements connect functions into a system. A map of separate buildings becomes more useful when we understand the flows between them. Not every town arranges its activities in the same way, so the model is a way to explain connections rather than a universal plan.

Brief check: What connects homes and workplaces in this example?
Listen for: People travelling between them.

Networks have nodes and links

On screen: Node: a connection point. / Link: the connection between points.

A transport network can be described using nodes and links. A station or junction is a node; a route between them is a link. A journey may pass through several nodes, where travellers transfer between services. Trace the network from one destination to another and show how a missing link can interrupt the route. The usefulness of a link depends on its availability and capacity, not merely on being drawn. This vocabulary also helps describe flows of goods, water or information through other geographical systems.

Brief check: Is a station a node or a link?
Listen for: A node: a point where connections meet.

A disruption can spread through the network

On screen: A closed link changes available routes. / Other services may face extra demand.

Close one bridge in a model town. Travellers may use another crossing, making it busier, or may be unable to reach their destination. Explain the chain from the original closure to the changed movement and possible effect on work or services. Do not assume every location is equally affected: some have alternative links and others do not. A good diagram traces the particular connections rather than saying that everything stops. Evidence about route use and alternatives helps identify the places most affected.

Brief check: Why might another bridge become busier after a closure?
Listen for: Some travellers divert to the remaining crossing.

Capacity must match demand over time

On screen: Capacity per trip is not capacity per hour. / Frequency tells us how often the service runs.

A bus carrying thirty passengers can move thirty per trip, but hourly capacity depends on how many trips it makes. If sixty people need to travel each hour, one trip may be insufficient while two full trips could match the stated demand. Real planning also considers timing, direction and accessibility. Distinguish the size of the vehicle from service frequency. This explains why drawing an alternative bus route does not establish that it can carry everyone displaced by a rail or bridge disruption.

Brief check: What must we know besides seats per bus?
Listen for: The frequency and timing of trips compared with demand.

Build it together · Explain links between city functions

On screen: Explain links between city functions / A station connects travellers to offices, museums and services.

A station connects travellers to offices, museums and services. Draw an arrow labelled “carries workers” rather than just “link”. A useful network explains what moves, between which places, and why it matters.

The first names the movement and its function.

Teaching question: Which arrow label explains a city connection? Correct reasoning: Bus route carries visitors from station to museum. Contrast this with: Station and museum are both words. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: Which arrow label explains a city connection?
Listen for: Bus route carries visitors from station to museum. The first names the movement and its function.

Show the nodes and routes only after identifying the real activities they connect. This keeps a network explanation rooted in London rather than turning the topic into an anonymous set of lines.

Brief check: How can a station support a museum’s function?
Listen for: It can help residents and visitors reach the museum.

Towns have connected functions

On screen: Homes, work, shops and services have different roles. / People and goods move between them.

A town contains activities that serve different needs. Residential areas provide homes; shops supply goods; workplaces provide jobs; services include education and healthcare. Their locations matter because people travel between them. Trace a journey from home to school and another from a delivery depot to shops. These movements connect functions into a system. A map of separate buildings becomes more useful when we understand the flows between them. Not every town arranges its activities in the same way, so the model is a way to explain connections rather than a universal plan.

Brief check: What connects homes and workplaces in this example?
Listen for: People travelling between them.

Networks have nodes and links

On screen: Node: a connection point. / Link: the connection between points.

A transport network can be described using nodes and links. A station or junction is a node; a route between them is a link. A journey may pass through several nodes, where travellers transfer between services. Trace the network from one destination to another and show how a missing link can interrupt the route. The usefulness of a link depends on its availability and capacity, not merely on being drawn. This vocabulary also helps describe flows of goods, water or information through other geographical systems.

Brief check: Is a station a node or a link?
Listen for: A node: a point where connections meet.

A disruption can spread through the network

On screen: A closed link changes available routes. / Other services may face extra demand.

Close one bridge in a model town. Travellers may use another crossing, making it busier, or may be unable to reach their destination. Explain the chain from the original closure to the changed movement and possible effect on work or services. Do not assume every location is equally affected: some have alternative links and others do not. A good diagram traces the particular connections rather than saying that everything stops. Evidence about route use and alternatives helps identify the places most affected.

Brief check: Why might another bridge become busier after a closure?
Listen for: Some travellers divert to the remaining crossing.

Capacity must match demand over time

On screen: Capacity per trip is not capacity per hour. / Frequency tells us how often the service runs.

A bus carrying thirty passengers can move thirty per trip, but hourly capacity depends on how many trips it makes. If sixty people need to travel each hour, one trip may be insufficient while two full trips could match the stated demand. Real planning also considers timing, direction and accessibility. Distinguish the size of the vehicle from service frequency. This explains why drawing an alternative bus route does not establish that it can carry everyone displaced by a rail or bridge disruption.

Brief check: What must we know besides seats per bus?
Listen for: The frequency and timing of trips compared with demand.

Build it together · Trace a disruption through a network

On screen: Trace a disruption through a network / A closed station removes one access point but not every city function.

A closed station removes one access point but not every city function. Trace an alternative route, count extra changes and identify who bears the cost. Visitors and commuters may experience different effects.

The remaining connection may work with extra time or crowding; investigate its limits.

Teaching question: A station closes but a bus route remains open. What should planners compare? Correct reasoning: Alternative journey time and capacity. Contrast this with: Assume nobody can reach the area. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: A station closes but a bus route remains open. What should planners compare?
Listen for: Alternative journey time and capacity. The remaining connection may work with extra time or crowding; investigate its limits.

7B · Week 12 · Lesson 1 · sections 3.8

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 3.8

On screen: Imports enter; exports leave. / Track goods, people and information separately

Today's key idea: The UK connects to the wider world. Trade moves goods, travel moves people and communication moves information. Imports enter; exports leave the country being discussed. Connections have benefits, costs and dependencies. The same shipment is an export at one end and an import at the other. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Can the same shipment be one country’s export and another’s import?
Listen for: Yes. The terms depend on the country’s point of view.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

The UK connects to the wider world

On screen: Imports enter; exports leave. / Travel and communication create other links.

An import enters a country from elsewhere; an export is sent to another country. Describe the direction from the country’s point of view. Fruit brought into a UK shop is an import for the UK, while the exporting place describes the same connection differently. Goods are only one kind of international link. People travel for visits, work, study or other purposes, and messages connect places without moving a person or parcel along the same physical route. Trace goods, people and information using separate arrows. The UK’s relationship with other countries therefore includes trade, tourism and communication rather than one single supply chain. Our invented examples illustrate those relationships without claiming a current national trade total or travel schedule.

Brief check: Can the same shipment be one country’s export and another’s import?
Listen for: Yes. The terms depend on the country’s point of view.

Trade connects places

On screen: Goods move between producers and buyers. / Information and payments also connect them.

Trade involves the exchange of goods and services between people or places. A product can connect farms, factories, transport companies, shops and customers in different locations. Trace one simple chain and identify what moves at each connection. Goods move physically, while orders, information and payments may move through different channels. A product’s final shop is not necessarily where its materials came from. Geography investigates these spatial connections and their effects on places rather than treating a product as appearing fully made on a shelf.

Brief check: Does the place where an item is sold necessarily make its materials?
Listen for: No. Materials and production can come from other places.

Production has several stages

On screen: Raw material → processing → manufacture → sale. / Each stage can depend on an earlier one.

Use a familiar garment to illustrate production. Cotton can be grown, processed into fibre and fabric, made into clothing, transported and sold. These stages may occur in different places. Explain why a factory needs inputs before producing goods and why shops need deliveries before selling stock. The sequence is a classroom model, not a claim that every garment follows an identical chain. Some businesses combine stages or use different materials. The important idea is dependence between activities through flows of materials and products.

Brief check: Which stage may wait if fabric delivery stops?
Listen for: The manufacturing stage that needs the fabric.

A broken link has immediate and later effects

On screen: First: the next stage lacks its input. / Later: other stages may be affected.

If a shipment of material is delayed, the first direct effect is on the stage waiting for that material. A factory may use stored stock temporarily, so production does not necessarily stop immediately. Later, fewer finished goods may reach shops. Trace the effects in order and state the conditions, such as how long stock lasts. Avoid claiming that every consumer is instantly affected by one delay. The network and its available reserves determine how the disruption spreads through time and across places.

Brief check: Why might the factory continue briefly after a delivery delay?
Listen for: It may have stored inputs available.

Alternatives involve trade-offs

On screen: Another route may keep goods moving. / It may add distance, time or cost.

A different port or supplier can restore a connection, but it may create new costs or delays. Compare the avoided disruption with the additional distance, price and environmental effects. Availability alone does not make the alternative best. A suitable recommendation identifies which link it repairs and what conditions still need checking. Distinguish classroom figures from real prices or service schedules. When a trade network changes, some places may gain business while others lose it, so a local benefit does not automatically describe every affected place.

Brief check: Does an available alternative necessarily have no disadvantages?
Listen for: No. It can add cost, time or other effects.

Build it together · Track goods, people and information separately

On screen: Track goods, people and information separately / A shipment leaving A and entering B is an export for A and an import for B.

A shipment leaving A and entering B is an export for A and an import for B. A message may travel without the goods moving yet. Label the arrow type and whose viewpoint defines the trade word.

The goods enter the UK; the same movement is an export for the sending country.

Teaching question: A UK shop receives goods from another country. From the UK viewpoint, these are what? Correct reasoning: Imports. Contrast this with: Exports. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: A UK shop receives goods from another country. From the UK viewpoint, these are what?
Listen for: Imports. The goods enter the UK; the same movement is an export for the sending country.

METHOD A shipment leaving A and entering B is an export for A and an import for B. A message may travel without the goods moving yet. Label the arrow type and whose viewpoint defines the trade word.

Label the arrow type and whose viewpoint defines the trade word. Explain why one choice fits and why the other does not.
