Watch a second example · 3.8

On screen: From the receiving country’s view, what are the same goods?

Fictional trade: apples move from Country A to Country B. Payment moves back. An order message travels online. A worker separately travels to visit relatives. A port then closes.

From the receiving country’s view, what are the same goods? An import into Country B. The movement has not changed, only the viewpoint.

Related steps in this same case: From the sending country’s view, what are the goods? An export from Country A. The viewpoint matters.

From the receiving country’s view, what are the same goods? An import into Country B. The movement has not changed, only the viewpoint.

Identify a flow of information and a flow of people. The order message is information; the worker’s journey is movement of people.

Now change one condition · 3.8

On screen: Does a port closure automatically stop online messages?

Fictional trade: apples move from Country A to Country B. Payment moves back. An order message travels online. A worker separately travels to visit relatives. A port then closes.

Does a port closure automatically stop online messages? No. Different flows can use different networks.

Related steps in this same case: Does a port closure automatically stop online messages? No. Different flows can use different networks.

What might a supplier need to change after the closure? Route, transport mode, timing or stock arrangements; check capacity and cost before choosing.

Complete a two-way explanation of the trade link. Country A sends apples; Country B receives them and sends payment. Information coordinates the exchange.

The key question is: A UK shop receives goods from another country. From the UK viewpoint, these are what? The correct idea is: Imports. The goods enter the UK; the same movement is an export for the sending country. Hear one or two brief answers, correct the specific misconception, and close with the accurate geographical explanation.

On screen: Would a longer delivery route be worth its extra cost in this case? What would influence your view? / Say: “I would choose … because …”

Context for this discussion: A UK shop receives fruit from abroad; tourists arrive; two classes exchange messages.

Relevant explanation: Incoming fruit is a UK import; it is an export for the sending country. Messages move information.

3–25 min · Explain and reconnect

Quality of life has several dimensions

On screen: Health, safety, housing and access matter. / Income is one part of the picture.

Quality of life concerns how people live and experience their surroundings. Income matters, but health services, housing, safety, environmental conditions and access to opportunities also matter. A wealthy area may still have a long journey to a clinic or polluted surroundings. Introduce several indicators before judging a place. Explain that indicators measure selected aspects rather than a complete human experience. People can also value the same features differently, so factual measurements and personal priorities should be kept distinguishable.

Brief check: Does income alone tell us everything about quality of life?
Listen for: No. Other conditions and access also matter.

Explain the trade-off

On screen: A proposal can have benefits and costs. / Use evidence for both sides.

A new service may improve one condition while weakening another. For example, a larger central clinic could offer more facilities but increase travel for remote residents. Explain each effect through its mechanism rather than labelling the proposal simply good or bad. Then identify what evidence could help compare the effects: travel times, service capacity and the needs of different users. An opinion about priorities is legitimate, but it should be distinguished from a measurable claim about what the proposal will do.

Brief check: What should a balanced recommendation include?
Listen for: Supported benefits, supported costs and the needs of affected groups.

See the method · Update only the conclusions the new evidence supports

On screen: Update only the conclusions the new evidence supports / If clinic travel drops from 40 to 15 minutes, access improves by 25 minutes.

If clinic travel drops from 40 to 15 minutes, access improves by 25 minutes. It does not follow that housing, air quality or every resident's health improved. Change the specific claim and retain the unknowns.

One improved indicator does not establish every outcome for every person.

Teaching question: A new clinic cuts average travel time. What can be concluded directly? Correct reasoning: Average access time improved. Contrast this with: Every resident's quality of life is now best. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. London is the UK’s capital

On screen: London is in south-east England, on the River Thames. / Its capital role includes national government.

London is the United Kingdom’s capital and lies in south-east England on the River Thames. Locate it within England, then within the UK, before discussing its functions. Parliament meets at Westminster, giving a concrete example of the city’s national government role. London is also a place where people live, work, study and visit. A capital is not defined as a place where everyone in the country lives or as the only city with important activities. Its role connects a particular location to national decision-making. Link the map location to the river and transport connections, while avoiding the assumption that river location alone completely explains the history or importance of the city.

Brief check: Does being the capital mean all UK residents live there?
Listen for: No. It describes the city’s national role.

Capacity must match demand over time

On screen: Capacity per trip is not capacity per hour. / Frequency tells us how often the service runs.

A bus carrying thirty passengers can move thirty per trip, but hourly capacity depends on how many trips it makes. If sixty people need to travel each hour, one trip may be insufficient while two full trips could match the stated demand. Real planning also considers timing, direction and accessibility. Distinguish the size of the vehicle from service frequency. This explains why drawing an alternative bus route does not establish that it can carry everyone displaced by a rail or bridge disruption.

Brief check: What must we know besides seats per bus?
Listen for: The frequency and timing of trips compared with demand.

The first names the movement and its function.

Teaching question: Which arrow label explains a city connection? Correct reasoning: Bus route carries visitors from station to museum. Contrast this with: Station and museum are both words. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

The UK connects to the wider world

On screen: Imports enter; exports leave. / Travel and communication create other links.

An import enters a country from elsewhere; an export is sent to another country. Describe the direction from the country’s point of view. Fruit brought into a UK shop is an import for the UK, while the exporting place describes the same connection differently. Goods are only one kind of international link. People travel for visits, work, study or other purposes, and messages connect places without moving a person or parcel along the same physical route. Trace goods, people and information using separate arrows. The UK’s relationship with other countries therefore includes trade, tourism and communication rather than one single supply chain. Our invented examples illustrate those relationships without claiming a current national trade total or travel schedule.

Brief check: Can the same shipment be one country’s export and another’s import?
Listen for: Yes. The terms depend on the country’s point of view.

Alternatives involve trade-offs

On screen: Another route may keep goods moving. / It may add distance, time or cost.

A different port or supplier can restore a connection, but it may create new costs or delays. Compare the avoided disruption with the additional distance, price and environmental effects. Availability alone does not make the alternative best. A suitable recommendation identifies which link it repairs and what conditions still need checking. Distinguish classroom figures from real prices or service schedules. When a trade network changes, some places may gain business while others lose it, so a local benefit does not automatically describe every affected place.

Brief check: Does an available alternative necessarily have no disadvantages?
Listen for: No. It can add cost, time or other effects.

See the method · Choose a response to a broken connection

On screen: Choose a response to a broken connection / If a port closes, a new sea route, stored supplies or reduced demand may help in different ways.

If a port closes, a new sea route, stored supplies or reduced demand may help in different ways. Identify what is interrupted first. A working internet connection cannot physically replace a delayed food shipment.

Information can coordinate action, but goods need a usable physical route.

Teaching question: Which response directly moves goods around a closed port? Correct reasoning: Use another available port and compare added cost. Contrast this with: Send the shop more emails only. London is the UK’s capital

On screen: London is in south-east England, on the River Thames. / Its capital role includes national government.

London is the United Kingdom’s capital and lies in south-east England on the River Thames. Locate it within England, then within the UK, before discussing its functions. Parliament meets at Westminster, giving a concrete example of the city’s national government role. London is also a place where people live, work, study and visit. A capital is not defined as a place where everyone in the country lives or as the only city with important activities. Its role connects a particular location to national decision-making. Link the map location to the river and transport connections, while avoiding the assumption that river location alone completely explains the history or importance of the city.

Brief check: Does being the capital mean all UK residents live there?
Listen for: No. It describes the city’s national role.

Capacity must match demand over time

On screen: Capacity per trip is not capacity per hour. / Frequency tells us how often the service runs.

A bus carrying thirty passengers can move thirty per trip, but hourly capacity depends on how many trips it makes. If sixty people need to travel each hour, one trip may be insufficient while two full trips could match the stated demand. Real planning also considers timing, direction and accessibility. Distinguish the size of the vehicle from service frequency. This explains why drawing an alternative bus route does not establish that it can carry everyone displaced by a rail or bridge disruption.

Brief check: What must we know besides seats per bus?
Listen for: The frequency and timing of trips compared with demand.

The UK connects to the wider world

On screen: Imports enter; exports leave. / Travel and communication create other links.

An import enters a country from elsewhere; an export is sent to another country. Describe the direction from the country’s point of view. Fruit brought into a UK shop is an import for the UK, while the exporting place describes the same connection differently. Goods are only one kind of international link. People travel for visits, work, study or other purposes, and messages connect places without moving a person or parcel along the same physical route. Trace goods, people and information using separate arrows. The UK’s relationship with other countries therefore includes trade, tourism and communication rather than one single supply chain. Our invented examples illustrate those relationships without claiming a current national trade total or travel schedule.

Brief check: Can the same shipment be one country’s export and another’s import?
Listen for: Yes. The terms depend on the country’s point of view.

Alternatives involve trade-offs

On screen: Another route may keep goods moving. / It may add distance, time or cost.

A different port or supplier can restore a connection, but it may create new costs or delays. Compare the avoided disruption with the additional distance, price and environmental effects. Availability alone does not make the alternative best. A suitable recommendation identifies which link it repairs and what conditions still need checking. Distinguish classroom figures from real prices or service schedules. When a trade network changes, some places may gain business while others lose it, so a local benefit does not automatically describe every affected place.

Brief check: Does an available alternative necessarily have no disadvantages?
Listen for: No. It can add cost, time or other effects.

3–25 min · Explain and reconnect

Quality of life has several dimensions

On screen: Health, safety, housing and access matter. / Income is one part of the picture.

Quality of life concerns how people live and experience their surroundings. Income matters, but health services, housing, safety, environmental conditions and access to opportunities also matter. A wealthy area may still have a long journey to a clinic or polluted surroundings. Introduce several indicators before judging a place. Explain that indicators measure selected aspects rather than a complete human experience. People can also value the same features differently, so factual measurements and personal priorities should be kept distinguishable.

Brief check: Does income alone tell us everything about quality of life?
Listen for: No. Other conditions and access also matter.

Explain the trade-off

On screen: A proposal can have benefits and costs. / Use evidence for both sides.

A new service may improve one condition while weakening another. For example, a larger central clinic could offer more facilities but increase travel for remote residents. Explain each effect through its mechanism rather than labelling the proposal simply good or bad. Then identify what evidence could help compare the effects: travel times, service capacity and the needs of different users. An opinion about priorities is legitimate, but it should be distinguished from a measurable claim about what the proposal will do.

Brief check: What should a balanced recommendation include?
Listen for: Supported benefits, supported costs and the needs of affected groups.

The UK connects to the wider world

On screen: Imports enter; exports leave. / Travel and communication create other links.

An import enters a country from elsewhere; an export is sent to another country. Describe the direction from the country’s point of view. Fruit brought into a UK shop is an import for the UK, while the exporting place describes the same connection differently. Goods are only one kind of international link. People travel for visits, work, study or other purposes, and messages connect places without moving a person or parcel along the same physical route. Trace goods, people and information using separate arrows. The UK’s relationship with other countries therefore includes trade, tourism and communication rather than one single supply chain. Our invented examples illustrate those relationships without claiming a current national trade total or travel schedule.

Brief check: Can the same shipment be one country’s export and another’s import?
Listen for: Yes. The terms depend on the country’s point of view.

Alternatives involve trade-offs

On screen: Another route may keep goods moving. / It may add distance, time or cost.

A different port or supplier can restore a connection, but it may create new costs or delays. Compare the avoided disruption with the additional distance, price and environmental effects. Availability alone does not make the alternative best. A suitable recommendation identifies which link it repairs and what conditions still need checking. Distinguish classroom figures from real prices or service schedules. When a trade network changes, some places may gain business while others lose it, so a local benefit does not automatically describe every affected place.

Brief check: Does an available alternative necessarily have no disadvantages?
Listen for: No. It can add cost, time or other effects.

Landscape evidence file

7B · Week 18 · Lesson 1 · sections 4.1

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 4.1

On screen: Past cold periods brought extensive ice to parts of Britain. / Build a past-ice explanation from several clues

Today's key idea: Britain has a glacial history. Past ice can leave landforms and deposits long after it melts. Evidence must be tied to the place being investigated. A broad valley, scratches and deposits support an ice interpretation, but do not establish a precise date by themselves. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Was the ice extent identical everywhere throughout Britain’s history?
Listen for: No. Extent and timing varied.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Britain has a glacial history

On screen: Past cold periods brought extensive ice to parts of Britain. / The present landscape contains evidence of those changes.

Britain experienced repeated periods of glaciation during the Quaternary, with extensive ice affecting much of northern and central Britain at different times. The school-plan question about twenty thousand years ago introduces a landscape very different from today’s. Do not treat Britain as entirely covered by an identical glacier at every stage: extent and timing varied. The important introductory connection is between colder past conditions, moving ice and surviving landforms or deposits. Many valleys now occupied by rivers were modified by earlier ice. To reconstruct a particular place at a particular date, we need dated and mapped geological evidence rather than only a modern photograph. This gives the past-ice investigation a regional context before pupils examine individual clues.

Brief check: Was the ice extent identical everywhere throughout Britain’s history?
Listen for: No. Extent and timing varied.

Ice can change a landscape

On screen: Moving ice can erode and transport material. / Landforms can remain after the ice melts.

A glacier is moving land ice, and it can change the ground beneath and around it. Its erosion can alter valley shapes, while transported material can be deposited as the ice melts. The ice does not have to remain for all traces of its activity to disappear. Introduce the difference between an active process and a landform left behind. A modern valley photograph may contain clues to past ice, but identifying that history requires more than assuming every mountain valley was made entirely by glaciers.

Brief check: Can a landform remain after the glacier disappears?
Listen for: Yes. The resulting shape or deposits can remain.

Use several clues for past ice

On screen: Valley shape is one clue. / Deposits and mapped evidence add information.

A broad valley with steep sides may be consistent with glacial erosion, but one view does not provide a complete history. Deposits, rock surfaces, surrounding landforms and geological mapping can add independent evidence. Explain how several compatible clues support a claim more strongly than a single vague resemblance. A deposit also needs interpretation: not all sediment in a glaciated area was dropped directly by ice. We should identify what each source shows and which part of the historical explanation it supports.

Brief check: Why use more than one clue?
Listen for: Different evidence can test and strengthen the proposed explanation.

Separate appearance from history

On screen: “The valley has steep sides” is an observation. / “Ice eroded it” is a historical explanation.

Point to the visible shape and describe it before offering a cause. The photograph can show a broad floor and steep sides, but it cannot directly show an event that happened before the photograph was taken. Historical explanation connects the appearance to processes using further evidence. Keep the two sentence types distinct so pupils understand why an accurate description is valuable without being complete proof of a cause. A confident explanation should be proportional to the sources available, not to how familiar the picture seems.

Brief check: Can a photograph directly show when a valley was eroded?
Listen for: Not by its shape alone.

Time and change need evidence

On screen: Ask when ice was present. / Ask what changed before and after it.

To reconstruct a landscape’s history, arrange evidence in time as well as space. A dated deposit can help establish when material was laid down. Earlier and later sources can show changes in ice extent or valley conditions. Explain that a landform may reflect several processes acting at different times. A river can occupy a valley previously modified by ice. The present process and the earlier process therefore need not be competing explanations of exactly the same stage. Specify the part of the history being claimed.

Brief check: Can a river now flow through a valley previously modified by ice?
Listen for: Yes. Processes can act at different times.

Build it together · Build a past-ice explanation from several clues

On screen: Build a past-ice explanation from several clues / A broad valley is an observation; past glacial erosion is an interpretation.

A broad valley is an observation; past glacial erosion is an interpretation. Scratched rock, transported debris and dated deposits can strengthen the interpretation together. No single shape gives an exact age by itself.

Multiple relevant sources can support an interpretation; age needs suitable dating evidence.

Teaching question: Which addition strengthens a past-ice investigation? Correct reasoning: Mapped striations and deposits considered with valley shape. Contrast this with: A precise ice age guessed from one photograph. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: Which addition strengthens a past-ice investigation?
Listen for: Mapped striations and deposits considered with valley shape. Multiple relevant sources can support an interpretation; age needs suitable dating evidence.

A modern valley photograph may contain clues to past ice, but identifying that history requires more than assuming every mountain valley was made entirely by glaciers.

Brief check: Can a landform remain after the glacier disappears?
Listen for: Yes. The resulting shape or deposits can remain.

Use several clues for past ice

On screen: Valley shape is one clue. / Deposits and mapped evidence add information.

A broad valley with steep sides may be consistent with glacial erosion, but one view does not provide a complete history. Deposits, rock surfaces, surrounding landforms and geological mapping can add independent evidence. Explain how several compatible clues support a claim more strongly than a single vague resemblance. A deposit also needs interpretation: not all sediment in a glaciated area was dropped directly by ice. We should identify what each source shows and which part of the historical explanation it supports.

Brief check: Why use more than one clue?
Listen for: Different evidence can test and strengthen the proposed explanation.

Separate appearance from history

On screen: “The valley has steep sides” is an observation. / “Ice eroded it” is a historical explanation.

Point to the visible shape and describe it before offering a cause. The photograph can show a broad floor and steep sides, but it cannot directly show an event that happened before the photograph was taken. Historical explanation connects the appearance to processes using further evidence. Keep the two sentence types distinct so pupils understand why an accurate description is valuable without being complete proof of a cause. A confident explanation should be proportional to the sources available, not to how familiar the picture seems.

Brief check: Can a photograph directly show when a valley was eroded?
Listen for: Not by its shape alone.

Time and change need evidence

On screen: Ask when ice was present. / Ask what changed before and after it.

To reconstruct a landscape’s history, arrange evidence in time as well as space. A dated deposit can help establish when material was laid down. Earlier and later sources can show changes in ice extent or valley conditions. Explain that a landform may reflect several processes acting at different times. A river can occupy a valley previously modified by ice. The present process and the earlier process therefore need not be competing explanations of exactly the same stage. Specify the part of the history being claimed.

Brief check: Can a river now flow through a valley previously modified by ice?
Listen for: Yes. Processes can act at different times.

Build it together · Match the strength of a claim to its evidence

On screen: Match the strength of a claim to its evidence / “Ice covered this place exactly 12,000 years ago” includes extent and date.

“Ice covered this place exactly 12,000 years ago” includes extent and date. A photograph of a valley shape does not establish either precisely. Ask for deposit mapping, dating and evidence of ice movement.

Qualify an interpretation when the evidence does not establish timing or extent.

Teaching question: Which revision is justified by a valley photograph alone? Correct reasoning: The shape is consistent with past glacial erosion; more evidence is needed. Contrast this with: The photo proves the exact date the glacier vanished. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: Which revision is justified by a valley photograph alone?
Listen for: The shape is consistent with past glacial erosion; more evidence is needed. Qualify an interpretation when the evidence does not establish timing or extent.

Keep the glacier in balance

7B · Week 19 · Lesson 1 · sections 4.2

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 4.2

On screen: They need conditions in which snow and ice can remain. / Calculate glacier mass balance

Today's key idea: Where can glaciers persist?. Snow persists and compacts into glacier ice where accumulation exceeds losses over time. Ice flows under gravity. Mass balance is accumulation minus loss. A retreating snout does not mean the ice flows uphill. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Why can glaciers exist in some high mountains outside polar regions?
Listen for: High elevation can provide cold conditions, alongside sufficient snow accumulation.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Where can glaciers persist?

On screen: They need conditions in which snow and ice can remain. / They occur in polar regions and some high mountains.

Glaciers occur where conditions allow enough snow and ice to persist and accumulate. Polar regions provide examples, as do high mountain areas in several parts of the world. A high mountain near the Equator can have colder conditions than nearby low land, so latitude alone is insufficient to explain every glacier location. Temperature, elevation and snowfall all matter. A cold dry place may receive little snow, while a place with large snowfall may support ice under a different balance of conditions. Start by locating polar regions and mountain examples on the world view, then explain the accumulation and loss relationship. The existence of ice does not make every frozen lake a glacier: glacier ice also moves under its own weight.

Brief check: Why can glaciers exist in some high mountains outside polar regions?
Listen for: High elevation can provide cold conditions, alongside sufficient snow accumulation.

Snow can become glacier ice

On screen: Snow accumulates and is compressed. / A glacier moves under its own weight.

Where snow persists and accumulates, it can become compacted into denser ice over time. A glacier forms and moves under its own weight. It is not simply any patch of snow that lasts for a few days. Explain the distinction between stored ice and its movement. Ice can flow slowly even when the glacier’s front appears nearly stationary. The front, called the snout or terminus, is a boundary whose position depends on both ice arriving and ice being lost near it.

Brief check: Is a stationary-looking front proof that no ice moves?
Listen for: No. Flow and front position are different.

Accumulation and ablation

On screen: Accumulation adds snow or ice. / Ablation removes glacier mass.

Accumulation adds mass, commonly through snowfall. Ablation removes mass through processes such as melting, sublimation or ice breaking away in relevant settings. In the classroom model we simplify these processes to additions and losses. Make that simplification explicit before using tokens or blocks. The glacier can gain or lose stored mass depending on the balance over a stated period. Its actual response also depends on where the changes happen and how ice flows, so a simple total is useful without representing every physical detail.

Brief check: What does accumulation do to glacier mass?
Listen for: It adds mass.

Calculate a simplified balance

On screen: Balance = additions − losses. / A negative result means net loss in this model.

Suppose the model gains nine units and loses six over the same period. Nine minus six is three units of net gain. Reverse the values and the balance becomes negative three. State the units and period, then explain the sign rather than asking pupils only to perform subtraction. A zero balance means the stated additions and losses are equal, not that all processes stop. Ice can continue entering and leaving while the total remains unchanged. This connects a calculation to the process it represents.

Brief check: Does a zero balance mean no ice is added or lost?
Listen for: No. Equal additions and losses can occur.

Movement and retreat can coexist

On screen: Ice can flow forwards. / The snout can retreat when loss exceeds supply there.

At the front, compare the arrival of ice with the rate at which it is removed. If more is lost than supplied, the boundary can move backwards even while ice flows towards it. Use a moving conveyor with an end being removed as an analogy, then identify its limits: real glaciers involve complex flow and changing geometry. Avoid saying that glacier retreat is ice flowing uphill. Retreat describes the boundary’s position, while flow describes the motion of the ice itself. A simple annual balance does not predict an exact retreat distance.

Brief check: Can a glacier retreat while ice still flows towards its front?
Listen for: Yes. Loss at the front can exceed incoming supply.

Build it together · Calculate glacier mass balance

On screen: Calculate glacier mass balance / If additions are 8 units and losses 5, the store gains 3.

If additions are 8 units and losses 5, the store gains 3. If the next year adds 4 and loses 6, it loses 2; the two-year net gain is 1. Balance is additions minus losses, not their sum.

Losses exceed additions by 3, reducing the ice store.

Teaching question: Additions are 6 units and losses 9. What is the balance? Correct reasoning: -3 units. Contrast this with: 15 units. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: Additions are 6 units and losses 9. What is the balance?
Listen for: -3 units. Losses exceed additions by 3, reducing the ice store.

MODEL EXPLANATION +3 then −3; net zero over two years. Real length responses can lag behind mass changes.

METHOD If additions are 8 units and losses 5, the store gains 3. If the next year adds 4 and loses 6, it loses 2; the two-year net gain is 1. Balance is additions minus losses, not their sum.

7B · Week 20 · Lesson 1 · sections 4.3

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 4.3

On screen: Weathering breaks rock down in place. / Distinguish plucking, transport and abrasion

Today's key idea: Erosion differs from weathering. Plucking removes rock blocks; abrasion scrapes the bed with debris carried by moving ice; transport moves that debris. Use a process chain: moving ice and debris → action on rock → visible result. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Which term involves removing material?
Listen for: Erosion.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Erosion differs from weathering

On screen: Weathering breaks rock down in place. / Erosion removes and transports material.

Weathering breaks rock down where it lies. Erosion includes removal by an agent such as moving ice or water. A glacier can pick up material already loosened by weathering and move it to another location. Distinguish the terms using one rock at the valley side: breaking it into pieces is not the same as carrying those pieces away. In an actual landscape, the processes can interact. Keeping their roles clear helps pupils build an explanation of change rather than treating every kind of rock damage as one identical action.

Brief check: Which term involves removing material?
Listen for: Erosion.

Plucking removes rock fragments

On screen: Ice can grip loosened rock. / Movement can pull fragments away.

Plucking is the removal of rock fragments by moving glacier ice. Water can enter cracks and freezing conditions can help loosen rock, while ice can become attached to parts of the bed. As the glacier moves, fragments may be pulled away. Use the diagram to show the original crack, the removed fragment and its new position. This is a simplified account: conditions beneath a glacier vary. The key distinction is removal of pieces rather than merely scratching the surface. Those pieces can then become tools for further erosion.

Brief check: What does plucking remove?
Listen for: Fragments of rock from the bed or sides.

Abrasion wears the surface

On screen: Rock carried by ice can scrape the bed. / Friction can scratch and smooth rock.

Abrasion occurs when debris carried by the glacier rubs or scrapes the ground. Compare it with sandpaper wearing a surface: the particles do the scraping as the moving material presses them against the rock. Glacial scratches can provide evidence of past motion, but their interpretation requires an appropriate source and context. Explain how plucking can supply fragments that later contribute to abrasion. The two processes are connected without being the same action. A classroom scraper illustrates friction but does not reproduce the full glacier system.

Brief check: How does abrasion differ from plucking?
Listen for: Abrasion wears or scratches surfaces; plucking removes fragments.

A model must control the comparison

On screen: Change one factor at a time. / Keep force and material comparable.

If we compare a rough and smooth scraper but push the rough one much harder, we cannot isolate roughness as the explanation for different wear. Force changed too. Explain a fair comparison using the same surface, movement and force while changing the feature being tested. The model then supports a limited statement about that setup. It cannot establish the exact erosion rate of a real glacier. Useful models clarify a mechanism, and their limitations tell us which extra processes and conditions are missing.

Brief check: Can roughness alone explain a result if force also changed?
Listen for: No. The comparison changed more than one factor.

Build it together · Distinguish plucking, transport and abrasion

On screen: Distinguish plucking, transport and abrasion / Plucking removes blocks loosened from bedrock; transport carries debris; abrasion occurs when debris held by moving ice scrapes the bed.

Plucking removes blocks loosened from bedrock; transport carries debris; abrasion occurs when debris held by moving ice scrapes the bed. Label each action separately so “erosion” does not hide the mechanism.

Moving debris can wear and scratch rock surfaces.

Teaching question: Which action best represents abrasion? Correct reasoning: Rock fragments carried in ice scrape bedrock. Contrast this with: A glacier simply holds still without contact. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: Which action best represents abrasion?
Listen for: Rock fragments carried in ice scrape bedrock. Moving debris can wear and scratch rock surfaces.

On screen: What happens when ice melts and releases the debris?

A fictional glacier carries sharp rock fragments at its base. The fragments scrape the bed. Elsewhere, ice removes a loosened block.

What happens when ice melts and releases the debris? Deposition: the carried material is left behind.

7B · Week 21 · Lesson 1 · sections 4.4

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 4.4

On screen: A tributary valley can meet a deeper main trough. / Explain widening and deepening in cross-section

Today's key idea: Hanging valleys show different erosion levels. A glacial trough has a broad floor and steep sides compared with a typical river-cut V-shaped valley. Moving ice can erode both sides and floor. A cross-section shows a slice across, not a route along the valley. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Why can the tributary valley floor lie above the main floor?
Listen for: The main glacier may have eroded its valley more deeply.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Hanging valleys show different erosion levels

On screen: A tributary valley can meet a deeper main trough. / Its floor may remain above the main valley floor.

A smaller tributary glacier may erode less deeply than a larger glacier in the main valley. After the ice disappears, the tributary valley floor can lie above the deeper main trough. This is called a hanging valley. Trace the two floors and their height difference. A stream may drop from the higher tributary towards the lower main floor, sometimes creating a waterfall. The explanation concerns different amounts of erosion in connected valleys; it is not a valley floating without support. Use the cross-section or a suitable diagram to show the relationship clearly before introducing the name. The landform joins local shapes to the wider glacier system that once occupied the valleys.

Brief check: Why can the tributary valley floor lie above the main floor?
Listen for: The main glacier may have eroded its valley more deeply.

Truncated spurs mark altered valley sides

On screen: Ridges can project into an earlier valley. / Glacial erosion can cut back their ends.

A spur is a ridge projecting from a valley side. A river valley may wind around interlocking spurs, while a large glacier moving through the valley can erode their projecting ends. The cut-back faces are called truncated spurs. Show a plan view with projecting ridges before the altered trough. Explain why this landform needs a different view from a simple profile across the floor. It helps pupils connect three-dimensional landscape features rather than treating every glacial feature as the same letter-shaped cross-section. In a real landscape, suitable evidence is needed to identify the shape and its history; the schematic clarifies the proposed mechanism.

Brief check: What part of the spur is described as truncated?
Listen for: Its projecting end has been cut back.

A valley cross-section looks across

On screen: Compare the floor and both sides. / The viewing direction matters.

A cross-section shows the shape across a valley rather than along its length. Mark one side, the floor and the other side. A photograph looking down the valley may not reveal that profile clearly, so source choice matters. A river and glacier can both occupy a valley without producing the same typical cross-section. Begin with description: is the floor narrow or broad, and how do the sides rise? Then connect the form to the processes that may have modified it, using suitable evidence.

Brief check: Which view best tests a cross-section claim?
Listen for: A view or profile across the valley.

River valleys are often V-shaped

On screen: River erosion cuts into the valley floor. / Slope processes affect the sides.

Many upper river valleys have narrow floors and sloping sides, giving a V-shaped cross-section. Downward river erosion and material moving from the sides both contribute to the form. Explain that the letter is a simplified description, not an exact geometry found everywhere. Other factors such as rock, structure and past processes affect actual valleys. Point to the narrow channel and the slopes so pupils understand what the label describes. A V shape is a useful pattern for comparison rather than proof that one agent explains the entire history.

Brief check: What part of a typical V-shaped profile is narrow?
Listen for: The valley floor.

Glaciers widen and deepen valleys

On screen: Ice occupies much of the valley. / Erosion can make a broad trough.

A valley glacier can occupy a large part of a valley rather than being confined to a narrow water channel. Erosion at the bed and sides can deepen and widen the valley, producing a glacial trough with a broad floor and steep sides. The common U-shaped label summarises that cross-section. Trace the contact areas before showing the changed profile. Do not say ice merely sits in the valley and leaves the shape unchanged. The form results from interaction between moving ice, carried debris and the rock it encounters.

Brief check: Why can ice affect more of the valley profile than a narrow channel?
Listen for: A glacier can occupy and erode a much broader part of the valley.

Describe the form before claiming the cause

On screen: Broad floor and steep sides describe shape. / Further evidence supports the glacial history.

A pupil can correctly describe a broad floor without yet proving its origin. Link the description to a process explanation, then identify evidence that would support past glacier activity. Compare a suitable cross-profile with a view along the floor and explain why one source answers the shape question more directly. Real valleys can have complex histories and later river changes. A useful answer states the form observed, the proposed process and the evidence available, instead of using the word glacier as a substitute for explanation.

Brief check: Does every broad valley photograph prove a complete glacial history?
Listen for: No. Use appropriate additional evidence.

Build it together · Explain widening and deepening in cross-section

On screen: Explain widening and deepening in cross-section / Draw the valley as if sliced across.

Draw the valley as if sliced across. River erosion can form a narrow V; glacial erosion can widen the floor and steepen sides into a trough. Arrows should point at the surfaces removed, not imply ice deposits the valley.

Cross-section displays floor width and side slopes directly.

Teaching question: Which view best shows a valley's U-shaped cross-section? Correct reasoning: A slice across the valley. Contrast this with: Only a line following the river from above. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: Which view best shows a valley's U-shaped cross-section?
Listen for: A slice across the valley. Cross-section displays floor width and side slopes directly.

A smaller tributary glacier may erode less deeply than a larger glacier in the main valley. After the ice disappears, the tributary valley floor can lie above the deeper main trough. This is called a hanging valley. Trace the two floors and their height difference. A stream may drop from the higher tributary towards the lower main floor, sometimes creating a waterfall. The explanation concerns different amounts of erosion in connected valleys; it is not a valley floating without support. Use the cross-section or a suitable diagram to show the relationship clearly before introducing the name. The landform joins local shapes to the wider glacier system that once occupied the valleys.

Brief check: Why can the tributary valley floor lie above the main floor?
Listen for: The main glacier may have eroded its valley more deeply.

Truncated spurs mark altered valley sides

On screen: Ridges can project into an earlier valley. / Glacial erosion can cut back their ends.

A spur is a ridge projecting from a valley side. A river valley may wind around interlocking spurs, while a large glacier moving through the valley can erode their projecting ends. The cut-back faces are called truncated spurs. Show a plan view with projecting ridges before the altered trough. Explain why this landform needs a different view from a simple profile across the floor. It helps pupils connect three-dimensional landscape features rather than treating every glacial feature as the same letter-shaped cross-section. In a real landscape, suitable evidence is needed to identify the shape and its history; the schematic clarifies the proposed mechanism.

Brief check: What part of the spur is described as truncated?
Listen for: Its projecting end has been cut back.

A valley cross-section looks across

On screen: Compare the floor and both sides. / The viewing direction matters.

A cross-section shows the shape across a valley rather than along its length. Mark one side, the floor and the other side. A photograph looking down the valley may not reveal that profile clearly, so source choice matters. A river and glacier can both occupy a valley without producing the same typical cross-section. Begin with description: is the floor narrow or broad, and how do the sides rise? Then connect the form to the processes that may have modified it, using suitable evidence.

Brief check: Which view best tests a cross-section claim?
Listen for: A view or profile across the valley.

River valleys are often V-shaped

On screen: River erosion cuts into the valley floor. / Slope processes affect the sides.

Many upper river valleys have narrow floors and sloping sides, giving a V-shaped cross-section. Downward river erosion and material moving from the sides both contribute to the form. Explain that the letter is a simplified description, not an exact geometry found everywhere. Other factors such as rock, structure and past processes affect actual valleys. Point to the narrow channel and the slopes so pupils understand what the label describes. A V shape is a useful pattern for comparison rather than proof that one agent explains the entire history.

Brief check: What part of a typical V-shaped profile is narrow?
Listen for: The valley floor.

Glaciers widen and deepen valleys

On screen: Ice occupies much of the valley. / Erosion can make a broad trough.

A valley glacier can occupy a large part of a valley rather than being confined to a narrow water channel. Erosion at the bed and sides can deepen and widen the valley, producing a glacial trough with a broad floor and steep sides. The common U-shaped label summarises that cross-section. Trace the contact areas before showing the changed profile. Do not say ice merely sits in the valley and leaves the shape unchanged. The form results from interaction between moving ice, carried debris and the rock it encounters.

Brief check: Why can ice affect more of the valley profile than a narrow channel?
Listen for: A glacier can occupy and erode a much broader part of the valley.

Describe the form before claiming the cause

On screen: Broad floor and steep sides describe shape. / Further evidence supports the glacial history.

A pupil can correctly describe a broad floor without yet proving its origin. Link the description to a process explanation, then identify evidence that would support past glacier activity. Compare a suitable cross-profile with a view along the floor and explain why one source answers the shape question more directly. Real valleys can have complex histories and later river changes. A useful answer states the form observed, the proposed process and the evidence available, instead of using the word glacier as a substitute for explanation.

Brief check: Does every broad valley photograph prove a complete glacial history?
Listen for: No. Use appropriate additional evidence.

A plan view shows bends and route direction; a cross-section shows width and slopes. A river can curve in plan while lying inside a U-shaped valley. These descriptions are compatible because the viewing directions differ.

A valley's transverse profile is different from its route when viewed from above.

Teaching question: Does a curved river in plan disprove a U-shaped valley? Correct reasoning: No; plan shape and cross-section answer different questions. Contrast this with: Yes; every view must look like the letter U. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: Does a curved river in plan disprove a U-shaped valley?
Listen for: No; plan shape and cross-section answer different questions. A valley's transverse profile is different from its route when viewed from above.

7B · Week 22 · Lesson 1 · sections 4.5

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 4.5

On screen: A corrie is a bowl-like hollow. / Explain a corrie and the ridge between hollows

Today's key idea: A corrie is a mountain hollow. A corrie is a bowl-shaped glacial hollow; erosion can steepen its back wall and deepen its floor. An arête is a narrow ridge between eroded hollows or valleys. Shape results from erosion on different sides. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Is the corrie the ridge or the hollow?
Listen for: The hollow.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

A corrie is a mountain hollow

On screen: A corrie is a bowl-like hollow. / Ice can erode its bed and back wall.

A corrie, also called a cirque, is a bowl-like hollow in a mountain landscape. Snow can collect in a suitable hollow and develop into ice. Erosion can deepen the floor and steepen the back wall, while a rock lip may remain towards the entrance. Point to these parts separately so the word names a landform rather than any mountain lake. Water may occupy a corrie after the ice has gone, but a lake is not required for the hollow to be identified.

Brief check: Is the corrie the ridge or the hollow?
Listen for: The hollow.

An arête is a sharp ridge

On screen: Erosion acts on neighbouring hollows. / A narrow ridge can remain between them.

An arête is a narrow, sharp ridge. When neighbouring corries or glacial valleys erode towards a divide, the ridge between them can become sharper. Show two eroded hollows and trace the remaining high ground. The arête is the material left between the erosion areas, not the bowl itself. This explains why correct labels depend on the part of the landscape being named. Use a finger or pointer to distinguish hollow, wall and ridge before expecting pupils to recall the terminology.

Brief check: Which feature remains between neighbouring eroded hollows?
Listen for: An arête.

Several ridges can meet at a peak

On screen: Erosion can act on several sides. / A sharp peak may remain between them.

Where erosion works around a mountain from several directions, a sharply pointed peak can remain. The common term pyramidal peak describes this form. Compare it with an arête: one is a peak, the other a ridge. Trace each in the diagram and explain how they connect to surrounding hollows. A schematic makes the relationships easier to see but does not prove the complete origin of every real pointed mountain. Rock structure and other processes also affect actual shapes, so apply the terms using relevant landscape evidence.

Brief check: How is a peak different from a ridge?
Listen for: A peak is a summit; a ridge is an extended line of high ground.

Connect each name to the process

On screen: Corrie: hollow. Arête: ridge. / Peak: summit left between eroded areas.

Return to the whole mountain after teaching its parts. Point to one feature and describe its position relative to the others. Then explain which areas were eroded and which high ground remained. This prevents a list of unfamiliar words from replacing understanding. A good description locates the feature, while a good explanation connects it to erosion around it. If a pupil labels the hollow arête, correct the part of the landscape being named rather than merely repeating the vocabulary louder.

Brief check: Why is labelling a hollow “arête” incorrect?
Listen for: The arête is the ridge; the hollow is the corrie.

Build it together · Explain a corrie and the ridge between hollows

On screen: Explain a corrie and the ridge between hollows / A corrie is an armchair-like hollow shaped by glacial erosion, with a steep back wall.

A corrie is an armchair-like hollow shaped by glacial erosion, with a steep back wall. When neighbouring hollows erode back towards each other, a narrow ridge can remain between them: an arête.

The feature is the remaining ridge, not the hollow or a sediment pile.

Teaching question: What does an arête describe? Correct reasoning: A narrow ridge between eroded hollows or valleys. Contrast this with: A pile of river mud on flat ground. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: What does an arête describe?
Listen for: A narrow ridge between eroded hollows or valleys. The feature is the remaining ridge, not the hollow or a sediment pile.

What the ice leaves behind

7B · Week 23 · Lesson 1 · sections 4.6

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 4.6

On screen: An erratic differs from the local bedrock. / Explain deposition when ice loses its load

Today's key idea: Erratics link deposits to transport. When glacier ice melts it releases carried debris. Till commonly contains mixed, unsorted particle sizes. Moraines are accumulations of glacial debris; their positions can help interpret former ice margins. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: How does an erratic differ from local bedrock?
Listen for: It has been transported and is of a different rock type from the surrounding bedrock.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Erratics link deposits to transport

On screen: An erratic differs from the local bedrock. / Its rock type can help investigate where it came from.

A glacial erratic is a transported rock that differs from the local bedrock where it now lies. Its presence can prompt a question about movement from another source area. Compare the rock type with surrounding ground, then investigate a possible matching source and evidence of glacial transport. Difference alone should be interpreted in context rather than used as complete proof of every detail of a journey. An erratic connects the three stages of removal, transport and deposition: the rock began somewhere, moved and was left behind. It also differs from a moraine, which is an accumulation of debris rather than the name for one particular transported block.

Brief check: How does an erratic differ from local bedrock?
Listen for: It has been transported and is of a different rock type from the surrounding bedrock.

Glaciers transport debris

On screen: Material can travel on, within or beneath ice. / Transport differs from its original removal.

Glaciers can carry material in several positions: on the surface, within the ice or near the bed. Rock may enter from erosion beneath the glacier or from valley sides. Removal, transport and deposition are distinct stages. A fragment can be eroded in one place and deposited elsewhere after a period of movement. Trace one fragment through this sequence. Its final location therefore does not automatically show where it originated. This distinction helps explain why deposited material can provide clues about past glacier movement.

Brief check: Does a deposited fragment necessarily come from the place where it now lies?
Listen for: No. It may have been transported.

Deposition leaves material behind

On screen: Melting ice releases carried debris. / Direct glacial deposits can be poorly sorted.

When debris-bearing ice melts, its carried material can be left behind. Directly deposited glacial material, often called till, commonly contains a mixture of particle sizes rather than neatly separated layers. Explain why ice can carry fine and coarse material together. A simple mixed pile models that idea, but real deposits vary and need field evidence. Do not use poor sorting as the only possible clue or assume every mixed deposit is glacial. Interpret it alongside location, landforms and other geological information.

Brief check: What does “poorly sorted” mean here?
Listen for: Different particle sizes are mixed together.

Moraines mark accumulations of debris

On screen: Some lie along glacier sides. / Others form near the front or where ice streams meet.

A moraine is an accumulation of glacial debris. Lateral moraines lie along glacier sides. Where glacier streams join, debris from their adjacent margins can form a medial moraine. Accumulations near an end position include terminal or end moraines. Use location to distinguish the names instead of treating them as separate kinds of rock. A ridge of debris may help reconstruct a former ice margin, but interpreting its age and origin needs appropriate evidence. The visible position is the starting observation, not the entire historical conclusion.

Brief check: What helps distinguish lateral and end moraines?
Listen for: Their positions relative to the glacier.

Meltwater can sort sediment

On screen: Moving water carries different sizes differently. / Sorted layers may reflect meltwater deposition.

Meltwater flows away from ice and can transport and deposit sediment. Flowing water can sort particles because different sizes and densities settle under different conditions. A strongly layered, sorted deposit therefore raises a different interpretation from a simple direct release of mixed debris by melting ice. Location near a glacier does not mean every deposit was laid down directly by ice. Compare the mechanisms and ask which observations each predicts. The answer should match the deposit’s features and context rather than rely only on the region’s label.

Brief check: What alternative should we consider for sorted sediment near a glacier?
Listen for: Transport and deposition by meltwater.

Build it together · Explain deposition when ice loses its load

On screen: Explain deposition when ice loses its load / Ice can carry particles of many sizes together.

Ice can carry particles of many sizes together. As it melts, debris may be released as unsorted till; a moraine is an accumulation of glacial debris. Contrast deposition with the earlier removal and transport.

Direct deposition by ice need not sort particles like flowing meltwater can.

Teaching question: Why can a direct ice deposit contain mixed sizes? Correct reasoning: Ice can carry and release fine and coarse debris together. Contrast this with: Every particle must first become identical in size. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: Why can a direct ice deposit contain mixed sizes?
Listen for: Ice can carry and release fine and coarse debris together. Direct deposition by ice need not sort particles like flowing meltwater can.

A valley visitor plan

7B · Week 24 · Lesson 1 · sections 4.7

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 4.7

On screen: Broad floors and steep sides affect movement. / Connect landform, visitors and measurable pressure

Today's key idea: A glacial valley can become a visitor landscape. The Lake District includes glacial landscapes. Physical features can attract visitors and influence routes. Visitor management weighs access, erosion, livelihoods and landscape protection. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: How can steep sides affect visitor movement?
Listen for: They can limit suitable routes and access.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

A glacial valley can become a visitor landscape

On screen: Broad floors and steep sides affect movement. / The landform remains after ice retreats.

A glacial trough can provide striking scenery and routes through mountain country after its glacier disappears. A broad floor and steep sides affect where paths, roads and settlements can lie. Langdale in the Lake District provides a named example of a glacial valley landscape, while the visitor counts in our exercises are fictional. Separate the real place and landform from invented measurements. Explain how physical geography shapes opportunities and constraints for people rather than treating landscape and tourism as unrelated topics.

Brief check: How can steep sides affect visitor movement?
Listen for: They can limit suitable routes and access.

Visitors create benefits and pressures

On screen: Visitors can support local businesses. / Concentrated use can affect paths and habitats.

Visitors may support accommodation, shops, guiding and other local services. Repeated foot traffic can also wear paths, disturb sensitive areas and create waste or congestion. Explain the mechanism behind each effect. More people walking on a path can increase pressure, but visitor numbers alone do not establish its damage level. Surface, weather and maintenance matter too. A balanced account recognises benefits and costs without assuming that tourism is always either harmful or beneficial in every place and under every condition.

Brief check: Do visitor counts alone measure path damage?
Listen for: No. We need information about condition and other relevant factors.

A snapshot needs a context

On screen: Counts need a time and place. / Repeat counts before describing a general pattern.

Eighty visitors on one path and twenty on another describe the observation period in the source. They do not prove the first is always four times busier. Check whether counts cover equal times and comparable locations, then consider day, season and weather. Repeat observations to investigate variation. The same number of visitors can also affect different habitats differently. Use the figures to raise a management question while avoiding a conclusion that goes beyond what was measured. Geographical decisions join counts to the places in which they occur.

Brief check: What must be equal for a simple count comparison?
Listen for: The observation periods and counting rules should be comparable.

Management must consider sensitivity

On screen: A quiet path may still be fragile. / Compare access, habitat and maintenance.

Sending visitors from a crowded path to a quiet one may reduce pressure at the first location but create harm at the second. Low use does not establish unlimited capacity. Examine habitat sensitivity, route surface, accessibility and maintenance needs before recommending diversion. Measures might include repairing a surface, clearer signs, seasonal protection or directing use towards suitable routes. Each should be connected to the problem it addresses. Ask who benefits and what new pressure may be created, rather than selecting a measure because it sounds generally environmentally friendly.

Brief check: Should every spare visitor be sent to the quieter path?
Listen for: No. Check its sensitivity and capacity first.

Pressure and condition must both be measured over comparable observations.

Teaching question: Which pair best tests whether heavy use is affecting a path? Correct reasoning: Repeated visitor counts and path-condition measurements. Contrast this with: One attractive photograph only. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: Which pair best tests whether heavy use is affecting a path?
Listen for: Repeated visitor counts and path-condition measurements. Pressure and condition must both be measured over comparable observations.

A water-store budget

7B · Week 24 · Lesson 2 · sections 4.8

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 4.8

On screen: Snow and ice hold water over time. / Model a glacier as a changing water store

Today's key idea: Ice is a water store. Glaciers store freshwater and influence river flow, landscapes and livelihoods. Effects of change vary by season and place; short-term melt increases do not guarantee long-term supply. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Is river flow the same quantity as water stored in ice?
Listen for: No. One is a flow and the other a store.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Ice is a water store

On screen: Snow and ice hold water over time. / Melting releases water to other stores and flows.

A glacier stores water as ice. Snowfall can add to that store, while melting can release liquid water. A store is an amount held at a time; a flow is movement into or out of it. Show a storage box with incoming and outgoing arrows. This distinction helps us understand why a large river flow does not necessarily mean the ice store is growing. Water in the river may come from rainfall as well as melting. Follow each input separately before making a claim about the stored ice.

Brief check: Is river flow the same quantity as water stored in ice?
Listen for: No. One is a flow and the other a store.

Water can have several inputs

On screen: Rainfall can contribute to runoff. / Snowmelt and ice melt can also contribute.

A mountain river can receive rainfall runoff, snowmelt, glacier melt and other contributions. Their importance varies through time and between basins. In the classroom model, label the separate arrows rather than combining them into an unexplained total. A wet year may increase river flow even while glacier mass decreases. To explain an observed change, identify which inputs were measured and which were not. The question is not simply whether a glacier exists nearby, but how water reaches the river under the stated conditions.

Brief check: Can extra rainfall increase flow while stored ice falls?
Listen for: Yes. Several inputs can affect river flow.

Net loss can release stored water

On screen: Losses can exceed additions. / A high outflow does not prove a growing store.

Suppose a model receives eight units and releases twelve during the same period. It has used four units from storage, so its stored amount decreases. Write additions minus losses and connect the negative balance to the storage box. This illustrates the idea without predicting exact real discharge or future trends. Melting stored ice can temporarily contribute water even while reducing the remaining ice. An increase in outflow is therefore not automatically good evidence that the store is increasing or that the same flow can continue indefinitely.

Brief check: If outflow exceeds input, what happens to storage?
Listen for: It decreases by the difference in this simplified balance.

Water supply depends on timing

On screen: People need water when and where they use it. / Seasonal patterns matter as well as annual totals.

A yearly water total can conceal periods of shortage or high flow. Households, farming, hydropower and ecosystems may need water at different times. Explain why changes in snow and ice storage can alter the timing of release, not merely the total amount. A recommendation needs seasonal flow information and demand, while long-term predictions require more than one classroom calculation. Separate measured trends from a single unusual year. This connects the physical water system to human needs without pretending the simple diagram includes every management factor.

Brief check: Why is an annual total alone insufficient for supply planning?
Listen for: It can hide when water is available and when it is needed.

A store starting at 40 units, gaining 7 and losing 10, ends at 37. Separate stored water from water released this period. Model units illustrate a balance, not an actual glacier forecast.

50 + 4 - 9 = 45; losses leave the store.

Teaching question: Start 50, add 4, lose 9. What is the final store? Correct reasoning: 45 units. Contrast this with: 63 units. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Listen for: 45 units. 50 + 4 - 9 = 45; losses leave the store.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 5.1

On screen: Source: where the river begins. / Use river-network vocabulary correctly

Today's key idea: A river has a connected course. A river flows from its source through a drainage network towards its mouth. Tributaries join the main channel. The Thames flows through London towards the North Sea; a schematic explains a system, not exact geography. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Does downstream always mean towards the bottom of a map?
Listen for: No. Follow the river’s actual flow direction.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

A river has a connected course

On screen: Source: where the river begins. / Mouth: where it enters another water body.

A river carries water along a connected course from its source towards its mouth. The source is where the named river begins, while the mouth is where it enters another water body. Downstream means following the flow; upstream is towards the source against that direction. Trace the course before naming individual parts. A map may show bends and junctions, but page position alone does not define downstream. Water generally moves from higher towards lower elevation, so we must use the network and flow information rather than assume rivers always run towards the bottom of the page.

Brief check: Does downstream always mean towards the bottom of a map?
Listen for: No. Follow the river’s actual flow direction.

Tributaries join the main river

On screen: Tributary: a smaller river that joins another. / Confluence: the place where rivers meet.

A tributary contributes water to another river. The confluence is the junction where they meet. Trace one tributary into the main channel and then continue downstream. The water does not stop at the junction. This connectivity matters when explaining how rainfall, sediment or pollution from one part of the basin can affect another. The direction of movement matters: a pollutant introduced below a town does not automatically travel upstream to it in our simple flow model. Locate the entry point before tracing any claimed effect.

Brief check: What is a confluence?
Listen for: The junction where rivers meet.

A drainage basin collects water

On screen: The basin drains towards a river system. / A watershed divides neighbouring basins.

A drainage basin is the area from which water drains into a river system. Its boundary, often called a watershed or drainage divide in UK school geography, separates it from neighbouring basins. Trace water from a slope into a tributary and then the main river. Land use anywhere in the connected basin may influence water reaching the channel. The river line is therefore only part of the geographical system. Our schematic makes the network clear but does not give an exact surveyed basin boundary unless that information is supplied.

Brief check: Is the basin only the water inside the river channel?
Listen for: No. It includes the land draining towards the system.

Use a named river and a separate model

On screen: The Thames flows through London towards the North Sea. / A schematic explains connections, not exact bends.

The Thames has its source in the Cotswolds and flows through London towards its estuary and the North Sea. Locate the named places on an appropriate map. Then use the simple source-to-mouth schematic to explain tributaries and confluences. Keep its purpose clear: a straight arrow can show a connection without reproducing the river’s exact shape or distances. A named real river and a fictional exercise network can be used in the same lesson if pupils know which facts belong to which source.

Brief check: Does a simple source-to-mouth arrow show every real bend of the Thames?
Listen for: No. It is a schematic connection.

Build it together · Use river-network vocabulary correctly

On screen: Use river-network vocabulary correctly / A tributary joins the main river at a confluence.

A tributary joins the main river at a confluence. The source begins the river; the mouth is where it enters another water body. Follow the arrows downstream instead of treating every branching line as a river splitting.

A confluence is a junction; a watershed is a drainage divide.

Teaching question: Two streams join. What is the meeting point called? Correct reasoning: A confluence. Contrast this with: A watershed. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.
