7B · Week 25 · Lesson 2 · sections 5.2

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 5.2

On screen: Water can be stored in oceans, ice, soil and groundwater. / Explain water-cycle arrows as changes or movements

Today's key idea: Water moves between stores. Evaporation turns liquid water into vapour; cooling can cause condensation; precipitation returns water to land or sea. Water reaches channels through surface runoff and subsurface pathways; stores delay movement. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Is soil water a store or a transfer?
Listen for: A store.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Water moves between stores

On screen: Water can be stored in oceans, ice, soil and groundwater. / Processes move water between stores.

The water cycle describes water moving between places and changing state. Oceans, lakes, ice, soil and groundwater are stores. A store holds water; a process moves it or changes its form. Trace one possible route rather than suggesting that every drop follows the same circle at the same speed. Water can remain in different stores for very different times. A classroom diagram simplifies a large connected system, so its arrows should help explain specific transfers rather than become a sequence memorised without meaning.

Brief check: Is soil water a store or a transfer?
Listen for: A store.

Evaporation, condensation and precipitation

On screen: Evaporation: liquid becomes water vapour. / Condensation forms droplets; precipitation falls.

Energy can cause liquid water to become water vapour through evaporation. Vapour is a gas and is not the same as visible cloud droplets. When air cools sufficiently, condensation can form droplets or, under suitable conditions, ice particles. Precipitation includes water falling from clouds as rain, snow or other forms. Trace these processes with their correct state changes. Do not say clouds are simply invisible gas that falls unchanged. The explanation should connect energy, state and movement using accessible words before introducing the technical terms.

Brief check: Is visible cloud made only of invisible water vapour?
Listen for: No. Visible cloud contains droplets or ice particles.

Infiltration and runoff are different paths

On screen: Infiltration: water enters the ground. / Runoff: water flows over the surface.

When rain reaches land, some water may enter the soil through infiltration. Some may move across the surface as runoff. Vegetation can intercept rainfall, and stored water can later evaporate or move through the ground. The balance depends on rainfall and the condition of the surface and soil. Already saturated soil has less available storage, so further rain may produce more surface runoff. Point to the alternative arrows and explain why the same rainfall amount need not create the same rapid river response everywhere.

Brief check: What can saturation change during further rainfall?
Listen for: It can reduce additional storage and increase surface runoff.

The basin model has a boundary

On screen: A simple split can show runoff and infiltration. / Real basins include more stores and transfers.

Our interactive model divides a stated rainfall input into simplified pathways. Check that the parts add to the input within that model. Then identify what it leaves out: time delays, storage changes, evaporation and complex drainage routes may matter in a real basin. This is not a reason to reject the model; it tells us the question it can answer. It illustrates how changing a surface condition can change the split, but does not predict the exact discharge of a named river after a real storm.

Brief check: Does the classroom split predict every real river response?
Listen for: No. It omits important processes and timing.

Evaporation changes liquid to vapour using energy; condensation changes vapour to liquid droplets. Precipitation moves water down from the atmosphere. Give each arrow its own process name rather than calling every movement evaporation.

Condensation changes state; infiltration is water entering the ground.

Teaching question: Which process turns water vapour into liquid droplets? Correct reasoning: Condensation. Contrast this with: Infiltration. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Listen for: Condensation. Condensation changes state; infiltration is water entering the ground.

Ice is a water store

On screen: Snow and ice hold water over time. / Melting releases water to other stores and flows.

A glacier stores water as ice. Snowfall can add to that store, while melting can release liquid water. A store is an amount held at a time; a flow is movement into or out of it. Show a storage box with incoming and outgoing arrows. This distinction helps us understand why a large river flow does not necessarily mean the ice store is growing. Water in the river may come from rainfall as well as melting. Follow each input separately before making a claim about the stored ice.

Brief check: Is river flow the same quantity as water stored in ice?
Listen for: No. One is a flow and the other a store.

Water supply depends on timing

On screen: People need water when and where they use it. / Seasonal patterns matter as well as annual totals.

A yearly water total can conceal periods of shortage or high flow. Households, farming, hydropower and ecosystems may need water at different times. Explain why changes in snow and ice storage can alter the timing of release, not merely the total amount. A recommendation needs seasonal flow information and demand, while long-term predictions require more than one classroom calculation. Separate measured trends from a single unusual year. This connects the physical water system to human needs without pretending the simple diagram includes every management factor.

Brief check: Why is an annual total alone insufficient for supply planning?
Listen for: It can hide when water is available and when it is needed.

See the method · Compare short-term flow with long-term storage

On screen: Compare short-term flow with long-term storage / More melt may increase release now while reducing the stored ice available later.

More melt may increase release now while reducing the stored ice available later. A bank account analogy helps: a larger withdrawal today does not prove a larger future balance. Actual runoff also depends on precipitation and season.

A short-term flow increase does not establish a permanent supply increase.

Teaching question: Why is “more melt now means more water forever” weak? Correct reasoning: It ignores depletion of the ice store and other water inputs. Contrast this with: Water stores cannot ever change. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: Why is “more melt now means more water forever” weak?
Listen for: It ignores depletion of the ice store and other water inputs. A short-term flow increase does not establish a permanent supply increase.

A river has a connected course

On screen: Source: where the river begins. / Mouth: where it enters another water body.

A river carries water along a connected course from its source towards its mouth. The source is where the named river begins, while the mouth is where it enters another water body. Downstream means following the flow; upstream is towards the source against that direction. Trace the course before naming individual parts. A map may show bends and junctions, but page position alone does not define downstream. Water generally moves from higher towards lower elevation, so we must use the network and flow information rather than assume rivers always run towards the bottom of the page.

Brief check: Does downstream always mean towards the bottom of a map?
Listen for: No. Follow the river’s actual flow direction.

Use a named river and a separate model

On screen: The Thames flows through London towards the North Sea. / A schematic explains connections, not exact bends.

The Thames has its source in the Cotswolds and flows through London towards its estuary and the North Sea. Locate the named places on an appropriate map. Then use the simple source-to-mouth schematic to explain tributaries and confluences. Keep its purpose clear: a straight arrow can show a connection without reproducing the river’s exact shape or distances. A named real river and a fictional exercise network can be used in the same lesson if pupils know which facts belong to which source.

Brief check: Does a simple source-to-mouth arrow show every real bend of the Thames?
Listen for: No. It is a schematic connection.

A confluence is a junction; a watershed is a drainage divide.

Brief check: Two streams join. What is the meeting point called?
Listen for: A confluence. A confluence is a junction; a watershed is a drainage divide.

Water moves between stores

On screen: Water can be stored in oceans, ice, soil and groundwater. / Processes move water between stores.

The water cycle describes water moving between places and changing state. Oceans, lakes, ice, soil and groundwater are stores. A store holds water; a process moves it or changes its form. Trace one possible route rather than suggesting that every drop follows the same circle at the same speed. Water can remain in different stores for very different times. A classroom diagram simplifies a large connected system, so its arrows should help explain specific transfers rather than become a sequence memorised without meaning.

Brief check: Is soil water a store or a transfer?
Listen for: A store.

The basin model has a boundary

On screen: A simple split can show runoff and infiltration. / Real basins include more stores and transfers.

Our interactive model divides a stated rainfall input into simplified pathways. Check that the parts add to the input within that model. Then identify what it leaves out: time delays, storage changes, evaporation and complex drainage routes may matter in a real basin. This is not a reason to reject the model; it tells us the question it can answer. It illustrates how changing a surface condition can change the split, but does not predict the exact discharge of a named river after a real storm.

Brief check: Does the classroom split predict every real river response?
Listen for: No. It omits important processes and timing.

Different pathways and stores produce different travel times.

Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

3–25 min · Explain and reconnect

Ice is a water store

On screen: Snow and ice hold water over time. / Melting releases water to other stores and flows.

A glacier stores water as ice. Snowfall can add to that store, while melting can release liquid water. A store is an amount held at a time; a flow is movement into or out of it. Show a storage box with incoming and outgoing arrows. This distinction helps us understand why a large river flow does not necessarily mean the ice store is growing. Water in the river may come from rainfall as well as melting. Follow each input separately before making a claim about the stored ice.

Brief check: Is river flow the same quantity as water stored in ice?
Listen for: No. One is a flow and the other a store.

Water supply depends on timing

On screen: People need water when and where they use it. / Seasonal patterns matter as well as annual totals.

A yearly water total can conceal periods of shortage or high flow. Households, farming, hydropower and ecosystems may need water at different times. Explain why changes in snow and ice storage can alter the timing of release, not merely the total amount. A recommendation needs seasonal flow information and demand, while long-term predictions require more than one classroom calculation. Separate measured trends from a single unusual year. This connects the physical water system to human needs without pretending the simple diagram includes every management factor.

Brief check: Why is an annual total alone insufficient for supply planning?
Listen for: It can hide when water is available and when it is needed.

A river has a connected course

On screen: Source: where the river begins. / Mouth: where it enters another water body.

A river carries water along a connected course from its source towards its mouth. The source is where the named river begins, while the mouth is where it enters another water body. Downstream means following the flow; upstream is towards the source against that direction. Trace the course before naming individual parts. A map may show bends and junctions, but page position alone does not define downstream. Water generally moves from higher towards lower elevation, so we must use the network and flow information rather than assume rivers always run towards the bottom of the page.

Brief check: Does downstream always mean towards the bottom of a map?
Listen for: No. Follow the river’s actual flow direction.

Use a named river and a separate model

On screen: The Thames flows through London towards the North Sea. / A schematic explains connections, not exact bends.

The Thames has its source in the Cotswolds and flows through London towards its estuary and the North Sea. Locate the named places on an appropriate map. Then use the simple source-to-mouth schematic to explain tributaries and confluences. Keep its purpose clear: a straight arrow can show a connection without reproducing the river’s exact shape or distances. A named real river and a fictional exercise network can be used in the same lesson if pupils know which facts belong to which source.

Brief check: Does a simple source-to-mouth arrow show every real bend of the Thames?
Listen for: No. It is a schematic connection.

Build a drainage basin

7B · Week 29 · Lesson 1 · sections 5.3

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 5.3

On screen: Channel form and valley shape change along the river. / Draw a drainage divide from high ground

Today's key idea: Compare upper, middle and lower course. A drainage basin is the area drained by a river and its tributaries; a watershed separates neighbouring basins. A river profile often becomes gentler downstream, but local exceptions exist. Width, depth and discharge are different measurements. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Should a general downstream pattern replace checking the actual measurements?
Listen for: No. Use the model alongside the source evidence.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Compare upper, middle and lower course

On screen: Channel form and valley shape change along the river. / Tributaries and local conditions affect the pattern.

The upper course is nearer the source, while the lower course is nearer the mouth; the middle course lies between. In many school examples, the upper valley is narrower and the channel smaller, while tributaries add water downstream and the lower channel becomes wider and deeper. The valley floor may also broaden. Treat these as patterns to investigate rather than absolute rules at every point. Rock, local slope, water inputs and human alterations can produce variation. Describe the actual source evidence before applying a general model. Course position provides a geographical framework for comparing channel measurements; width, depth and discharge then help explain what differs and why.

Brief check: Should a general downstream pattern replace checking the actual measurements?
Listen for: No. Use the model alongside the source evidence.

A channel has width, depth and velocity

On screen: Width and depth describe channel size. / Velocity describes water speed.

A river’s width and depth describe the channel cross-section, while velocity is the speed of flowing water. These are different quantities. A wide river is not necessarily carrying more water each second than a narrower but deeper and faster one. Point to the width across the surface and depth down into the section, then follow the flow arrow to show velocity. Measurements need units and representative methods because depth and speed can vary across a real channel. Our simple rectangular model makes the relationship easier to calculate.

Brief check: Does width alone establish how much water passes each second?
Listen for: No. Depth and velocity also matter.

Discharge is volume per time

On screen: Discharge measures water passing a section. / This model uses area × mean velocity.

Discharge is the volume of water passing a cross-section per unit of time. In a simplified rectangular section, width times depth gives area. Multiply that area by mean velocity to estimate discharge. Metres times metres gives square metres, and multiplying by metres per second gives cubic metres per second. Explain the units using a block of water moving past the section. Real channels require suitable measurements of shape and velocity, so the model’s neat numbers are a teaching example rather than a complete field method.

Brief check: What does discharge measure?
Listen for: Volume of water passing per unit of time.

Compare all the relevant quantities

On screen: A larger area can carry more water. / Faster flow can also increase discharge.

Compare two model rivers by calculating each discharge, not by choosing the one that looks widest. A section of ten square metres at two metres per second carries twenty cubic metres per second in the model. A section of twenty square metres at half a metre per second carries ten. The example shows why a visible dimension alone is insufficient. Keep the area and velocity labels beside the calculation. If the source omits necessary values, “we need more information” is a valid conclusion rather than an invitation to guess.

Brief check: Can we choose the greater discharge without depth or velocity information?
Listen for: Not reliably from width alone.

River changes vary along the course

On screen: Inputs and channel conditions change downstream. / Use evidence instead of absolute rules.

Tributaries can add water downstream, while channel size and flow conditions can change. These patterns help explain river variation, but they are not a guarantee that every measurement increases at every point and moment. Rainfall, withdrawals, storage and channel form can affect observations. State whether the source describes a particular section, time or general pattern. A measurement taken during one event should not automatically become a permanent characteristic of the whole river. This keeps the calculation connected to the geographical context in which it was made.

Brief check: Does one high-flow measurement describe the river at all times?
Listen for: No. Time and conditions affect flow.

Build it together · Draw a drainage divide from high ground

On screen: Draw a drainage divide from high ground / A drainage basin is land draining to an outlet.

A drainage basin is land draining to an outlet. A watershed divides neighbouring basins; rain falling on opposite sides may enter different streams. The divide is not the river itself.

The ridge can separate downhill flow paths.

Teaching question: Rain falls on opposite sides of a ridge separating two basins. What may happen? Correct reasoning: It drains towards different rivers. Contrast this with: It must all flow along the ridge top. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: Rain falls on opposite sides of a ridge separating two basins. What may happen?
Listen for: It drains towards different rivers. The ridge can separate downhill flow paths.

Sediment journey

7B · Week 29 · Lesson 2 · sections 5.4

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 5.4

On screen: Erosion removes material. / Distinguish removing, moving and dropping sediment

Today's key idea: Rivers erode, transport and deposit. Erosion removes material; transport carries it; deposition lays it down. Moving water carries material in different ways; changes in flow and sediment size influence what is moved or deposited. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Is moving material the same process as leaving it behind?
Listen for: No. Transport and deposition are different.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Rivers erode, transport and deposit

On screen: Erosion removes material. / Transport moves it; deposition leaves it behind.

A river can remove material, carry it and deposit it farther along its course. These are distinct processes that can occur in different parts of the same system. Trace one particle from a bank into moving water and then to a deposit. The river does not need to be either eroding or depositing everywhere at once. Local flow and available material influence what happens. Naming the process accurately helps us explain a landform rather than treating every visible change as erosion.

Brief check: Is moving material the same process as leaving it behind?
Listen for: No. Transport and deposition are different.

Erosion has different mechanisms

On screen: Water can remove weakened material. / Carried particles can abrade the bed and banks.

Flowing water can act on the channel directly and use carried sediment to wear surfaces. Hydraulic action describes the force of water on the channel, while abrasion involves carried material scraping or striking the bed and banks. Solution removes some soluble material chemically, and attrition wears transported particles as they collide. Introduce the actions through the diagram before adding the terms. These processes can work together, and their importance depends on flow, rock and sediment conditions. A list of names should not replace the explanation of what each action does.

Brief check: Which process uses carried particles to wear the channel?
Listen for: Abrasion.

Particles move in different ways

On screen: Large particles can roll; smaller ones can bounce. / Fine material can be suspended; dissolved material travels in solution.

Traction describes particles rolling or sliding along the bed. Saltation involves bouncing movement. Fine particles can be held in suspension, while dissolved material travels in solution. Show each position relative to the bed and water column. The transport mode depends on particle properties and flow conditions, so size alone is not a universal rule. A clear model can compare particles under stated similar conditions. If density changes as well as size, we cannot claim that size alone explains all the differences in movement.

Brief check: Is dissolved material simply a visible particle floating at the surface?
Listen for: No. It travels in solution.

Deposition depends on carrying capacity

On screen: Slower or changed flow can release sediment. / Different materials settle under different conditions.

When flow conditions no longer keep material moving, sediment may be deposited. Coarser particles often settle before finer ones under a simple comparable setup, but density, shape and flow also matter. Explain what stays constant in the demonstration before making a prediction. A pile of sediment can show deposition without telling us the complete history of its transport. Use the source conditions to interpret the sequence and avoid saying every particle follows an identical rule in every river. The mechanism is a change in the ability to carry material.

Brief check: Why should density be considered in a settling comparison?
Listen for: It can affect settling as well as particle size.

Build it together · Distinguish removing, moving and dropping sediment

On screen: Distinguish removing, moving and dropping sediment / Erosion removes material, transport moves it and deposition leaves it behind.

Erosion removes material, transport moves it and deposition leaves it behind. The same grain can experience all three at different places or times. Attach action verbs to a grain's story rather than just name locations.

It is moving with the flow rather than being left behind.

Teaching question: A grain is carried downstream without settling. Which process is shown? Correct reasoning: Transport. Contrast this with: Deposition. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: A grain is carried downstream without settling. Which process is shown?
Listen for: Transport. It is moving with the flow rather than being left behind.

METHOD Erosion removes material, transport moves it and deposition leaves it behind. The same grain can experience all three at different places or times. Attach action verbs to a grain's story rather than just name locations.

Now change one condition · 5.4

On screen: Does deposition mean sediment has ceased to exist?

Fictional sediment story: a grain is loosened from a bank, carried downstream, then settles where flow conditions can no longer keep it moving.

Does deposition mean sediment has ceased to exist? No. It remains in a deposit and may be moved again later.

7B · Week 30 · Lesson 1 · sections 5.4

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 5.4

On screen: Erosion removes material. / Predict settling with stated assumptions

Today's key idea: Rivers erode, transport and deposit. Erosion removes material; transport carries it; deposition lays it down. Moving water carries material in different ways; changes in flow and sediment size influence what is moved or deposited. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Is moving material the same process as leaving it behind?
Listen for: No. Transport and deposition are different.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Rivers erode, transport and deposit

On screen: Erosion removes material. / Transport moves it; deposition leaves it behind.

A river can remove material, carry it and deposit it farther along its course. These are distinct processes that can occur in different parts of the same system. Trace one particle from a bank into moving water and then to a deposit. The river does not need to be either eroding or depositing everywhere at once. Local flow and available material influence what happens. Naming the process accurately helps us explain a landform rather than treating every visible change as erosion.

Brief check: Is moving material the same process as leaving it behind?
Listen for: No. Transport and deposition are different.

Erosion has different mechanisms

On screen: Water can remove weakened material. / Carried particles can abrade the bed and banks.

Flowing water can act on the channel directly and use carried sediment to wear surfaces. Hydraulic action describes the force of water on the channel, while abrasion involves carried material scraping or striking the bed and banks. Solution removes some soluble material chemically, and attrition wears transported particles as they collide. Introduce the actions through the diagram before adding the terms. These processes can work together, and their importance depends on flow, rock and sediment conditions. A list of names should not replace the explanation of what each action does.

Brief check: Which process uses carried particles to wear the channel?
Listen for: Abrasion.

Particles move in different ways

On screen: Large particles can roll; smaller ones can bounce. / Fine material can be suspended; dissolved material travels in solution.

Traction describes particles rolling or sliding along the bed. Saltation involves bouncing movement. Fine particles can be held in suspension, while dissolved material travels in solution. Show each position relative to the bed and water column. The transport mode depends on particle properties and flow conditions, so size alone is not a universal rule. A clear model can compare particles under stated similar conditions. If density changes as well as size, we cannot claim that size alone explains all the differences in movement.

Brief check: Is dissolved material simply a visible particle floating at the surface?
Listen for: No. It travels in solution.

Deposition depends on carrying capacity

On screen: Slower or changed flow can release sediment. / Different materials settle under different conditions.

When flow conditions no longer keep material moving, sediment may be deposited. Coarser particles often settle before finer ones under a simple comparable setup, but density, shape and flow also matter. Explain what stays constant in the demonstration before making a prediction. A pile of sediment can show deposition without telling us the complete history of its transport. Use the source conditions to interpret the sequence and avoid saying every particle follows an identical rule in every river. The mechanism is a change in the ability to carry material.

Brief check: Why should density be considered in a settling comparison?
Listen for: It can affect settling as well as particle size.

When flow loses transporting power, deposition can occur. In a simplified comparison of similar-density particles, larger grains often settle before fine suspended material. Shape, turbulence and density can change real behaviour.

Different particles have different settling and transport behaviour; the model holds other factors similar.

Teaching question: With otherwise comparable grains and slowing flow, which is more likely to settle first? Correct reasoning: Coarser sediment. Contrast this with: All grains must settle simultaneously. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Listen for: Coarser sediment. Different particles have different settling and transport behaviour; the model holds other factors similar.

Six landform process cards

7B · Week 31 · Lesson 1 · sections 5.5

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 5.5

On screen: Erosion can undercut a step. / Connect landforms to more than one process

Today's key idea: Waterfalls can retreat upstream. Different river landforms develop through erosion, transport and deposition over time. The six source cards cover waterfalls, gorges, meanders, oxbow lakes, floodplains and natural levees. The model demonstrates only bend migration and a possible cut-off. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: What does retreat mean for the waterfall’s position?
Listen for: It moves upstream over successive erosion and collapse.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Waterfalls can retreat upstream

On screen: Erosion can undercut a step. / Collapse and removal can move the fall backwards.

A waterfall is a steep drop in a river’s course. In a common school model with contrasting rock resistance, erosion can remove weaker material below a harder layer. Undercutting leaves an overhang, which can collapse. The river removes debris and the sequence can repeat, moving the waterfall upstream. Trace the undercut, collapse and retreat in order. This is one explanatory model rather than the only origin of every waterfall. A gorge can remain behind the retreating fall, showing the connection between a process sequence and two landforms.

Brief check: What does retreat mean for the waterfall’s position?
Listen for: It moves upstream over successive erosion and collapse.

Meanders have different conditions on each side

On screen: Outer bend: erosion often dominates. / Inner bend: deposition often dominates.

A meander is a bend in a river. Flow is commonly faster and deeper towards the outer bend, where erosion can wear the bank. Slower conditions near the inner bend can favour deposition. Point to both sides of the same bend, then trace how their different processes can shift its shape. The exact flow pattern is more complex than the simplified arrows. The important introductory idea is that erosion and deposition can occur beside each other, producing change through a connected system rather than separate unrelated events.

Brief check: Which side commonly receives deposition in the simple bend model?
Listen for: The inner bend.

An oxbow lake needs a cut-off and isolation

On screen: A narrowing neck can be crossed by a new channel. / Deposits can block the old bend’s entrances.

As a meander develops, its neck can narrow. A shorter channel may cut through, especially during high flow. The old bend is not automatically an isolated lake at the instant the new channel appears. Deposition can block its connections, leaving an oxbow lake. Show neck narrowing, breakthrough and isolation as separate stages. This sequence explains why a short new channel and a fully disconnected water body describe different conditions. A correct answer must identify which stage the source actually shows rather than simply naming the final landform.

Brief check: Does a new shortcut always mean the old bend is already isolated?
Listen for: No. Its entrances may still be connected.

Flood deposits can build floodplains and levees

On screen: Floodwater spreads beyond the channel. / Sediment settles as the flow changes.

When a river overtops its banks, water spreads across the surrounding valley floor. Flow commonly slows away from the channel, allowing sediment to settle. Repeated deposition can contribute to a floodplain. Coarser sediment often settles near the banks, helping build natural levees, while finer material may travel farther. Explain that a natural levee is a deposit-built bank feature, not a constructed wall. Floodplains also have complex histories involving channel movement and other processes, so one flood does not instantly create an entire mature landscape.

Brief check: Is a natural levee the same thing as a concrete flood wall?
Listen for: No. It forms from deposited sediment.

Build it together · Connect landforms to more than one process

On screen: Connect landforms to more than one process / At a meander, erosion often affects the outer bank while deposition builds the inner bank.

At a meander, erosion often affects the outer bank while deposition builds the inner bank. A floodplain can receive flood deposits. Name the process and its location; saying “the river erodes everywhere” misses the contrast.

Different flow conditions around a bend favour different processes.

Teaching question: Which pair fits a simplified meander bend? Correct reasoning: Outer-bank erosion and inner-bank deposition. Contrast this with: Deposition everywhere with no bank erosion. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: Which pair fits a simplified meander bend?
Listen for: Outer-bank erosion and inner-bank deposition. Different flow conditions around a bend favour different processes.

MODEL EXPLANATION Waterfall/gorge involve erosion and retreat; meander/oxbow involve erosion, deposition and cut-off; floodplain/levee involve flood deposition.

METHOD At a meander, erosion often affects the outer bank while deposition builds the inner bank. A floodplain can receive flood deposits. Name the process and its location; saying “the river erodes everywhere” misses the contrast.

The key question is: What must happen before a bend becomes an isolated oxbow lake? The correct idea is: A new channel bypasses the bend and the old entrances become blocked. Cut-off and isolation explain the feature; it is not merely a circular river on a map. Hear one or two brief answers, correct the specific misconception, and close with the accurate geographical explanation.

Context for this discussion: A waterfall retreats upstream leaving a gorge. A meander neck narrows, a shorter channel breaks through, and deposits isolate the old bend. Floodwater deposits material on the floodplain; coarser material often settles near banks.

Relevant explanation: Label retreat and gorge behind the fall; neck narrowing, breakthrough and isolation; deposits near the banks can build natural levees.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 5.6

On screen: Navigation, recreation and energy are possible uses. / Balance a finite supply and make trade-offs explicit

Today's key idea: Rivers provide more than water supply. Rivers supply water and support transport, power, food, habitats and recreation. Uses can compete. An allocation decision must consider downstream needs and uncertainty, not only the largest user. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Does every river section automatically provide shipping and hydropower?
Listen for: No. Each use needs suitable physical and practical conditions.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Rivers provide more than water supply

On screen: Navigation, recreation and energy are possible uses. / Each use needs suitable conditions.

People use rivers for water supply, transport, recreation and, in suitable systems, power generation. Farming and industry may depend on water drawn from a basin, while a navigable channel can connect inland places to ports. Recreation can include activities beside or on the water. Hydropower uses moving water and a height difference within an engineered system. Not every river provides all these uses in the same way. Depth, flow, location, infrastructure and water quality influence what is possible. Explain the condition each use needs before comparing the benefits. This restores the broader topic of river uses before the class examines competition for a shared water supply.

Brief check: Does every river section automatically provide shipping and hydropower?
Listen for: No. Each use needs suitable physical and practical conditions.

Water has competing uses

On screen: Homes, farms and industry need water. / Ecosystems also depend on water.

Water supports drinking, sanitation, farming, industry and ecosystems. These uses can compete when supply is limited or unevenly distributed. Identify who uses the water before deciding how to allocate it. Demand is not simply what one person prefers; it concerns amounts required over time and for particular purposes. A classroom token budget makes the shared limit visible but does not capture every legal, environmental or practical factor of real management. Keep that distinction clear while using the model to explain why a shared resource needs coordinated decisions.

Brief check: Who can be affected besides households and businesses?
Listen for: Ecosystems and other users dependent on the water.

A water budget has a shared total

On screen: Add all allocations. / The sum must fit the available supply in this model.

If supply is eighty units, allocations of twenty, thirty, twenty and twenty total ninety. Each individual amount is below eighty, but their combined use exceeds the shared supply by ten. Write the running total so pupils see where the limit is crossed. Feasibility depends on the whole package. The model assumes a stated period and comparable units; changing either would change the interpretation. It does not prove that every real allocation can be moved freely between users or places without infrastructure and other conditions.

Brief check: Why is checking each allocation separately insufficient?
Listen for: All users share the same limited total.

Reducing demand can differ from increasing supply

On screen: Efficiency can reduce water needed. / New supply can have costs and environmental effects.

Management can seek to reduce demand, increase usable supply or change distribution. Fixing leaks and using water efficiently aim to reduce waste; storage or transfer can alter availability. Each option has mechanisms, costs and limits. A transfer may help one place while affecting the donor basin, and stored water still depends on inputs. Explain the specific shortage before choosing an option. A measure that sounds useful in general may not address the timing, quality or location problem in the actual source.

Brief check: Does building storage create water without any input?
Listen for: No. It stores water that must enter the system.

Fairness requires explaining priorities

On screen: Minimum needs and effects matter. / Different allocations can be feasible but unequal.

Several allocations can fit the same supply, yet have very different effects. Explain which needs a proposal protects and which uses it reduces. Invite opinions about priorities after establishing the numerical facts. There may be more than one defensible allocation, but each must meet the model’s limit and account for its effects. An argument should connect a chosen amount to a need rather than claim fairness solely because all categories receive equal tokens. Equal amounts and equitable outcomes are not necessarily the same in a resource decision.

Brief check: Can two different allocations both fit the supply?
Listen for: Yes. Compare their reasons and effects as well as feasibility.

If requests total 90 units and supply is 80, the shortfall is 10. A proposal must sum to at most 80 and state which needs are reduced. Arithmetic checks feasibility; fairness needs reasons and local evidence.

Total demand is 90; subtract available supply to find the gap.

7B · Week 32 · Lesson 2 · sections 5.7

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 5.7

On screen: River water meets coastal water. / Explain why estuary conditions vary

Today's key idea: An estuary connects river and sea. An estuary is a tidal river mouth where freshwater and seawater mix. Tides influence water levels and movement. Estuaries can support ports, habitats and settlements; these uses may create competing demands. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Why is an estuary different from an isolated inland pond?
Listen for: It connects river inputs with coastal water and tidal influence.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

An estuary connects river and sea

On screen: River water meets coastal water. / Tides influence water levels and movement.

An estuary is a coastal area where river water meets and mixes with seawater, with conditions influenced by tides. Fresh and salt water are not necessarily mixed evenly at every place or time. River flow, tide and the shape of the estuary influence the pattern. Locate the Thames towards its mouth and the North Sea, then contrast that environment with a small upstream channel. The estuary is part of a connected system: it receives river inputs and interacts with coastal conditions. This explains why both upstream activity and marine processes can affect it. Our schematic shows that connection; it does not supply the exact salinity or water level at a named point today.

Brief check: Why is an estuary different from an isolated inland pond?
Listen for: It connects river inputs with coastal water and tidal influence.

The Thames Estuary has human and ecological roles

On screen: Shipping and riverside activities use its connections. / Habitats also depend on its changing water and sediment conditions.

The Thames Estuary connects the river and London region to the North Sea. Shipping and riverside activities use those connections, while its water and sediment environments support habitats. Depth, tidal conditions and access influence navigation. Mudflats and other intertidal areas experience alternating coverage and exposure as water levels change. Explain how a project intended to improve navigation could also alter sediment or habitat conditions. The question is about two roles of the same place, not unrelated benefits and disadvantages. A wider channel or dredging proposal should be evaluated against its stated purpose and its effects on the estuary system. Detailed claims about present traffic, habitat extent or water quality need appropriate sources rather than invented classroom figures.

Brief check: Can improving navigation have effects on habitats in the same estuary?
Listen for: Yes. Channel or sediment changes can affect both.

Rivers support human activities

On screen: Transport, farming and settlements use rivers. / Uses depend on location and river conditions.

Rivers provide water and can support transport, recreation and other activities. Their usefulness depends on depth, flow, water quality, access and surrounding land. A navigable lower section does not mean every tributary can carry large ships. Trace how a river connects activities in different places. It can also create hazards, so proximity brings possible benefits and costs. Explain one use through the condition it requires instead of presenting rivers as uniformly useful everywhere for every purpose.

Brief check: Does a useful shipping channel imply every river section is navigable?
Listen for: No. Conditions differ along the system.

Engineering changes the river system

On screen: Dredging changes the channel. / Walls and embankments change local flow conditions.

Engineering alters the river or its surroundings to serve a purpose. Dredging can deepen a channel for navigation, while walls or embankments may limit local overflow. The intervention changes a connected system, so effects can extend beyond the immediate project. Explain the intended mechanism first, then consider sediment, habitat, maintenance and flow elsewhere. A supported local benefit does not establish that every other effect is positive. The evaluation needs the relevant places, users and time period rather than only the project’s stated aim.

Brief check: Why examine areas beyond the project site?
Listen for: A connected river system can carry effects elsewhere.

Benefits and environmental costs can coexist

On screen: A deeper channel may help ships. / Habitat or sediment movement may change.

A deeper navigation channel can help vessels while also changing habitat or sediment conditions. These statements need not contradict each other. Separate each outcome and identify the evidence supporting it. Do not erase an observed cost merely because an intended benefit was achieved. Compare alternatives and possible mitigation, while recognising that mitigation may not remove every effect. An opinion about the preferred trade-off should follow an accurate account of both sides. This is a geographical evaluation of consequences for places and users, not a simple vote on whether engineering is good.

Brief check: Does finding one benefit disprove an environmental cost?
Listen for: No. Both outcomes can occur.

Recommendations need conditions and monitoring

On screen: Match the intervention to the problem. / Check what happens after implementation.

A recommendation should identify the problem, the mechanism of the proposed response and the conditions on which it depends. If depth limits shipping, channel changes may address that problem; they do not automatically solve poor water quality or every flood risk. Monitoring after implementation helps test expected benefits and unexpected effects. Specify a relevant measure rather than saying only “check it”. Water depth, habitat condition or downstream flow may answer different questions. The evidence need follows the claim we want to test.

Brief check: What should monitoring measure?
Listen for: The relevant intended outcome and possible adverse effects.

7B · Week 33 · Lesson 1 · sections 5.8

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 5.8

On screen: A channel can overflow. / Control one variable in a runoff experiment

Today's key idea: Flooding means water covers normally dry land. Flooding occurs when water covers normally dry land. Rainfall, saturated ground, surfaces and channel capacity affect risk. A cause is not the same as an impact. One factor rarely explains every flood. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Is every flood caused by the same process?
Listen for: No. The mechanism must be identified.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Flooding means water covers normally dry land

On screen: A channel can overflow. / Other flood mechanisms also exist.

Flooding occurs when water covers land that is normally dry. A river can overflow when water exceeds the capacity of its channel at a location. Surface-water flooding can also occur when drainage cannot remove water quickly enough. Coastal conditions can create other mechanisms. Start with the source’s actual process rather than assuming every flood has the same cause. A risk explanation should connect water input, movement or storage to where people and property are exposed. This makes the difference between naming rain and explaining how flooding develops.

Brief check: Is every flood caused by the same process?
Listen for: No. The mechanism must be identified.

Rain reaches the channel through pathways

On screen: Saturated ground has less available storage. / Rapid runoff can increase the river’s response.

Prolonged or intense rainfall can increase water entering a basin. If the ground is saturated, additional rainfall may move more readily across the surface. Trace rainfall to runoff to the channel before discussing overflow. Timing matters: water arriving quickly can create a larger peak than the same total spread over a long time. Our simple rainfall model illustrates a pathway, not an exact flood forecast. Channel conditions and other stores also affect the response, so rainfall alone is not the full explanation.

Brief check: Why can the rate of arrival matter as well as total rainfall?
Listen for: Rapid arrival can produce a larger peak flow.

Land use can change the response

On screen: Paving can reduce infiltration locally. / Drainage can route water differently.

Replacing permeable ground with paving can reduce local infiltration and alter runoff pathways. Drains may move water quickly towards a channel, although the outcome depends on design and conditions. Compare the same rainfall input before and after a surface change so pupils understand the mechanism being tested. Do not say identical rainfall guarantees identical runoff. The surface and drainage system mediate the response. A real explanation requires evidence of the relevant land-use and drainage changes rather than inferring them from a flood photograph alone.

Brief check: Can runoff change even if rainfall stays the same?
Listen for: Yes. Surface and drainage conditions can change.

Causes and impacts are different

On screen: Cause: a factor contributing to flooding. / Impact: what happens because of the event.

Heavy rain and restricted channel capacity can contribute to a flood. Damaged homes, closed roads and interrupted services are impacts. Build the sequence from trigger through pathway to outcome. “Rain caused damage” skips the process that connects them. Impacts also depend on what is exposed and how people can respond. Two floods with similar water levels can produce different harm if buildings, warning systems or access differ. Describe immediate and later impacts separately so repairs and lost activity do not become confused with the initial flood mechanism.

Brief check: Are damaged homes a cause or an impact?
Listen for: An impact.

40-minute teaching route: introduction 3, explanations 22, board demonstration 6, changed example 5, brief responses 3, dismissal 1. Timings are estimates, not measured classroom duration. Use the supplied subject explanations; do not stretch a single question to fill a stage.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 5.8

On screen: A channel can overflow. / Connect causes to impacts through a mechanism

Today's key idea: Flooding means water covers normally dry land. Flooding occurs when water covers normally dry land. Rainfall, saturated ground, surfaces and channel capacity affect risk. A cause is not the same as an impact. One factor rarely explains every flood. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Is every flood caused by the same process?
Listen for: No. The mechanism must be identified.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Flooding means water covers normally dry land

On screen: A channel can overflow. / Other flood mechanisms also exist.

Flooding occurs when water covers land that is normally dry. A river can overflow when water exceeds the capacity of its channel at a location. Surface-water flooding can also occur when drainage cannot remove water quickly enough. Coastal conditions can create other mechanisms. Start with the source’s actual process rather than assuming every flood has the same cause. A risk explanation should connect water input, movement or storage to where people and property are exposed. This makes the difference between naming rain and explaining how flooding develops.

Brief check: Is every flood caused by the same process?
Listen for: No. The mechanism must be identified.

Rain reaches the channel through pathways

On screen: Saturated ground has less available storage. / Rapid runoff can increase the river’s response.

Prolonged or intense rainfall can increase water entering a basin. If the ground is saturated, additional rainfall may move more readily across the surface. Trace rainfall to runoff to the channel before discussing overflow. Timing matters: water arriving quickly can create a larger peak than the same total spread over a long time. Our simple rainfall model illustrates a pathway, not an exact flood forecast. Channel conditions and other stores also affect the response, so rainfall alone is not the full explanation.

Brief check: Why can the rate of arrival matter as well as total rainfall?
Listen for: Rapid arrival can produce a larger peak flow.

Land use can change the response

On screen: Paving can reduce infiltration locally. / Drainage can route water differently.

Replacing permeable ground with paving can reduce local infiltration and alter runoff pathways. Drains may move water quickly towards a channel, although the outcome depends on design and conditions. Compare the same rainfall input before and after a surface change so pupils understand the mechanism being tested. Do not say identical rainfall guarantees identical runoff. The surface and drainage system mediate the response. A real explanation requires evidence of the relevant land-use and drainage changes rather than inferring them from a flood photograph alone.

Brief check: Can runoff change even if rainfall stays the same?
Listen for: Yes. Surface and drainage conditions can change.

Causes and impacts are different

On screen: Cause: a factor contributing to flooding. / Impact: what happens because of the event.

Heavy rain and restricted channel capacity can contribute to a flood. Damaged homes, closed roads and interrupted services are impacts. Build the sequence from trigger through pathway to outcome. “Rain caused damage” skips the process that connects them. Impacts also depend on what is exposed and how people can respond. Two floods with similar water levels can produce different harm if buildings, warning systems or access differ. Describe immediate and later impacts separately so repairs and lost activity do not become confused with the initial flood mechanism.

Brief check: Are damaged homes a cause or an impact?
Listen for: An impact.

Damage is a consequence; rainfall contributes to the water input.

0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 5.9

On screen: Separate real facts from classroom figures. / Organise a case file without mixing fact and invention

Today's key idea: A case study needs a trustworthy source. A case study connects location, causes, impacts and responses using specific evidence. Different flood mechanisms need different measures. The Thames Barrier helps manage tidal flood risk; it cannot prevent every kind of flooding. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Can an invented count be reported as a verified historical Thames figure?
Listen for: No. It belongs to the fictional exercise.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

A case study needs a trustworthy source

On screen: Separate real facts from classroom figures. / Name the event, place and source.

A case study connects processes to a particular place and event. Real dates and counts need sources that support them. Our invented flood log practises organising an explanation, but it must not become a historical claim about the Thames. State which information is factual background and which belongs to the fictional exercise. This distinction allows meaningful practice without misleading pupils. A neat table or detailed number does not make a source authentic; provenance concerns where the information came from and what it represents.

Brief check: Can an invented count be reported as a verified historical Thames figure?
Listen for: No. It belongs to the fictional exercise.

Organise causes, impacts and responses

On screen: Cause → process → impact. / Response: what people do before, during or after.

Organise the event as a sequence. Prolonged rain can be a trigger; channel overflow is part of the flooding mechanism; flooded homes and road closure are impacts. Warnings, diversion and repairs are responses, although they occur at different times and serve different purposes. A warning can help preparation but does not remove rainfall. A diversion can maintain some travel without repairing a house. Sorting the log makes these relationships clear, and an explanation should then connect the categories rather than simply list them.

Brief check: Does a road diversion remove the original rainfall?
Listen for: No. It responds to a transport impact.

The Thames Barrier has a specific role

On screen: It helps protect London from tidal and combined flood risk. / It does not stop every flood across the basin.

The Thames Barrier helps protect London against tidal and combined tidal and river flood risk under its operating arrangements. Its location and mechanism matter. It is not a device that removes every rainstorm, clears every drain or prevents all upstream flooding. Compare a barrier, a blocked local drain and rainfall farther upstream. Each problem has a different pathway and may require a different response. Teaching the barrier’s real role accurately is more useful than calling it a universal solution or suggesting it has no benefit because it has limits.

Brief check: Would a tidal barrier automatically clear a blocked local drain?
Listen for: No. It addresses a different mechanism.

Match responses to mechanisms

On screen: Warnings help people prepare. / Drainage maintenance and repairs address different needs.

A response should address the source’s actual problem. Warning residents can help them act, but they also need time, information and practical means to respond. Drainage maintenance can address a blockage; it does not guarantee protection from every river flood. Repairs address damage after the event rather than preventing the original trigger. Ask what each response changes and what it leaves unchanged. This mechanism-based comparison supports an informed recommendation without assuming that the most familiar named measure is always the right one.

Brief check: Why can a warning be insufficient on its own?
Listen for: People may lack the transport, time or means to act.

Sort a fictional event into trigger, mechanism, impacts and responses. Label dates and counts by their source. An invented classroom log can practise reasoning but must not become a claimed historical Thames event.

Source identity is part of accurate case-study reporting.

Contrast this with: As a verified historical Thames total. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. 0–3 min · Introduce the topic

Today we will understand · 5.10

On screen: Measures have different purposes. / Choose a feasible package and explain its limits

Today's key idea: Flood management aims to reduce risk. Flood management can reduce likelihood, exposure or harm. No single measure removes every risk. Compare cost, effectiveness, environmental effects and local suitability; warnings support response rather than stopping water. Start by pointing to the named features. Say each new term, give its plain-English meaning and connect it to something visible. Invite one short answer to the check below; use it to decide which idea needs a second explanation. Pupils stay seated and do not need to copy this slide.

Brief check: Does having a flood measure guarantee zero risk?
Listen for: No. Capacity and conditions still matter.

3–25 min · Teach the Geography

Flood management aims to reduce risk

On screen: Measures have different purposes. / No single measure guarantees zero risk.

Flood management can seek to reduce the likelihood of flooding, reduce exposure or help people prepare and recover. Different measures act on different parts of that chain. Storage may hold water temporarily; barriers may limit a particular inflow; warning systems help people respond. Start by identifying the flood mechanism and affected area. The existence of a measure does not mean all risk disappears. Its capacity, location, maintenance and the event conditions influence performance. A realistic explanation names the intended benefit and the limits that remain.

Brief check: Does having a flood measure guarantee zero risk?
Listen for: No. Capacity and conditions still matter.

Hard and soft approaches have trade-offs

On screen: Structures can alter channels or barriers. / Land use and preparation can change exposure or response.

Hard engineering commonly uses built structures or channel alterations. Other approaches include land-use planning, restoring storage areas and warning or preparation. The categories describe broad approaches rather than a ranking of automatically good and bad measures. Compare how each option acts on the problem in the source. A wall may protect one location while changing flow elsewhere; a storage area needs land and sufficient capacity. Explain the mechanism, then consider costs, environmental effects and people affected. A mixed package may be appropriate if its components address distinct needs.

Brief check: Should a category name alone decide which measure is best?
Listen for: No. Compare mechanisms and local conditions.

A feasible package must fit the shared budget

On screen: Add the complete package cost. / Affordability comes before comparing preferences.

If a package includes warnings, storage and a wall, add all their costs. Checking that each item individually costs less than the budget is insufficient. A fifty-token budget cannot fund a sixty-token total. Once feasibility is established, compare how well the package addresses the actual risks. The cheapest package may fail to protect the required area, while the most expensive feasible one may create unnecessary costs. Our tokens are invented classroom data; real costs and permissions require appropriate information beyond the model.

Brief check: What is wrong with checking only each individual price?
Listen for: The combined package can exceed the shared budget.

Evaluate effects across places and time

On screen: Who benefits? Who may face new risk? / What maintenance and evidence are needed?

A flood wall may protect one neighbourhood but shift faster flow towards another. A responsible evaluation includes that transferred risk rather than counting only the local benefit. Consider the system, affected groups, long-term maintenance and environmental effects. A larger budget creates options but does not prove which is best. State what further evidence would help, such as flow modelling, capacity or land-use information. Invite opinions about priorities after explaining the supported outcomes. A recommendation should make its reasoning and remaining uncertainty clear enough to review.

Brief check: Does a benefit at one site establish a benefit everywhere?
Listen for: No. Effects can be uneven or transferred.

3–25 min · Explain and reconnect

Flooding means water covers normally dry land

On screen: A channel can overflow. / Other flood mechanisms also exist.

Flooding occurs when water covers land that is normally dry. A river can overflow when water exceeds the capacity of its channel at a location. Surface-water flooding can also occur when drainage cannot remove water quickly enough. Coastal conditions can create other mechanisms. Start with the source’s actual process rather than assuming every flood has the same cause. A risk explanation should connect water input, movement or storage to where people and property are exposed. This makes the difference between naming rain and explaining how flooding develops.

Brief check: Is every flood caused by the same process?
Listen for: No. The mechanism must be identified.

Causes and impacts are different

On screen: Cause: a factor contributing to flooding. / Impact: what happens because of the event.

Heavy rain and restricted channel capacity can contribute to a flood. Damaged homes, closed roads and interrupted services are impacts. Build the sequence from trigger through pathway to outcome. “Rain caused damage” skips the process that connects them. Impacts also depend on what is exposed and how people can respond. Two floods with similar water levels can produce different harm if buildings, warning systems or access differ. Describe immediate and later impacts separately so repairs and lost activity do not become confused with the initial flood mechanism.

Brief check: Are damaged homes a cause or an impact?
Listen for: An impact.

On screen: Separate real facts from classroom figures. / Name the event, place and source.

Our invented flood log practises organising an explanation, but it must not become a historical claim about the Thames. A neat table or detailed number does not make a source authentic; provenance concerns where the information came from and what it represents.

Drainage maintenance can address a blockage; it does not guarantee protection from every river flood. Repairs address damage after the event rather than preventing the original trigger. Ask what each response changes and what it leaves unchanged. This mechanism-based comparison supports an informed recommendation without assuming that the most familiar named measure is always the right one.

Demonstrate the relevant operation or connection aloud before inviting an answer. The case is a teaching example; no pupil needs to produce a written response.

Flood management aims to reduce risk

On screen: Measures have different purposes. / No single measure guarantees zero risk.

Flood management can seek to reduce the likelihood of flooding, reduce exposure or help people prepare and recover. Different measures act on different parts of that chain. Storage may hold water temporarily; barriers may limit a particular inflow; warning systems help people respond. Start by identifying the flood mechanism and affected area. The existence of a measure does not mean all risk disappears. Its capacity, location, maintenance and the event conditions influence performance. A realistic explanation names the intended benefit and the limits that remain.

Brief check: Does having a flood measure guarantee zero risk?
Listen for: No. Capacity and conditions still matter.

Evaluate effects across places and time

On screen: Who benefits? Who may face new risk? / What maintenance and evidence are needed?

A flood wall may protect one neighbourhood but shift faster flow towards another. A responsible evaluation includes that transferred risk rather than counting only the local benefit. Consider the system, affected groups, long-term maintenance and environmental effects. A larger budget creates options but does not prove which is best. State what further evidence would help, such as flow modelling, capacity or land-use information. Invite opinions about priorities after explaining the supported outcomes. A recommendation should make its reasoning and remaining uncertainty clear enough to review.

Brief check: Does a benefit at one site establish a benefit everywhere?
Listen for: No. Effects can be uneven or transferred.

3–25 min · Explain and reconnect

Flooding means water covers normally dry land

On screen: A channel can overflow. / Other flood mechanisms also exist.

Flooding occurs when water covers land that is normally dry. A river can overflow when water exceeds the capacity of its channel at a location. Surface-water flooding can also occur when drainage cannot remove water quickly enough. Coastal conditions can create other mechanisms. Start with the source’s actual process rather than assuming every flood has the same cause. A risk explanation should connect water input, movement or storage to where people and property are exposed. This makes the difference between naming rain and explaining how flooding develops.

Brief check: Is every flood caused by the same process?
Listen for: No. The mechanism must be identified.

Causes and impacts are different

On screen: Cause: a factor contributing to flooding. / Impact: what happens because of the event.

Heavy rain and restricted channel capacity can contribute to a flood. Damaged homes, closed roads and interrupted services are impacts. Build the sequence from trigger through pathway to outcome. “Rain caused damage” skips the process that connects them. Impacts also depend on what is exposed and how people can respond. Two floods with similar water levels can produce different harm if buildings, warning systems or access differ. Describe immediate and later impacts separately so repairs and lost activity do not become confused with the initial flood mechanism.

Brief check: Are damaged homes a cause or an impact?
Listen for: An impact.

A case study needs a trustworthy source

On screen: Separate real facts from classroom figures. / Name the event, place and source.

A case study connects processes to a particular place and event. Real dates and counts need sources that support them. Our invented flood log practises organising an explanation, but it must not become a historical claim about the Thames. State which information is factual background and which belongs to the fictional exercise. This distinction allows meaningful practice without misleading pupils. A neat table or detailed number does not make a source authentic; provenance concerns where the information came from and what it represents.

Brief check: Can an invented count be reported as a verified historical Thames figure?
Listen for: No. It belongs to the fictional exercise.

Match responses to mechanisms

On screen: Warnings help people prepare. / Drainage maintenance and repairs address different needs.

A response should address the source’s actual problem. Warning residents can help them act, but they also need time, information and practical means to respond. Drainage maintenance can address a blockage; it does not guarantee protection from every river flood. Repairs address damage after the event rather than preventing the original trigger. Ask what each response changes and what it leaves unchanged. This mechanism-based comparison supports an informed recommendation without assuming that the most familiar named measure is always the right one.

Brief check: Why can a warning be insufficient on its own?
Listen for: People may lack the transport, time or means to act.

3–25 min · Explain and reconnect

Flooding means water covers normally dry land

On screen: A channel can overflow. / Other flood mechanisms also exist.

Flooding occurs when water covers land that is normally dry. A river can overflow when water exceeds the capacity of its channel at a location. Surface-water flooding can also occur when drainage cannot remove water quickly enough. Coastal conditions can create other mechanisms. Start with the source’s actual process rather than assuming every flood has the same cause. A risk explanation should connect water input, movement or storage to where people and property are exposed. This makes the difference between naming rain and explaining how flooding develops.

Brief check: Is every flood caused by the same process?
Listen for: No. The mechanism must be identified.

Causes and impacts are different

On screen: Cause: a factor contributing to flooding. / Impact: what happens because of the event.

Heavy rain and restricted channel capacity can contribute to a flood. Damaged homes, closed roads and interrupted services are impacts. Build the sequence from trigger through pathway to outcome. “Rain caused damage” skips the process that connects them. Impacts also depend on what is exposed and how people can respond. Two floods with similar water levels can produce different harm if buildings, warning systems or access differ. Describe immediate and later impacts separately so repairs and lost activity do not become confused with the initial flood mechanism.

Brief check: Are damaged homes a cause or an impact?
Listen for: An impact.

10 infiltrate; the remaining 30 run off in this two-part model.

Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Listen for: 30 units. 10 infiltrate; the remaining 30 run off in this two-part model.
