A case study needs a trustworthy source

On screen: Separate real facts from classroom figures. / Name the event, place and source.

A case study connects processes to a particular place and event. Real dates and counts need sources that support them. Our invented flood log practises organising an explanation, but it must not become a historical claim about the Thames. State which information is factual background and which belongs to the fictional exercise. This distinction allows meaningful practice without misleading pupils. A neat table or detailed number does not make a source authentic; provenance concerns where the information came from and what it represents.

Brief check: Can an invented count be reported as a verified historical Thames figure?
Listen for: No. It belongs to the fictional exercise.

Match responses to mechanisms

On screen: Warnings help people prepare. / Drainage maintenance and repairs address different needs.

A response should address the source’s actual problem. Warning residents can help them act, but they also need time, information and practical means to respond. Drainage maintenance can address a blockage; it does not guarantee protection from every river flood. Repairs address damage after the event rather than preventing the original trigger. Ask what each response changes and what it leaves unchanged. This mechanism-based comparison supports an informed recommendation without assuming that the most familiar named measure is always the right one.

Brief check: Why can a warning be insufficient on its own?
Listen for: People may lack the transport, time or means to act.

See the method · Match a response to the flood mechanism

On screen: Match a response to the flood mechanism / A tidal barrier addresses incoming high water at its protected location; it does not remove every upstream rainfall or drainage problem.

A tidal barrier addresses incoming high water at its protected location; it does not remove every upstream rainfall or drainage problem. Warnings help preparation, while drainage work addresses a different pathway.

Measures have different mechanisms and geographical coverage.

Teaching question: A local drain is blocked after rain. What directly addresses that blockage? Correct reasoning: Appropriate drainage maintenance. Contrast this with: Assume a distant tidal barrier clears it. Explain which fact or step makes the second response fail. Point to the specific part of the visual rather than asking pupils to guess from the title. Use the model's own quantities; the following case supplies different information.

Brief check: A local drain is blocked after rain. What directly addresses that blockage?
Listen for: Appropriate drainage maintenance. Measures have different mechanisms and geographical coverage.

Method note: A tidal barrier addresses incoming high water at its protected location; it does not remove every upstream rainfall or drainage problem. Warnings help preparation, while drainage work addresses a different pathway.

Read the source in small sections. Link each named place, measurement or process to the diagram. Keep the source visible when referring to a number. Demonstrate the relevant operation or connection aloud before inviting an answer. The case is a teaching example; no pupil needs to produce a written response.

Flood management aims to reduce risk

On screen: Measures have different purposes. / No single measure guarantees zero risk.

Flood management can seek to reduce the likelihood of flooding, reduce exposure or help people prepare and recover. Different measures act on different parts of that chain. Storage may hold water temporarily; barriers may limit a particular inflow; warning systems help people respond. Start by identifying the flood mechanism and affected area. The existence of a measure does not mean all risk disappears. Its capacity, location, maintenance and the event conditions influence performance. A realistic explanation names the intended benefit and the limits that remain.

Brief check: Does having a flood measure guarantee zero risk?
Listen for: No. Capacity and conditions still matter.

Evaluate effects across places and time

On screen: Who benefits? Who may face new risk? / What maintenance and evidence are needed?

A flood wall may protect one neighbourhood but shift faster flow towards another. A responsible evaluation includes that transferred risk rather than counting only the local benefit. Consider the system, affected groups, long-term maintenance and environmental effects. A larger budget creates options but does not prove which is best. State what further evidence would help, such as flow modelling, capacity or land-use information. Invite opinions about priorities after explaining the supported outcomes. A recommendation should make its reasoning and remaining uncertainty clear enough to review.

Brief check: Does a benefit at one site establish a benefit everywhere?
Listen for: No. Effects can be uneven or transferred.

On screen: What may continue after water recedes?

Fictional event log: heavy rain on saturated ground; river overflow; 108 homes flooded; road closed for 52 days; warnings issued; repairs continued afterwards. This is not a historical report about a named flood.

Teacher demonstration · Mistake clinic · Choose a feasible package and explain its limits

On screen: Choose a feasible package and explain its limits / Follow your teacher’s explanation of the places, facts and steps.

Review case: A package costs 25 + 20 + 15 tokens with a budget of 50. Is it feasible? Proposed answer: “Yes; each item individually costs less than 50.”. Method note: With 50 tokens, a 10-token warning system and 30-token storage area cost 40, leaving 10. Warnings help people respond; storage may hold water. Neither guarantees zero harm in every event.

Now change one condition · 5.10

On screen: Budget rises to 100. Compare two possible packages.

Fictional flood options: warnings 10 tokens; storage area 40; wall 80. Budget 550. Warnings help people respond; storage may hold water at a suitable site; a wall can block flow locally but may transfer risk.

Budget rises to 100. Compare two possible packages. Warnings + wall = 90; warnings + storage = 50. Explain different functions and limits, not just price.

Related steps in this same case: Budget rises to 100. Compare two possible packages. Warnings + wall = 90; warnings + storage = 50. Explain different functions and limits, not just price.

What should be checked before choosing the storage site? Capacity, land suitability, affected people/ecosystems and connection to the flood pathway.

Make a conditional recommendation. Choose a feasible package matched to the local mechanism, stating one benefit and one remaining risk or evidence need.
